}# Data files associated with A Dependency Map Enhanced with Next-Generation 3D Cancer Models


## Overview ##
This file set includes metadata files (6 files) and analysis result files (29 files) associated with Neiswender, Maffa, Brenan et al. "A Dependency Map Enhanced with Next-Generation 3D Cancer Models" (Nature, 2026). The custom analysis code used for generating these results is available at a GitHub repository (https://github.com/broadinstitute/DepMap-NextGen-Public).  


In addition, raw profiling data of the models (including data for mutation, copy number, gene expression, and gene dependency) and processed data files required for running the custom code are available at DepMap portal (https://depmap.org/portal/data_page/?tab=allData; file set name "NextGen Model Manuscript 2026").


## Metadata Files ##


### minipool_guide_metadata.csv
This table provides the barcode sequence (“Construct_Barcode”) and target gene (“Gene”) for each of the 2000 sgRNAs included in the minipool library. See Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9a for the schematic and graphical representations of this library, respectively. This library targets 1,000 genes, including 250 test genes, 650 negative control genes, and 100 positive control (i.e., common essential) genes.


### minipool_library_composition.csv
This table shows the membership of each of the nine core functional classes (“Integrin”, “ECM Adhesion”, “Actin Regulation”, “Adherens Junction”, “Tight Junction”, “Lipid Metabolism”, ”Wnt Signaling”, “PI3K mTOR Signaling”, and “Cell Cycle”) targeted by the minipool library. The majority of the test genes of this library belong to one or more of these core functional classes, while the rest of them (“Other”) do not belong to any of these classes but are still included in the library based on specific interests. See Extended Data Fig. 9a for the graphical representations of this library.


### minipool_screen_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including model ID (“DepMap ID”), growth format, and type of culture medium (“Serum status” and “Culture medium”), as well as the QC results for each of the minipool screens (n = 18). These QC results include log2-fold change correlation between the replicates (“replicate LFC correlation”), total sequencing reads (“Total reads”), and two metrics based on the gene effect distributions of negative and positive controls (“NNMD” and “ROC-AUC”).


### minipool_sequence_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including model ID (“DepMap ID”), growth format, and type of culture medium (“Serum status” and “Culture medium”), as well as the QC results for each of the minipool screen sequencing attempts (n = 34). Note that 16 out of the 18 minipool screens were conducted with technical duplicates. One of the replicates (0178_Adh_Nat_Serum_Dome_RepB) was removed from the further analysis due to the low NNMD score. The read count of the PCR products of genomic DNA prepared from Cas12a-null 293T cells that were infected with the minipool library (HEK_CasNull_MP_control) is also displayed.


### model_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including model ID, lineage (“OncotreeLineage”), primary disease (“OncotreePrimaryDisease”), subtype (“OncotreeSubtype”), growth pattern (Adherent, Mixed, Suspension or Unknown for traditional and Dome or Spheroid for NextGen models), as well as the availability of WGS/RNAseq/CRISPR profiling results for the traditional (n = 1685) and NextGen (n = 314) models used in the study. For the models profiled by the CRISPR screen, the screen type (“CRISPRScreenType”), classified into five types based on the model type and culture condition—namely, 2DS (adherent/suspension culture of the traditional cell line models), 2DO (coat culture of the NextGen organoid models), 3DO (dome culture of the NextGen organoid models), 2DN (coat culture of the NextGen CNS models), and 3DN (spheroid culture of the NextGen CNS models)—is also indicated. Note that "GrowthPattern" indicates the format of culture used for the derivation of the respective model, which can be different from the format of culture used for screening and omics profiling (the latter is indicated by "CRISPRScreenType"; also see "Culture Format" column of Supplementary Table 1).


### screen_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including the model ID, library, screen type, model lineage (“OncotreeLineage”), model primary disease (“OncotreePrimaryDisease”), model subtype(“OncotreeSubtype”), and growth pattern, for all the CRISPR screens of traditional (screen n = 1387; PassesQC = “TRUE”) and NextGen (n = 147) models whose results are analyzed in the study. The availability of gene expression (“HasExprData”) and CN data in the corresponding model is also indicated. The screen type was classified into five types based on the model type and culture condition, namely, 2DS (adherent/suspension culture of the traditional cell line models), 2DO (coat culture of the NextGen organoid models), 3DO (dome culture of the NextGen organoid models), 2DN (coat culture of the NextGen CNS models), and 3DN (spheroid culture of the NextGen CNS models). Note that "GrowthPattern" indicates the format of culture used for the derivation of the respective model, which can be different from the format of culture used for screening and omics profiling (the latter is indicated by "ScreenType"; also see "Culture Format" column of Supplementary Table 1).



## Analytical Result Files ##


### biomarker_expression_tumor_vs_normal.csv
For the three representative biomarker-associated dependencies shown in Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5 (HNRNPH1 and PROX1 expression addiction and ENO1/ENO2 paralog dependency), the expression of the biomarker (HNRNPH1, PROX1 and ENO2, respectively) was compared between the tumor samples and lineage-matched normal samples of the “TCGA TARGET GTEx” cohort downloaded from the Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net; n = 3192 [normal], 4143 [tumor]; only samples from nine tissue types, biliary tract, colorectal, breast, CNS/brain, esophagus/stomach, ovary, pancreas, prostate and uterus, were analyzed). The sample number (“normalN” and “tumorN”) and mean expression score (“Mean_normal” and “Mean_tumor”) for the normal and tumor groups, as well as the absolute difference in mean expression (“absDelta”), are indicated. Statistical significance of the difference in expression between the two groups was scored using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”).


### celligner_geneset_scores.csv
Expression scores for each of the 41 gene expression meta-programs identified by Gavish et al. (Nature, 2023 [PMID: 37258682]) as well as Basal and Classical programs defined by Moffitt et al. (Nat Genet, 2015 [PMID: 26343385]) were calculated from the gene expression data of the DepMap models (traditional and NextGen; n = 1914) and TCGA-plus tumor samples (n = 12236). See “Scoring the activity of gene-expression MPs” subsection of Methods for the strategy used for the calculation. The scores shown here underlie all the plots involving the meta-program expression scores, including those shown in Figs. 3a,b, 4a-e,g and Extended Data Figs. 6c,d, 7b-j, 8a,b.  


### celligner_nearest_neighbor_table.csv
For each of the DepMap models (n = 1909) and Novartis PDX models (n = 445; Gao et al. Nat Med, 2015 [PMID: 26479923]) (“input”), the identities (sample ID [“target”] and lineage [“target_lineage”]) of the 100 (25 for PDX models) nearest tumor samples (of the TCGA-plus/Met500 cohort [n = 13104]) on the Celligner UMAP embedding were recorded. This file was used for the Celligner-based model lineage prediction (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Figs. 2b,c).


### celligner_prediction_accuracy.csv
For each of the solid tumor models of DepMap NextGen (n = 304), DepMap traditional (n = 1346), and Novartis PDX (n = 443), their lineages were inferred from the lineages of the 25 (or more; indicated in the “neighbors_considered” column) nearest tumor samples on the Celligner embedding. DepMap models of the Ampulla of Vater and Vulva/Vagina lineages were removed from the further analysis due to the scarcity of tumor samples with corresponding lineages (n = 4 and 0, respectively; “immediate_fail”). The scores shown here underlie the Celligner lineage prediction accuracy plots shown in Extended Data Fig. 2a.


### celligner_undiff_cluster.csv
For each of the DepMap traditional (n = 1367) and NextGen models (n = 382), Novartis PDX models (n = 443), and TCGA-plus/Met500 tumor samples (n = 11029) of solid tumors, their residence in the undifferentiated cluster on the Celligner embedding is indicated (“undiff_cluster”). Note that some models have multiple gene expression profiles and the residence in the undifferentiated cluster was recorded per individual profiles. The undifferentiated cluster was defined on the basis of the relative abundance of the DepMap models and TCGA-plus/Met500 tumor samples as well as the mean  HALLMARK_EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION ssGSEA enrichment score among the DepMap models in the individual clusters identified on Celligner (cluster n = 79). Four clusters (clusters #28, 59, 62 and 67) were collectively designated as “undifferentiated cluster”. See “Lineage prediction with Celligner” subsection of Methods for the details of this procedure. The scores shown here underlie the plots for the proportion of samples in the undifferentiated cluster shown in  Extended Data Fig. 2c.


### expression_addiction_tests_full.csv
For each of the genes scored for both dependency and expression in the NextGen models (gene n = 17889), the Pearson correlation (r) between the dependency and the expression of the dependency gene itself (“NextGenPearsonR”) and the significance of correlation (by two-tailed Pearson correlation; “NextGenPValue”) were calculated. The corresponding Pearson correlation in the traditional models (“TraditionalPearsonR”) was also scored. In addition, the dependency class of the gene based on the dependency profiles across the DepMap NextGen models is indicated (“NextGenDepClass”; see “Classification of dependency profiles” subsection of Methods). Note that only the genes in the three strong dependency classes (“NextGenDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3786) were plotted in Fig. 2a.


### integrin_fak_colocalization_test.csv
To assess the colocalization between integrin subunits (integrin beta1, integrin alphaV) and FAK in the KP3 cells grown in either plastic (2D) or dome (3D) cultures, the images of integrin staining and FAK staining from the same region were loaded onto Fiji (ImageJ ver 1.54p) and the regions of interest (ROIs) were manually defined by drawing boundaries around single cells. Three metrics for protein colocalization—intensity correlation quotient (“Li’s ICQ”; Li et al. J Neurosci, 2004 [PMID: 15102922]), thresholded Manders' Coefficient 1 (“Mander’s tM1”), and Pearson correlation (“PearsonR”)—between the two stainings within the ROI was calculated using the Coloc2 plugin (ver 3.1.0) for Fiji. Data from four sample types ("Class"), integrin alphaV-staining, plastic (AV2D), integrin alphaV-staining, dome (AV3D), integrin beta1-staining, plastic (B12D), and integrin beta1-staining, dome (B13D), are shown Li’s ICQ values are plotted on Extended Data Fig. 10b.


### major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_gene_full.csv
For the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]; CDKN2B was removed since this gene was not evaluated in the NextGen model CRISPR screen), their dependency was compared between the 3D organoids cultured as dome (n = 94) and lineage-matched traditional 2D adherent models (n = 433). Statistical significance of the difference in dependency was scored using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”). For the cancer genes whose mutation (hotspot mutation for the oncogenes and damaging mutation for the TSGs) is annotated, the same analysis was conducted after removing the mutant models to see if the differing dependencies between the 2D models and 3D organoids holds even when we focus our analysis to the models with WT alleles of the respective gene (“mutfree_q” and “mf_confirmation”; also see “major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_gene_full.csv”). The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Extended Data Fig. 8d.


### major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_mutfree_full.csv
For the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]), their dependency was compared between the 3D organoids cultured as dome and lineage-matched traditional 2D adherent models after removing the mutant models of the respective gene (see “major_onc_tsg_alteration_matrix.csv”). The numbers of models used in the comparison (i.e., non-mutant models) are shown in the “2D_N” and “3D_N” columns. Statistical significance of the difference in dependency was scored using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”). 


### major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_pathway_full.csv
For the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]), we classified them into one of the 10 oncogenic signaling pathways based on the function of the protein they encode. For the groups of oncogenes and the groups of TSGs that belong to the same pathway (13 groups), mean dependency scores for the genes within the same group were calculated for the individual models. Subsequently, the mean dependency scores (i.e., mean of the means) of the NextGen 3D organoids (n = 94) and lineage-matched traditional 2D models (n = 433) were compared. Statistical significance of the difference in mean dependency scores was assessed using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”). The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Extended Data Fig. 8f.


### major_onc_tsg_alteration_matrix.csv
For each of the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]), mutation (hotspot mutation for oncogenes and damaging mutations for TSGs) of the respective gene per individual models in the NextGen 3D organoids (n = 94) and lineage-matched traditional 2D cell lines (n = 433) were scored. The values indicate the allele frequency of the mutations: 0 = no mutation; 1, 0 < (allele frequency) ≤ 0.95; 2, (allele frequency) > 0.95. This matrix was used to remove mutant models in “major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_mutfree_full.csv”.


### minipool_chronos_gene_effects.csv
Chronos gene dependency scores were determined based on the results of the minipool screens (screen n = 18) for each of the 1,000 genes evaluated in these screens (100 positive control genes, 650 negative control genes, and 250 test genes). These Chronos scores provided the basis for the minipool screen analyses whose results are presented in Figs. 5d-g, Extended Data Figs. 9c-g.


### minipool_growth_format_culture_medium_per_class.csv
After calculating the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene dependencies as coefficients of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods; the coefficient values are shown in “minipool_regression_coefficients. csv”), two analyses were conducted to evaluate the gene class-specific effects of these two components (i.e., growth format and culture medium) of culture conditions: 1) Mann-Whitney U test to compare the distributions of coefficients between in-class and out-of-class test genes for each of the nine core functional classes of minipool targets (results shown in Extended Data Figs. 9f,g); 2) F-test to compare the variances of the coefficients between in-class and out-of-class test genes for each of the nine core functional classes of minipool targets (results shown in Fig. 5g). This table summarizes the results of these two analyses, where columns starting with “GF” indicate the effects of growth formats and those starting with “CM” represent the effects of culture media. The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Fig. 5g and Extended Data Figs. 9f,g.


### minipool_growth_format_tests.csv
For each of the test genes assessed by the minipool screen (gene n = 250), the effect of the growth formats (Matrigel dome culture [dome] vs monolayer culture on plastic plates [plastic]) on gene dependency was extracted as a coefficient of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods; these coefficients are shown in “minipool_regression_coefficients. csv”) and the significance of the effect was scored by the two-sided linear regression t-test (“pvalue”). FDR (adjusted P-value) was calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. The mean Chronos scores in the screens on dome cultures (n = 11) and plastic cultures (n = 7) are also shown (“true_dome_mean” and “true_plastic_mean”, respectively). The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 9f.


### minipool_regression_coefficients.csv
For each of the genes assessed by the minipool screen (gene n = 1000), the effects of the growth formats (Matrigel dome culture [dome] vs monolayer culture on plastic plates [plastic) and the culture media (serum-free OPAC medium vs serum-containing RPMI/FBS medium) on gene dependency were extracted as coefficients of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods). This spreadsheet shows the coefficients representing the effect of growth formats (“C(Growth_Format)[T.Plastic]”) and the effect of culture media (“C(Serum_status)[T.Serum-free]”) for each gene. The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Figs 5d-g and Extended Data Figs. 9f,g.


### minipool_regression_pvalues.csv
In extracting the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene dependencies (gene n = 1000) via the linear regression model, the significance of these effects—against the null hypothesis that these components of culture conditions do not have any effect on gene dependency—were also scored using the two-sided linear regression t-test. This spreadsheet shows the P-values for the effect of growth formats (“C(Growth_Format)[T.Plastic]”) and the effect of culture media (“C(Serum_status)[T.Serum-free]”) per each gene. The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Figs 5d,e.


### minipool_serum_status_tests.csv
For each of the test genes assessed by the minipool screen (gene n = 250), the effect of the culture media (serum-free OPAC medium vs serum-containing RPMI/FBS medium) on gene dependency was extracted as a coefficient of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods; these coefficients are shown in “minipool_regression_coefficients. csv”) and the significance of the effect was scored by the two-sided linear regression t-test (“pvalue”). FDR (adjusted P-value) was calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. The mean Chronos scores in the screens with serum-containing RPMI/FBS (n = 9) and serum-free OPAC (n = 9) are also shown (“true_serum_mean” and “true_serum_free_mean”, respectively). The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 9g.


### next_gen_cancer_gene_annotations.csv
For all the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs; both annotated by the OncoKB; https://www.oncokb.org), the number of the NextGen models (with CRISPR profiles [n = 147]) that have relevant alterations—hotspot mutation and/or amplification for oncogenes and damaging mutation and/or deletion for TSGs—were scored. Oncogenes and TSGs with sufficient number of altered NextGen models (n ≥ 5 and at least one model with a hotspot mutation) were subjected to the analysis of dependencies associated with cancer gene alterations (shown in Fig. 2f). These included 6 oncogenes (CTNNB1, EGFR, ERBB2, KRAS, PIK3CA and TERT) and 13 TSGs (APC, ARID1A, CDKN2A, CIC, FBXW7, NF1, PIK3R1, PTEN, RB1, RNF43, SMAD4, TP53 and HLA-B).


### next_gen_dependency_lineage_tests.csv
In the analysis of dependencies associated with cancer gene alterations (shown in Fig. 2f), we tested if the observed association between the cancer gene alteration and dependency was consistently beyond the effects caused by lineage-bias of the cancer gene alteration. Specifically, we computed the differences in mean dependency between NextGen screens in each lineage and the remaining (i.e., out-of-lineage) NextGen screens, only considering lineages which have at least 5 models screened (breast, CNS/brain, colorectal, esophagus/stomach, pancreas and prostate). If the dependency difference observed across the two classes of models distinguished by the presence of a cancer gene alteration was outside the range of all dependency differences observed across all lineages, then we deemed the dependency-biomarker relationship to be driven by the cancer gene alteration. Otherwise, the dependency pattern was attributed to lineage effects. This spreadsheet shows the mean dependency difference between in-lineage vs out-of-lineage groups for each lineage:gene pair (n = 6 [lineage], 5536 [gene]). Also see “Identification of biomarker-associated dependencies” subsection of Methods.


### next_gen_vs_traditional_metaprogram_expression_tests.csv
For each of the 41 gene expression meta-programs identified by Gavish et al. (Nature, 2023 [PMID: 37258682]), the activity of the program was scored in the NextGen (n = 305) and lineage-matched traditional (n = 548) models. The activities of individual programs were then compared between the NextGen and traditional model groups both per lineage and with all the organoid lineages (i.e., all lineages except for CNS/brain) combined. The number of models (“NextGenN” and “TraditionalN”) and the mean expression scores (“NextGenMean” and “TraditionalMean”) for both model groups, as well as the difference in mean expression scores (“MeanDifference”) are indicated. Statistical significance of the difference was scored by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MannWhitneyPValue”) and FDR (adjusted P-value; “MannWhitneyFDR”) was calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure.


### onc_tsg_alteration_dependency_tests_full.csv
For oncogenes and TSGs that have sufficient number of NextGen models (n ≥ 5) with relevant alteration (hotspot mutation and/or amplification for oncogenes and damaging mutation and/or deletion for TSGs) (n = 13 [oncogene], 38 [TSG]), gene dependencies were compared between altered and unaltered NextGen models (n = 147 [model], 5536 [gene]). Mean dependency difference as well as the statistical significance of the difference, assessed by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test, were scored (“NextGenMeanDifference” and “NextGenMannWhitneyPValue”, respectively). The same comparison of gene dependency was conducted between the altered and unaltered traditional models (model n = 597) and the difference in mean dependency as well as the statistical significance of the difference were scored (“TraditionalMeanDifference” and “TraditionalMannWhitneyPValue”, respectively). Note that in the plot shown in Fig. 2f, only the oncogenes and TSGs that have at least one NextGen model with a hotspot mutation (n = 6 [oncogene], 13 [TSG]) and dependencies in the three strong dependency classes (“NextGenDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3786) were included.


### oncogene_gof_alteration_matrix.csv
For each of the cancer genes (oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes [TSGs]; annotated by the OncoKB; https://www.oncokb.org) (gene n = 741), the NextGen models (n = 147) and lineage-matched traditional models (n = 597) were classified based on the presence or absence of the gain-of-function (GOF) alteration of the gene (hotspot mutation and/or amplification). The values indicate the presence/absence of GOF alteration: 0 = absent; 1 = present. This made a basis for selecting oncogenes with sufficient representation of GOF models among the NextGen cohort (see “nextgen_cancer_gene_annotations.csv”) as well as the analysis for dependencies associated with oncogene GOF (Figs. 2f,g).


### organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tail_enrichment_tests_full.csv
The top 100 genes in either extreme of the distribution of mean dependency differences (3D organoids [n = 94] vs lineage-matched 2D models [n = 433]; gene n = 16691 excluding common essential genes) were combined to form a set of 200 genes with differential dependencies. Gene sets from the Hallmark and KEGG legacy collections were tested for enrichment among this set of 200 differential dependency genes using a hypergeometric test (or one-sided Fisher’s exact test). The number of differential dependency genes within each gene set (“OverlapSize”), the size of the gene set after removing essential genes (“EffectiveSetSize”), the original size of the gene set (“OriginalSetSize”), as well as the odds ratio and P-value from the hypergeometric test (“OddsRatio” and “FishersPValue”, respectively), are indicated. Only gene sets with EffectiveSetSize between 101 and 249 were included in the further analysis. The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Fig. 5a. Also see “Differential dependency analysis between 3D organoids and 2D models” subsection of Methods. 


### organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tests_full.csv
Gene dependencies were compared between the NextGen models that were grown as 3D organoids (n = 94) vs lineage-matched 2D adherent models (n = 433) (gene n = 18159). Mean dependency difference (“MeanDifference”), the statistical significance of the difference assessed by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MannWhitneyPValue”), as well as the adjusted P-values calculated by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MannWhitneyFDR”) were scored. Common essential genes, which were removed from the analysis of differential dependency genes (see “organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tail_enrichment_tests_full.csv”), were also labeled (“DropEssential”). This spreadsheet was used to compile the list of 200 differential dependency genes between 2D and 3D models (see “organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tail_enrichment_tests_full.csv”).


### organoids_vs_2d_top_geneset_similarity_matrix.csv
For the nine gene sets enriched for differential dependency genes (see Fig. 5a), their similarity was assessed by calculating the pairwise overlap coefficient, whose values are shown in this spreadsheet. Gene sets with pairwise overlap similarity > 0.3 (KEGG_FOCAL_ADHESION and KEGG_REGULATION_OF_ACTIN_CYTOSKELETON, HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT and  HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS) were merged to form functional clusters, resulting in two merged gene sets ("Adhesion/Cytoskeleton" and "Cell Cycle") and five ("Lipid Metabolism," "mTORC1," "OxPhos," "UV," and "SLE") gene sets that remained separate (see Extended Data Fig. 8h).


### paralog_dependency_tests_full.csv
For all the paralog pairs listed on the Ensembl genome browser 113 (https://www.ensembl.org/) with both genes scored for expression and dependency in the NextGen models (paralog pair n = 60527), we computed the Pearson correlation between the expression scores of one of the genes and dependency scores of the other across the NextGen models (model n = 146) (“NextGenPearsonR”). Statistical significance of the correlation was assessed by two-tailed Pearson correlation (“NextGenPValue”). The expression-dependency correlation of the same paralog pair was also scored in the data from the lineage-matched traditional model cohort (n = 572) and recorded (“TraditionalPearsonR”). Note that only genes in the three strong dependency classes (“NextGenDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3786) were plotted in Fig. 2d.


### pdac_classical_dependency_tests_full.csv
The correlation between gene dependency and expression of the PDAC-classical/MUC program across the cohort of the NextGen organoid models were scored for all the genes (n = 108 [model], 18159 [gene]) (“OrganoidPearsonR”). Statistical significance of the correlation was assessed by two-tailed Pearson correlation (“OrganoidPValue”). The membership in the MSigDB “GOBP: WNT_SIGNALING_PATHWAY” is also indicated (“WntSignaling”). Note that only genes in the three strong dependency classes based on the organoid screen data (“OrganoidDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3521) were plotted in Fig. 4d.


### tda_dependency_classification.csv
The dependency profiles of individual genes across the NextGen models were classified into either of the five classes (Non-dependency, Weakly selective, Strongly selective, High variance and Pan-dependency) based primarily on the strategy described in a prior publication (Krill-Burger et al. Genome Biol, 2023 [PMID: 37612728]) (also see “Classification of dependency profiles” subsection of Methods) (n = 18159 [gene], 147 [model]) (“NextGenClass”). The same classification strategy was also applied to the screens of the NextGen organoids (i.e., NextGen models out of the CNS/brain lineage) (n = 108 [organoid]) (“OrganoidsClass”). The variance of dependency scores as well as the dependency rank of each gene in their 90th percentile least depleted model (used for identifying “Pan-dependency” class; also see Dempster et al., bioRxiv, 2019; https://doi.org/10.1101/720243 for the details) were also recorded based both on the NextGen models dependency scores and organoid dependency scores (“NextGen90%ileLineRank” and “Organoids90%ileLineRank”, respectively).


### tumor_suppressor_lof_alteration_matrix.csv
For each of the cancer genes (oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes [TSGs]; annotated by the OncoKB; https://www.oncokb.org) (gene n = 741), the NextGen models (n = 147) and lineage-matched traditional models (n = 597) were classified based on the presence or absence of the loss-of-function (LOF) alteration of the gene (damaging mutation and/or deletion). The values indicate the presence/absence of LOF alteration: 0 = absent; 1 = present. This made a basis for selecting TSGs with sufficient representation of LOF models among the NextGen cohort (see “nextgen_cancer_gene_annotations.csv”) as well as the analysis for dependencies associated with TSG LOF (Fig. 2f).# Source verification notes (Phase 1, started 2026-10-28)

"""Phase-1 identifiability audit of the Broad minipool environmental panel.

Builds matched within-model contrasts (medium holding format fixed; format
holding medium fixed) from Chronos gene effects in original units, and
checks direction agreement with the authors' published regression
coefficients. Descriptive audit only -- no adaptive search, no claims.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
RAW = ROOT / "data" / "raw" / "broad_figshare"


def load():
    meta = pd.read_csv(RAW / "minipool_screen_metadata.csv")
    eff = pd.read_csv(RAW / "minipool_chronos_gene_effects.csv").set_index("ScreenID")
    lib = pd.read_csv(RAW / "minipool_library_composition.csv")
    return meta, eff, lib


def paired_deltas(meta: pd.DataFrame, eff: pd.DataFrame, contrast: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per-gene within-model paired differences for one contrast type."""
    rows = {}
    if contrast == "medium":  # OPAC - RPMI/FBS, same model + format
        groups = meta.groupby(["DepMap ID", "Growth Format"])
        key, a, b = "Culture medium", "OPAC", "RPMI/FBS"
    else:  # Dome - Plastic, same model + medium
        groups = meta.groupby(["DepMap ID", "Culture medium"])
        key, a, b = "Growth Format", "Dome", "Plastic"
    for gkey, g in groups:
        ga, gb = g[g[key] == a], g[g[key] == b]
        if len(ga) == 1 and len(gb) == 1:
            rows[f"{gkey[0]}|{gkey[1]}"] = eff.loc[ga.cell_line_name.iloc[0]] - eff.loc[gb.cell_line_name.iloc[0]]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)  # genes x pairs


def main() -> dict:
    meta, eff, lib = load()
    test_genes = lib.loc[lib["All test genes"] == True, "Gene"].tolist()  # noqa: E712
    out = {"n_screens": int(len(meta)), "n_models": int(meta["DepMap ID"].nunique()),
           "models": sorted(meta["DepMap ID"].unique()), "n_test_genes_in_library": len(test_genes)}
    frames = {}
    for contrast in ("medium", "format"):
        d = paired_deltas(meta, eff, contrast)
        frames[contrast] = d
        sub = d.loc[d.index.intersection(test_genes)]
        out[contrast] = {
            "n_pairs": int(d.shape[1]), "pair_keys": list(d.columns),
            "median_abs_delta_test_genes": float(sub.abs().median().median()),
            "frac_genes_sign_inconsistent": float(((sub > 0).any(axis=1) & (sub < 0).any(axis=1)).mean()),
        }
        d.to_csv(ROOT / "data" / f"paired_deltas_{contrast}.csv")
    # Direction check vs published regression coefficients (C5 precursor).
    coef = pd.read_csv(RAW / "minipool_regression_coefficients.csv")
    out["published_coef_columns"] = list(coef.columns)
    (ROOT / "data" / "identifiability_audit.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=2))
    print(json.dumps(out, indent=2))
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Direct testing is difficult and costly in organoids, which are small three-dimensional models grown from patient tumors. Using gene activity measurements from 852 conventional cancer models, we built predictive models for a preselected panel of 20 genes. Our primary evaluation asked whether the models could rank organoids by their dependence on each gene. Performance was weaker in organoids, but a small signal remained in 94 Broad organoids and in 148 Sanger organoids from 144 donors. Predictions for the Sanger organoids were fixed before the measured outcomes were accessed. A separate retrospective analysis examined whether the same predictions could rank the 20 genes within each organoid. This retrospective analysis showed modest improvement over tumor-lineage predictions for the full ranking, while improvement for the three strongest measured dependencies was observed only in Sanger. Pancreatic organoid results remained projections because direct measurements were unavailable. These findings provide limited evidence for ranking genes within the selected panel. They do not establish which experiments will succeed or which treatments will work in patients.</p><sec id="kwd-group1" sec-type="kwd-group" disp-level="2"><p><bold>Keywords:</bold> gene dependency, patient-derived organoids, functional genomics, transcriptomics, CRISPR screening, Elastic Net, external validation, cross-model transferability</p></sec></abstract><abstract id="abstract2"><title>Abstract</title><p>Transferability of transcriptome-based gene-dependency models from two-dimensional cancer models to organoids remains uncertain. Expression-only Elastic Net models for 20 preselected genes were selected using patient-grouped nested cross-validation in 681 models and evaluated in a locked 171-model holdout. Historical target selection used all 852 models, making holdout performance conditional internal confirmation rather than an unbiased generalization estimate. After refitting on all 852 models, frozen models underwent exploratory evaluation in 94 Broad organoids and blinded validation in 148 Sanger organoids from 144 donors. Predictions were sealed before Sanger outcome access. Primary target-wise Spearman correlations, ranking organoids per gene, averaged 0.4094, 0.1518, and 0.1015 in holdout, Broad, and Sanger, respectively. Sanger association exceeded the within-lineage permutation null (<italic>p</italic> = 0.00040), but improvement over lineage-only prediction remained uncertain (difference, 0.0462; 95% confidence interval, −0.0065–0.0986). <italic>CDK6</italic>, <italic>MDM4</italic>, and <italic>CCNE1</italic> passed false discovery rate correction in Sanger. Retrospective within-organoid gene ranking modestly improved over lineage-only prediction in both cohorts; top-three overlap improved only in Sanger. Pancreatic results remained unvalidated projections. Findings support weak cross-domain rank transfer and limited within-organoid ranking within the selected panel, without establishing genome-wide transferability, causal explanations for attenuation, or prospective experimental or therapeutic utility.</p></abstract><custom-meta-group><custom-meta><meta-name>status</meta-name><meta-value>released</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>display-pdf</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-olf</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-manuscript</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-preprint</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-journal-matter</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-scanned</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-retracted</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta><notes notes-type="article-notes"><sec id="historyarticle-meta1" sec-type="history" disp-level="2"><p>Received 2026 Sep 15; Revised 2026 Sep 30; Accepted 2026 Oct 5; Collection date 2026 Oct.</p></sec></notes></front><body><sec id="sec1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="1"><title>1. Introduction</title><p>Cancer comprises a heterogeneous group of diseases driven not only by genetic and epigenetic alterations but also by the reorganization of cellular signaling networks. This heterogeneity contributes to variable treatment responses among tumors with the same histological diagnosis and limits the effectiveness of target selection based solely on genomic alterations [<xref rid="B1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>]. Gene dependency refers to a cancer cell’s requirement to express a particular gene to survive or proliferate. Identifying such dependencies and synthetic-lethal relationships offers a strategy for exposing cancer-specific vulnerabilities while comparatively sparing normal cells [<xref rid="B2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>].</p><p>Large-scale functional genomic studies now enable the systematic interrogation of genes required for fitness across cancer models with diverse molecular backgrounds. The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) links molecular profiles of cancer cell lines to functional-screening data, enabling the identification of common and context-specific dependencies [<xref rid="B3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>]. Genome-scale loss-of-function screens using clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), collectively termed CRISPR–Cas9, have made systematic gene inactivation feasible in human cells [<xref rid="B5-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>,<xref rid="B6-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>]. High-resolution libraries have improved discrimination between core-essential genes and context-specific vulnerabilities [<xref rid="B7-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>], whereas copy-number-associated cutting toxicity has motivated correction methods such as CERES [<xref rid="B8-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>]. Large-scale ribonucleic acid (RNA) interference screens have provided complementary maps of dependency and synthetic lethality [<xref rid="B9-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>]. Although Broad and Sanger dependency datasets show broad concordance, gene-effect estimates can vary across screening libraries, experimental protocols, and computational processing [<xref rid="B10-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>,<xref rid="B11-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>]. Methods such as Chronos seek to improve dependency estimation by accounting for cell-population dynamics [<xref rid="B12-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>]. Nevertheless, genome-scale CRISPR screening remains costly, technically demanding, and sample-intensive, limiting its routine application across newly derived cancer models.</p><p>The Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) has established a molecular foundation for modeling associations among mutation, copy number, gene expression, treatment response, and gene dependency [<xref rid="B13-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. Although proteomic profiling expands this information space, messenger RNA expression remains an accessible readout of cellular state, measurable consistently across many cohorts [<xref rid="B15-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>]. This availability has motivated the computational prediction of dependencies in samples without direct functional screening. DeepDEP demonstrated that multi-omic profiles can predict cancer dependencies [<xref rid="B16-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>], while transcriptome-based dependency maps developed for The Cancer Genome Atlas showed that Elastic Net models can prioritize putative tumor vulnerabilities [<xref rid="B17-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>]. Other approaches have used synthetic data augmentation to address incomplete molecular profiles [<xref rid="B18-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">18</xref>]. However, expression-dependency associations can reflect tissue of origin and shared transcriptional programs [<xref rid="B19-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>], and domain shifts between cell lines and tumors can compromise transferability [<xref rid="B20-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>]. Thus, strong performance within cell-line collections should not be equated with generalizability across biological model systems. Elastic Net is well suited to high-dimensional data because it combines regularization, variable selection, and stability in the presence of correlated features [<xref rid="B21-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>]. Yet model selection and performance estimation on the same observations can produce optimistic bias, necessitating nested cross-validation [<xref rid="B22-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>]. Likewise, samples derived from the same patient or biological source must remain within a common data partition to prevent information leakage [<xref rid="B23-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>].</p><p>Conventional two-dimensional (2D) cultures are scalable and well-suited to functional screening, but they incompletely recapitulate cell–cell interactions, tissue architecture, and tumor-specific transcriptional states. Patient-derived organoids are three-dimensional (3D) culture systems that retain selected structural, genetic, and functional features of their tissue of origin [<xref rid="B24-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>,<xref rid="B25-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>]. Colorectal organoid biobanks have shown that interpatient molecular diversity and drug-response phenotypes can be preserved ex vivo [<xref rid="B26-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">26</xref>]. Comparisons with clinical outcomes also support the potential of gastrointestinal cancer organoids to reflect sensitivity or resistance to selected therapies [<xref rid="B27-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">27</xref>,<xref rid="B28-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">28</xref>]. These advantages make organoids valuable preclinical models for testing whether dependencies learned in 2D remain biologically relevant in more tissue-like systems. However, their epithelial predominance, incomplete representation of immune and stromal compartments, and sensitivity to culture conditions constrain direct extrapolation to patient tumors [<xref rid="B29-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">29</xref>].</p><p>In pancreatic cancer, long-term organoid cultures have been established from both normal and neoplastic tissues [<xref rid="B30-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">30</xref>], and growth-factor requirements have been shown to change with disease progression [<xref rid="B31-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">31</xref>]. The pancreatic organoid cohort reported by Tiriac et al. integrated RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiles with treatment-response phenotypes, enabling the analysis of molecular and functional subtypes [<xref rid="B32-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. Subsequent biobanks have further demonstrated the preservation of disease features and the feasibility of individualized drug screening [<xref rid="B33-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">33</xref>]. However, most such cohorts lack genome-scale measured CRISPR dependency outcomes. Consequently, applying an expression-based dependency model to RNA-seq data from these resources can provide biological projections or candidate hypotheses for functional testing, but cannot by itself establish measured gene dependency or therapeutic sensitivity.</p><p>Direct functional screening in organoids is technically challenging, yet genome-scale studies in intestinal organoids have identified genes associated with growth and treatment resistance [<xref rid="B34-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">34</xref>]. Pooled screens in human colon organoids have revealed tumor-suppressor and context-dependent selection effects [<xref rid="B35-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">35</xref>], and more recent work has identified dependencies involving WNT, mitogen-activated protein kinase, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, p53, and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) mismatch-repair pathways [<xref rid="B36-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">36</xref>]. Large-scale CRISPR knockout, CRISPR interference, and CRISPR activation screens in gastric organoids have further demonstrated the feasibility of examining gene-drug interactions in 3D systems [<xref rid="B37-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">37</xref>]. Next-generation model collections show that dependency profiles may differ between 2D and 3D culture conditions [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>]. Cancer dependencies can also be mapped systematically across tumor organoid biobanks [<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. Expanded patient-derived model resources can capture substantial tumor diversity [<xref rid="B40-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">40</xref>]. Together, these studies establish organoids as increasingly tractable functional genomics platforms while also underscoring that culture context can alter the biological relationships inferred from conventional cell lines.</p><p>Despite these advances, the extent to which transcriptome-dependency relationships learned in 2D cancer cell lines transfer to independent 3D organoid cohorts remains unresolved. A rigorous assessment requires model selection to be completed without access to 3D outcomes, predictions to be locked before outcome evaluation, and performance to be tested across independently generated CRISPR datasets. Here, we developed target-specific, expression-based Elastic Net models for a fixed panel of 20 genes using 852 pan-cancer 2D models. Candidate molecular representations were compared using patient-grouped nested cross-validation. The selected model was evaluated once in a locked 2D holdout for internal confirmation conditional on historical target selection. Without outcome-guided retraining, the frozen model was then examined exploratorily in Broad organoids and subjected to blinded independent external validation in a non-overlapping Sanger organoid cohort. Target-level findings from the two 3D cohorts were integrated in a retrospective transportability synthesis, and the locked models were subsequently projected onto an independent pancreatic organoid RNA-seq cohort lacking measured CRISPR outcomes. The primary hypothesis concerned ranking organoids by measured dependency for each gene, not ranking genes within an individual organoid. We hypothesized that this between-organoid signal would remain detectable but attenuated in 3D systems. A separate retrospective analysis evaluated gene ranking within individual organoids using the same frozen predictions. This secondary analysis addressed a different prediction task and did not replace the original primary evaluation.</p></sec><sec id="sec2-biology-15-01782" disp-level="1"><title>2. Materials and Methods</title><sec id="sec2dot1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.1. Study Design and Data Sources</title><p>This retrospective, multi-cohort computational study evaluated whether transcriptome-based gene-dependency rankings learned in 2D cancer models could be transferred to independent 3D organoid systems. The study used publicly available or openly released molecular, transcriptomic, and functional-genomics resources; it collected no new biospecimens and performed no new CRISPR screens. The primary workflow comprised five analytically distinct layers: (i) patient-grouped 2D model development and locking; (ii) exploratory transfer assessment in Broad organoids; (iii) outcome-blinded independent external validation in Sanger organoids; (iv) retrospective synthesis of the Broad and Sanger target-level results; and (v) secondary transcriptomic projection in a pancreatic organoid cohort without measured CRISPR dependency outcomes. The primary study design, data sources, and evidence hierarchy are shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f001" ref-type="fig">Figure 1</xref>. A separate retrospective analysis of gene ranking within organoids was defined after the external outcomes were available (<xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref>; <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S17–S19</xref>).</p><fig id="biology-15-01782-f001" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>Figure 1</label><caption><p>Study design, data sources, and evidence hierarchy. Target-specific Elastic Net models were developed from transcriptomic profiles and CRISPR Gene Effect values in 852 two-dimensional cancer models obtained from DepMap Public 26Q1 and the CCLE. Candidate representations were compared in 681 development models, and the selected expression-only representation was evaluated once on a locked 171-model internal holdout set; the final models were then refitted on all 852 models, keeping the targets, target-specific features, hyperparameters, and primary metric fixed. Historical target selection included the holdout models, so this evaluation provides internal confirmation conditional on the selected panel. Without retraining, these models were applied to 94 Broad NextGen organoids for exploratory evaluation and to 148 Sanger organoids representing 144 donors for blinded independent external validation. Sanger predictions were sealed using the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm before access to CRISPR outcomes. Broad and Sanger target-level results were subsequently combined in a retrospective transportability synthesis. The Tiriac pancreatic RNA-sequencing cohort comprised 55 samples and was used only for secondary projection because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable. The dashed border identifies this non-validation application cohort. The figure depicts the primary workflow; the model specification and prespecified primary metric remained unchanged. The separate retrospective within-organoid ranking analysis is described in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S17–S19</xref> and was not a new blinded validation. Colored boxes distinguish the five labeled stages, and arrows indicate their order in the workflow. CCLE, Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia; CRISPR, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats; DepMap, Cancer Dependency Map; RNA, ribonucleic acid; SHA-256, 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" xlink:href="biology-15-01782-g001.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/78de/13664187/76c7e31e9f46/biology-15-01782-g001.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1853?><?original-width 1467?><?scaled-height 1853?><?scaled-width 1467?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="biology-15-01782-g001.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/78de/13664187/c1ccb192f556/biology-15-01782-g001.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig><p>As shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f001" ref-type="fig">Figure 1</xref>, the first layer comprised 2D model development and locking using DepMap Public 26Q1 and CCLE molecular data [<xref rid="B3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>,<xref rid="B13-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. The analysis-ready population included 852 pan-cancer models with continuous CRISPR Gene Effect values for a fixed 20-gene target panel. Models were partitioned by PatientID, with ModelID used as a fallback only when PatientID was unavailable. This yielded 681 development models from 658 patient groups and 171 locked internal-holdout models from 165 patient groups. No PatientID was shared between partitions. Candidate molecular representations were compared exclusively within the development partition using patient-grouped, lineage-stratified 5 × 5 nested cross-validation. Before the locked-holdout outcomes were evaluated, the selected representation, target panel, target-specific feature identities, hyperparameters, primary metric, and prediction files were frozen. After the one-time holdout evaluation, the selected expression-only Elastic Net specification was refitted on all 852 models for downstream deployment. Only imputation, scaling, and coefficient parameters were re-estimated. The targets, features, hyperparameters, and primary metric remained fixed.</p><p>The second layer used 94 organoids from the Broad NextGen cancer model resource, with matched gene expression and CRISPR Gene Effect values for all 20 targets [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>]. The all-852 deployment model was applied without Broad-specific retraining, recalibration, feature substitution, or coefficient adaptation. Because PatientID was unavailable in the original Broad evaluation records, the organoid model was initially the analysis and resampling unit. Subsequently recovered partial donor information was examined retrospectively in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.3</xref>. Although the audited current run preserved a prediction-before-outcome sequence, Broad-94 had been accessible during earlier methodological work and was therefore classified as a retrospective exploratory transfer cohort rather than a pristine independent validation set.</p><p>The third layer used the Sanger tumor-derived organoid dependency map [<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. Following cross-resource identity auditing and conservative exclusion of Broad-linked and same-donor records, the final cohort contained 148 organoids from 144 donors. The fixed 20-target prediction matrix, cohort registry, protocol, and model and feature manifests were written and cryptographically sealed using the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA-256) before Sanger CRISPR outcomes were accessed. Sanger-148 was therefore treated as a one-time, outcome-blinded independent external-validation cohort, with donor structure retained in uncertainty estimation and sensitivity analyses.</p><p>In the fourth layer, the Broad-94 and Sanger-148 target-level rank correlations were combined only after the two cohorts had been evaluated separately [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>,<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. The retrospective transportability synthesis assessed directional concordance, pooled target-level associations, and between-cohort heterogeneity. It was not treated as a third external validation and did not alter any component of the frozen model. Because Broad/DepMap Chronos Gene Effect and Sanger corrected CRISPR log fold change (LFC) values are assay-specific scales, the synthesis focused on rank transfer rather than absolute numerical equivalence.</p><p>The fifth layer applied the same frozen models to 55 RNA-seq samples from the Tiriac pancreatic organoid cohort, accessed through the Genomic Data Commons (GDC) ORGANOID-PANCREATIC project [<xref rid="B32-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. The resource comprised 44 tumor samples from 38 independent tumor cases and 11 normal samples from 11 independent normal cases. Because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable, this layer was restricted to secondary transcriptomic projection and expression-domain diagnostics and was not used to estimate predictive accuracy or therapeutic sensitivity. Across all layers, no 3D observation contributed to 2D candidate selection, feature learning, hyperparameter tuning, or deployment coefficient estimation. After access to 3D data, no retraining, recalibration, target or feature reselection, hyperparameter retuning, or replacement of the prespecified primary metric was permitted. The secondary within-organoid endpoints were evaluated retrospectively and did not modify the frozen predictions or original primary results. Detailed cohort construction, preprocessing, modeling, and statistical procedures are provided in <xref rid="sec2dot2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.2</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.3</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.4</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot5-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.5</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot6-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.6</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot7-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.7</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot8-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.8</xref>, <xref rid="sec2dot9-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.9</xref> and <xref rid="sec2dot10-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10</xref>, and the archived code, frozen models, locked predictions, and verification records are described in <xref rid="sec2dot11-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.11</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot2-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.2. Development Cohort Construction and Target Panel Definition</title><p>The analysis-ready 2D resource comprised 852 pan-cancer models with gene-dependency outcomes available for a fixed 20-gene target panel. Each model was identified by ModelID. To prevent information leakage from biologically related models, we used PatientID as the grouping variable; when PatientID was unavailable, we used ModelID as the fallback group identifier. The patient-grouped partition and fixed target panel are detailed in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S1</xref>.</p><p>Using a locked 20% test fraction and global random seed 20260826, we divided the 852 models into 681 development models and 171 locked 2D holdout models, representing 658 and 165 unique patient groups, respectively. No PatientID overlapped between partitions. We used the development partition to compare candidate input representations, learn target-specific features, and select hyperparameters. Within the current model-development workflow, holdout outcomes were not accessed until the development decisions and prediction files had been locked. This restriction did not apply retrospectively to the earlier target-panel selection.</p><p>The response matrix comprised continuous CRISPR Gene Effect values for a 20-gene panel established before the present omics-candidate comparison. The panel included <italic>CDK6</italic>, <italic>STK11</italic>, <italic>CCND3</italic>, <italic>YAP1</italic>, <italic>MDM4</italic>, <italic>EP300</italic>, <italic>CTNNB1</italic>, <italic>EGFR</italic>, <italic>TSC2</italic>, <italic>TSC1</italic>, <italic>IGF1R</italic>, <italic>FGFR1</italic>, <italic>CCNE1</italic>, <italic>E2F3</italic>, <italic>ERBB3</italic>, <italic>NFE2L2</italic>, <italic>BRAF</italic>, <italic>KEAP1</italic>, <italic>MAPK1</italic>, and <italic>RAF1</italic>. No target was added to or removed from the panel during the current omics ablation, the Broad and Sanger 3D evaluations, or the Tiriac pancreatic organoid projection.</p><p>As documented in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S1</xref>, the panel had been defined in an earlier 2D workflow that used all 852 models. Consequently, the 171-model holdout was independent of the current candidate representation, feature selection, hyperparameters, and model-fitting decisions, but not fully independent of historical target panel selection. Its performance was therefore interpreted as internal confirmation conditional on the selected panel, not an unbiased estimate of generalization for the complete analysis pipeline. Independent 3D validation assessed new samples for the same preselected genes; it did not evaluate transferability to unselected genes or across the genome.</p><p>After the one-time holdout evaluation, we refitted the selected representation on all 852 models for downstream 3D deployment while retaining the fixed targets, target-specific feature identities, hyperparameters, and primary metric. Only preprocessing parameters and Elastic Net coefficients were re-estimated, as described in <xref rid="sec2dot5-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.5</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot3-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.3. Omics Data Preprocessing and Candidate Input Representations</title><p>The candidate omics blocks were derived from processed molecular data in DepMap Public 26Q1 and aligned to the 852 models defined in <xref rid="sec2dot2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.2</xref> [<xref rid="B3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B13-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. All matrices were ordered by ModelID and verified against the training registry. Gene-level features were tracked using Entrez Gene identifiers. For each target, the response variable was the continuous CRISPR Gene Effect value; no target-dependency outcome was included in any predictor matrix.</p><p>The gene-expression block comprised 19,215 protein-coding genes, represented as log2-transformed transcripts per million (TPM) values [log2(TPM + 1)], with no subsequent logarithmic transformation. The copy-number block comprised 19,955 whole-genome sequencing-derived gene-level linear, ploidy-relative values. Somatic variants were encoded separately as binary indicators of damage-mutation and hotspot-mutation carriers for 19,626 genes. OncotreeLineage was encoded as 29 binary indicators. The source blocks, encodings, initial dimensions, and candidate representations are summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S2</xref>.</p><p>As shown in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S2</xref>, lineage-only used the 29 lineage indicators as a non-molecular reference. Four molecular candidates were ordered by increasing representational complexity: expression-only (19,215 initial features); expression + copy number (39,170); expression + mutation (58,467), combining expression with damaging and hotspot indicators; and all omics + lineage (78,451), combining all four molecular blocks with lineage. The lineage-only reference was not eligible under the molecular one-standard-error selection rule.</p><p>Eligibility screening was relearned within every applicable training partition. Expression and copy-number features were excluded when the missing-value fraction in the training partition exceeded 0.20 or the variance was less than or equal to 1 × 10<sup>−8</sup>. The same variance threshold was applied to mutation indicators and to lineage indicators within the all-omics candidate set; all 29 indicators were retained for the lineage-only reference. For each target, nonfinite values were temporarily replaced with the training-partition means solely for univariate screening; the 300 eligible features with the largest absolute Pearson correlations were then retained.</p><p>For model fitting, missing values among the selected features were imputed using training-partition medians and standardized using means and standard deviations learned from the same training partition. These parameters were transferred unchanged to the corresponding validation or test observations. Filtering, screening, imputation, and standardization were repeated within each inner-training fold, each outer-training partition, and the 681-model development fit used for locked-holdout prediction. The 171 locked holdout models and all 3D data were excluded from learning feature eligibility, feature identities, imputation values, and scaling parameters.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot4-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.4. Patient-Grouped Nested Cross-Validation and Model Selection</title><p>Model development and candidate-representation comparison were performed exclusively in the 681-model development partition. To separate model selection from performance estimation, we used a prespecified 5 outer × 5 inner patient-grouped, lineage-stratified nested cross-validation design [<xref rid="B22-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>,<xref rid="B23-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>]. PatientID was retained as the group identifier, with ModelID used only as a fallback when PatientID was unavailable. No patient group crossed a training-validation boundary. Within each split, OncotreeLineage categories represented by fewer than five models were collapsed into Other_Rare for stratification only; the original lineage labels remained unchanged for modeling and reporting. Each development model contributed to exactly one outer-test prediction. The full frozen validation and tuning protocol is provided in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S3</xref>.</p><p>Within each outer-training partition, a separate five-fold inner validation was constructed. The eligibility filters, target-specific top-300 feature screening, median imputation, and standardization described in <xref rid="sec2dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.3</xref> were relearned in every inner-training fold and transferred unchanged to the corresponding inner-validation fold. Outer-test observations contributed to neither feature identities, preprocessing parameters, nor hyperparameter selection. Information flow was restricted to inner training, inner validation, hyperparameter selection, refitting on the complete outer-training partition, and one-time prediction of the outer-test partition.</p><p>A separate Elastic Net regression model was fitted for each of the 20 targets and each molecular representation [<xref rid="B21-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>]. The frozen search space was l1_ratio = {0.10, 0.50, 0.90} and alpha = {0.001, 0.01, 0.1}; we used a maximum of 20,000 iterations, a convergence tolerance of 0.0001, and cyclic coordinate updates. The inner objective was the mean target-specific Spearman correlation across the five inner-validation folds. We prioritized settings that converged in all inner folds; among them, we selected the setting with the highest mean inner Spearman correlation, resolving remaining ties in favor of a larger alpha and then a lower l1_ratio. When no setting converged in all five folds, we selected based on the number of converged folds, mean inner Spearman correlation, and larger alpha. We refit the chosen setting on the complete outer-training partition and applied it once to the outer-test partition. For the lineage-only reference, target-specific ridge regression was fitted to the 29 lineage indicators, with alpha = {0.1, 1, 10, 100} compared in the inner validation.</p><p>Predictions from the five outer-test folds were combined to generate out-of-fold (OOF) predictions for all 681 development models. The primary candidate score was the arithmetic mean of the 20 target-specific Spearman correlations, termed the macro target-wise Spearman correlation. We retained target-specific mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R<sup>2</sup>), calibration intercept, and calibration slope as secondary diagnostics, which did not alter model selection. Stability of the target-specific feature sets across outer folds was summarized using pairwise Jaccard similarity.</p><p>Candidate selection used only the development OOF predictions. Uncertainty for each candidate was estimated from 2000 bootstrap resamples of PatientID clusters. The one-standard-error threshold was defined as the highest observed molecular-candidate OOF macro Spearman correlation minus the candidate’s bootstrap standard error. Among molecular candidates meeting this threshold, we selected the least complex representation according to the prespecified order: expression-only, expression + copy number, expression + mutation, and all omics + lineage. Lineage-only was a non-molecular reference and was excluded from this rule.</p><p><xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S3</xref> further documents the development lock. For the selected candidate, the final l1_ratio and alpha pair for each target was the setting chosen most often across outer folds; ties were resolved by higher mean inner Spearman correlation, then by larger alpha. The 300 target-specific features were relearned using all 681 development models. Before indexing the 171-model outcome matrix for performance evaluation, we sealed the frozen protocol, split registry, selected representation, target-specific feature identities, hyperparameters, model manifest, and locked-holdout predictions using separate SHA-256 digests. No candidate, target, feature, hyperparameter, or primary metric was changed thereafter, and no 3D data were accessed during development.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot5-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.5. Locked 2D Holdout Evaluation and Deployment Model Finalization</title><p>After development selection had been locked, only the selected expression-only representation was applied to the 171-model 2D holdout. For each target, the 300 expression features were relearned in all 681 development models, and the final target-specific l1_ratio and alpha pair defined in <xref rid="sec2dot4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.4</xref> were fixed. Median imputation, standardization, and Elastic Net coefficients were fitted using the 681 development models and applied unchanged to the 171 holdout models. Predictions for the 20 targets were written together with ModelID, PatientID, and OncotreeLineage. Before the observed holdout CRISPR Gene Effect rows were indexed for evaluation, the prediction files, model manifest, and selected-feature registry were sealed with SHA-256 digests. The one-time holdout evaluation and deployment-model finalization protocol is summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S4</xref>.</p><p>The locked holdout outcomes were evaluated once after the prediction lock. The primary endpoint was the macro target-wise Spearman correlation. We calculated target-specific Spearman correlation, MAE, RMSE, R<sup>2</sup>, calibration intercept, and calibration slope as secondary diagnostics. We estimated uncertainty in the macro Spearman correlation from 2000 bootstrap resamples of PatientID clusters; we retained all rows belonging to a sampled patient group together, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles defined the 95% confidence interval (CI). The holdout-minus-development difference distribution was obtained by subtracting the development OOF bootstrap value from the holdout bootstrap value within each iteration. No model, feature, hyperparameter, or metric was changed during evaluation. Because historical target-panel selection used all 852 models, this stage provided internal confirmation conditional on that selection. We did not interpret its performance as an unbiased generalization estimate. The patient-cluster bootstrap did not account for uncertainty or optimism arising from historical target selection.</p><p>To evaluate information beyond tumor lineage, the lineage-only ridge reference described in <xref rid="sec2dot4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.4</xref> was refitted in the 681 development models and applied to the same 171 holdout models. The difference in macro Spearman correlation between the selected model and the lineage-only reference was estimated using common PatientID-cluster bootstrap resamples. When more than one model was associated with a patient, observed outcomes and predictions were additionally averaged at the PatientID level. With predictions fixed, complete 20-target outcome vectors were permuted among patient groups within each OncotreeLineage stratum for 2000 iterations. The one-sided empirical <italic>p</italic>-value was calculated as (1 + the number of null statistics greater than or equal to the observed statistic)/2001. The patient-aggregated macro Spearman correlation was retained as a sensitivity estimate.</p><p>After completing the locked 2D evaluation, we refitted the final model authorized for 3D application to all 852 models. The expression-only representation, fixed 20-target panel, 300 target-specific feature identities, target-specific l1_ratio and alpha settings, and primary metric were not reopened. We re-estimated only the median-imputation values, standardization parameters, and Elastic Net coefficients. Within the current model-fitting workflow, holdout outcomes entered coefficient estimation only in this final all-852 fit, after the internal performance estimate had been fixed. They were not used to revise candidate selection, targets, features, hyperparameters, or the reported 681-to-171 evaluation. A separate serialized bundle was recorded for each target, including feature identities and types, the imputer, scaler, fitted estimator, training-sample count, model role, and protocol hash. Nonconverged deployment fits were not accepted.</p><p>As documented in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S4</xref>, the locked internal-evaluation models and the all-852 deployment models were analytically distinct. The former supported only the 681-to-171 performance estimate; the latter constituted the final models applied without retraining to the 3D cohorts. The deployment-model manifest, selected-feature registry, target-specific model bundles, and final lock records were SHA-256 sealed before access to any new 3D data. Subsequent 3D applications prohibited retraining, recalibration, target or feature reselection, hyperparameter retuning, and metric switching; blind predictions had to be written and cryptographically sealed before outcome merging.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot6-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.6. Broad-94 Organoid Harmonization and Exploratory 3D Evaluation</title><p>The Broad-94 exploratory 3D cohort comprised 94 organoid models from the Broad NextGen resource, with both gene expression data and CRISPR Gene Effect outcomes for all 20 locked targets [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>]. ModelID was used for deterministic sample alignment and analysis. PatientID was unavailable in the original Broad evaluation records; therefore, the original analysis used organoid models as the inferential and resampling units. A later audit recovered partial donor information and identified a same-donor pair; the corresponding retrospective sensitivity analyses are described in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.3</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S22–S24</xref>. The frozen harmonization, prediction-lock, and exploratory-evaluation protocol is summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S5</xref>.</p><p>Cohort-size reconciliation found 95 unique 3D organoid (3DO) models in the archived Broad screen metadata. One model, ACH-003044, had PassesQC = False; the 94 quality-control-passing ModelIDs exactly matched the frozen registry. The prediction and outcome matrices each contained 94 × 20 values, and the long-format results contained 1880 unique model–target pairs. These records support the 94-model analytical cohort (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S22</xref>).</p><p>The expression-only deployment model, finalized in <xref rid="sec2dot5-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.5</xref> and refitted to all 852 2D models, was applied without Broad-specific retraining. For each target, the 300 locked expression features were matched to the Broad expression matrix using Entrez Gene identifiers and ordered exactly as stored in the corresponding model bundle. Feature coverage was defined as the proportion of the 300 frozen predictors present in the external expression matrix for each target. The prespecified 80% minimum (at least 240 of 300 predictors) was a pragmatic input-eligibility rule that limited unavailable predictors to 20% while allowing incomplete gene coverage across data resources. The cutoff was not optimized against external predictive performance and does not establish reliable prediction at 20% missingness. All 300 features were available for every Broad target, yielding 100% target-specific coverage. We applied the 2D-fitted median-imputation values, standardization parameters, Elastic Net coefficients, and l1_ratio and alpha settings unchanged. No Broad-fitted imputation, scaling, feature selection, coefficient adaptation, or target substitution was performed. This procedure generated a finite 94-organoid × 20-target prediction matrix.</p><p>To preserve an auditable prediction-before-outcome sequence in the current run, the prediction matrix and the model, feature, and lock manifests were written and SHA-256 sealed before the observed 3D outcome matrix was extracted. After sealing, only the 20 fixed Gene Effect columns were aligned to the predictions by ModelID. No model component or prespecified primary endpoint was changed after access to the outcome; the retrospective within-organoid endpoints are reported separately in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref>. Nevertheless, because Broad-94 had been used in prior methodological work, we did not classify the cohort as a previously unseen, blinded independent validation set; instead, we retained it for a retrospective exploratory assessment of 3D transportability.</p><p>The primary estimand was the macro target-wise Spearman correlation. We calculated target-specific Spearman correlation, MAE, RMSE, R<sup>2</sup>, calibration intercept, and calibration slope as secondary diagnostics and did not use them to reopen model selection.
