We estimated macro- and target-specific uncertainty from 5000 model-level bootstrap resamples performed with replacement within OncotreeLineage strata, preserving the observed lineage counts; 95% CIs were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The lineage-only ridge reference was applied to the same 94 organoids, and the expression-only-minus-lineage difference was estimated using paired bootstrap resamples. Target-specific partial Spearman correlations, adjusted for lineage indicators; lineage subgroup estimates for groups containing at least 7 models; and leave-one-lineage-out analyses were retained as secondary sensitivity analyses.</p><p>For the panel-wide permutation test, predictions were held fixed, and each organoid’s complete 20-target outcome vector was permuted among model rows within the same OncotreeLineage stratum for 5000 iterations, thereby preserving cross-target dependence and lineage composition. The one-sided empirical <italic>p</italic>-value was calculated as (1 + the number of null macro Spearman statistics greater than or equal to the observed statistic)/5001. Target-specific permutation <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted across the 20 targets using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. All Broad resampling procedures used random seed 20260829. As specified in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S5</xref>, rank transportability was the primary endpoint. Absolute-scale error, calibration, and lineage sensitivity were secondary diagnostics. Broad results were not used to retrain the model or select targets based on effect direction or statistical significance.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot7-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.7. Sanger-148 Cohort Construction and Blinded Independent External Validation</title><p>The independent Sanger 3D validation cohort was constructed from the RNA-seq and CRISPR-screening records of the tumor-derived organoid dependency map [<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. Before any Sanger target outcome was accessed, 162 organoids from 157 unique donors with both RNA-seq profiles and quality-controlled CRISPR-screening records were screened for eligibility. To prevent reuse of samples represented in the Broad exploratory layer or elsewhere in the Broad NextGen resource, Sanger sample and donor identifiers were cross-referenced against the Broad mapping records and the Broad-94 registry [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>,<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. Thirteen Broad-linked organoids and one additional organoid from the same donor as a Broad-linked model were conservatively excluded. The final cohort therefore comprised 148 organoids from 144 unique donors, with no exact Broad-94 identity or identifiable same-donor Broad overlap. Cohort construction, harmonization, and the outcome-blinded lock procedure are summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S6</xref>.</p><p>The final cohort included five tumor types: 81 colorectal organoids from 79 donors, 49 esophageal organoids from 49 donors, 11 ovarian organoids from 9 donors, 4 pancreatic organoids from 4 donors, and 3 gastric organoids from 3 donors. RNA-seq input and experimental CRISPR coverage for all 20 locked targets were available for every included organoid. Colorectal and esophageal subgroup analyses were prespecified as secondary, the ovarian subgroup was exploratory, and the pancreatic and gastric subgroups were treated as descriptive because of their small sample sizes. The primary external-validation analysis used all 148 organoids, with donor structure preserved in uncertainty estimation and sensitivity analyses.</p><p>Sanger TPM values were transformed as log2(TPM + 1) and aligned to the frozen expression-only feature space using Entrez Gene identifiers. For each target, the 300 expression features stored in the corresponding 2D deployment-model bundle were used in their locked order. Across targets, 3790 of 3845 unique locked genes were measured in the Sanger matrix; 55 genes were absent. Target-specific coverage ranged from 291 to 300 of 300 features (97.0–100%), exceeding the prespecified 80% minimum for all targets. Missing features were neither re-estimated from the external cohort nor replaced using Sanger-derived values; only the imputation and standardization objects learned in 2D data and the fixed Elastic Net coefficients were applied. A pre-outcome audit identified that the original coverage-key array had incorrectly counted the 55 entirely absent genes as present. The coverage metadata were corrected before outcome access, while the original and corrected blinded predictions remained bitwise identical.</p><p>Before the Sanger CRISPR outcomes were opened, the 148-organoid × 20-target blinded prediction matrix, cohort registry, protocol, model manifest, and feature manifest were written and sealed with SHA-256 digests; all 11 prespecified seal checks passed. Only after this lock was established were the Sanger outcomes accessed once and merged with the predictions in the frozen sample and target order, yielding 2960 finite prediction-outcome pairs. The external outcome was the corrected and scaled gene-level CRISPR LFC, with more negative values indicating stronger dependency. For the 13 organoids screened with two CRISPR libraries, the official Sanger covariate was applied: minLib was selected when the code was 1 and v1_1 when the code was 0. The available quality-controlled screen was used for single-library organoids. This externally defined selection rule was fixed before inspection of the target outcomes.</p><p>The primary external-validation estimand was the target-specific Spearman correlation between the blinded predictions and Sanger LFC values, followed by the arithmetic mean of the 20 target correlations (macro target-wise Spearman correlation). This primary estimand evaluates the ordering of organoids for a fixed gene and does not assess the ordering of genes within an organoid. Rank correlation was selected because the Sanger-corrected LFC and DepMap/Broad Chronos Gene Effect values are on assay-specific scales and were not assumed to be numerically comparable. Uncertainty was estimated with 5000 donor-cluster bootstrap resamples, retaining all organoids from a sampled donor together; 95% CIs were obtained from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. For the null distribution, repeated organoids were first averaged within donor, predictions were held fixed, and each donor-level 20-target observed-outcome vector was permuted within tumor-type/lineage strata for 5000 iterations. The two-sided empirical <italic>p</italic>-value was calculated as (1 + the number of absolute null macro correlations at least as large as the observed absolute macro correlation)/5001. Target-specific permutation <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted across the 20 targets using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure.</p><p>A lineage-only comparator, frozen before access to Sanger outcomes and based on patient-weighted 2D lineage means, was applied to the same cohort. We evaluated the expression-only-minus-lineage macro difference using paired donor-cluster bootstrap resamples, and we also calculated partial Spearman correlations adjusted for the primary tumor-type indicators. The influence of repeated donors was examined in two additional analyses: one retained the lexicographically first sample identifier per donor, and the other averaged predictions and outcomes within donor. An independent replay recomputed cohort size, donor count, overlap exclusions, feature coverage, target and prediction order, the complete 2960-pair grid, correlation statistics, bootstrap and permutation results, lineage adjustment, and file hashes; all 22 checks passed. As detailed in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S6</xref>, no model, target, feature, hyperparameter, or prespecified primary metric was changed after outcome unlock. The retrospective within-organoid endpoints were evaluated separately using the unchanged predictions.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot8-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.8. Retrospective Cross-Cohort Transportability Synthesis</title><p>The target-specific results from the Broad-94 exploratory evaluation and the Sanger-148 blinded independent external validation were combined retrospectively only after the two cohort-specific analyses had been completed [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>,<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. The fixed 20-target panel defined in <xref rid="sec2dot2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.2</xref> was aligned using Entrez Gene identifiers, and no targets were removed based on effect direction, magnitude, or statistical significance. Because Broad used Chronos Gene Effect values and Sanger used corrected CRISPR LFC values, the synthesis addressed target-specific rank transportability rather than absolute-scale equivalence. The Tiriac pancreatic projection was excluded from this synthesis because it did not contain measured genome-scale CRISPR outcomes. The synthesis protocol is summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S7</xref>.</p><p>Directional concordance was defined as a positive Spearman correlation for the same target in both Broad-94 and Sanger-148. The number of common-positive targets was compared with a one-sided exact binomial distribution with <italic>n</italic> = 20 and a null success probability of 0.50. This comparison was interpreted only as a descriptive sign benchmark: dependence among targets limits the binomial interpretation, and the synthesis was defined after the cohort-specific results were known. Agreement in relative target performance was evaluated separately using the two-sided Spearman correlation between the vectors of 20 Broad and 20 Sanger target-specific correlations.</p><p>For target-level pooling, each cohort-specific Spearman correlation was transformed to the Fisher-z scale. We derived inverse-variance weights from the cohort-specific uncertainty intervals obtained from the lineage-stratified Broad bootstrap and the donor-clustered Sanger bootstrap. Because Broad donor structure was incompletely ascertained, its original uncertainty weights may overstate precision; the synthesis is conditional on this unresolved model-level independence assumption. A fixed-effects pooled estimate was calculated for each target and then transformed back to the Spearman correlation scale. The resulting two-sided meta-analytic <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted across the 20 targets using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure. Because only two 3D cohorts were available, random-effects estimates and the I<sup>2</sup> heterogeneity statistic were retained as descriptive sensitivity measures and were not used as confirmatory decision criteria.</p><p>The panel-wide combined 3D estimate was defined as the arithmetic mean of the 20 fixed-effect target correlations. Sensitivity to target-panel composition was assessed by resampling the 20 locked targets with replacement for 20,000 iterations, then recalculating the combined macro correlation at each iteration. We reported the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as a descriptive 95% interval; this interval characterizes sensitivity to the composition of the fixed target panel and is not a new-patient or new-organoid sampling interval. Attenuation from 2D to 3D was calculated for each target by subtracting the corresponding locked 2D holdout correlation from the Broad or Sanger correlation, with panel-level summaries obtained using the same target-bootstrap structure.</p><p>To evaluate whether cross-target dependence could explain the common-positive count, we performed a post hoc, correlation-aware simultaneous permutation analysis. Predictions remained fixed. In Broad, each ModelID-level 20-target observed-outcome vector was retained as a block; in Sanger, repeated organoids were first averaged within donor, and each donor-level 20-target outcome vector was retained as a block. These vectors were permuted simultaneously among units within each cohort for 50,000 iterations, preserving the cross-target covariance structure. We recalculated the number of targets remaining positive in both cohorts at each iteration and calculated the one-sided empirical <italic>p</italic>-value with the plus-one correction. This analysis was explicitly treated as a post hoc sensitivity analysis and did not constitute a third external validation.</p><p>Within each cohort, we subtracted the target-specific lineage-only correlation from the corresponding expression-only correlation. We used a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the 20 paired differences to assess the incremental contribution of expression beyond lineage. A retrospective evidence classification was used for reporting only. Tier A required a positive correlation in both cohorts, a meta-analytic FDR q &lt; 0.05, and target-level FDR q &lt; 0.05 in at least one individual cohort. Tier B indicated positive correlations in both cohorts without fulfillment of all Tier A criteria. Tier C indicated a non-positive correlation in at least one cohort. As specified in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S7</xref>, the evidence tiers did not alter the locked panel or any model component, and no retraining, target or feature reselection, hyperparameter tuning, metric switching, or direction-based target removal was permitted during the synthesis.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot9-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.9. Secondary Transcriptomic Projection in the Tiriac Pancreatic Organoid Cohort</title><p>After completion of 2D model development, Broad-94 exploration, Sanger-148 blinded validation, and the retrospective cross-cohort synthesis, the frozen expression-only deployment models were applied to the Tiriac/ORGANOID-PANCREATIC cohort as a secondary biological projection [<xref rid="B32-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. Because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable, this analysis was prespecified as an application to an independent pancreatic transcriptome rather than external validation; predictive accuracy and CRISPR performance were not estimated. Fifty-five publicly available RNA-seq Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR) count files from the GDC project were obtained from the official public Amazon Simple Storage Service mirror. The cohort comprised 44 tumor samples representing 38 independent tumor cases and 11 samples from 11 independent normal cases; group membership was defined from the source TissueType metadata. Cohort preparation and projection procedures are summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S8</xref>.</p><p>The tpm_unstranded field in the STAR output was used as the abundance measure. Rows mapping to the same gene symbol were summed at the TPM level before log2(TPM + 1) transformation. The resulting sample-by-feature matrix was aligned to the locked expression features of the 20 target-specific Elastic Net deployment bundles finalized in all 852 2D models. The target panel, target-specific feature identities, stored imputation and standardization objects, hyperparameters, coefficients, and projection definitions were applied without modification. No Tiriac sample contributed to model fitting, feature selection, recalibration, retuning, or endpoint definition.</p><p>Of the 3845 unique locked features used across the 20 models, 3806 were observed in the Tiriac data. Target-specific coverage ranged from 292 to 300 of 300 selected features (97.33–100%), and every target met the prespecified 80% coverage threshold. Features absent from the Tiriac matrix were represented as not-a-number (NaN) values, filled with the medians stored in the frozen all-852 deployment models before the stored standardization, and then coefficients were applied. This preserved the training preprocessing rule without estimating replacement values from Tiriac. An independent computational replay reproduced the archived predictions exactly using training-median imputation (<xref rid="sec2dot10dot2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.2</xref>). This procedure produced a 55-sample × 20-target projection matrix. Source file identifiers, file sizes, source-provided integrity values, local SHA-256 digests, model and feature manifests, and prediction records were retained for provenance.</p><p>When multiple tumor organoid samples originated from the same GDC case, the 20 sample-level projections were averaged within the case, and the patient/case was used as the inferential unit. For each target, median case-level projections were calculated for 38 tumor cases and 11 normal cases, together with the tumor-minus-normal median difference. Uncertainty in this difference was estimated using 5000 case-level bootstrap resamples within the tumor and normal groups, with 95% percentile intervals. Tumor and normal projection distributions were compared using two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests, and the 20 <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure. Cliff’s delta was reported as an effect-size measure; under the prespecified orientation, a positive value indicated a more negative, and therefore stronger, projected dependency distribution in tumors. These analyses compared frozen model outputs rather than measured dependencies or model errors.</p><p>The 20-target median projection vector for Tiriac tumor cases was compared separately with the corresponding median prediction vectors for Broad-94 and Sanger-148. This comparison assessed whether the projected pancreatic target hierarchy was consistent across organoid applications. Concordance was quantified using two-sided Spearman correlations across the 20 targets. Because all compared values were predictions from the same locked model family and Tiriac lacked measured CRISPR outcomes, these correlations were interpreted as secondary evidence of target-ranking consistency rather than independent evidence of predictive accuracy.</p><p>Expression-domain shift was evaluated across the 3790 locked expression features that are jointly available in Tiriac, Broad-94, and Sanger-148. Multivariable separation among cohorts was visualized by principal component analysis (PCA). For Tiriac versus Broad-94 and Tiriac versus Sanger-148, a standardized mean difference (SMD) was calculated for each common feature, and shift magnitude was summarized using the median absolute SMD and the proportions of features with |SMD| &gt; 1 and |SMD| &gt; 2. The PCA and SMD diagnostics were descriptive and were not used to recalibrate the models, delete features, remove targets, or revise projections. <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S8</xref> defines the corresponding claim boundary: Tiriac results were described as projections or prioritizations and not as validated dependencies, confirmed dependencies, or therapeutic sensitivity.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot10-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.10. Statistical Analysis</title><p>Statistical analyses preserved the prespecified role and strongest available biological independence unit of each study layer. In the development, locked 2D holdout, Broad-94, and Sanger-148 analyses, the primary rank-based measure was the Spearman correlation between predicted and observed outcomes for each target and the arithmetic mean of the 20 target correlations (macro target-wise Spearman correlation). MAE, RMSE, R<sup>2</sup>, calibration intercept, and calibration slope were secondary diagnostics in the development, locked-holdout, and Broad analyses and did not reopen model selection. Because Sanger-corrected LFC and DepMap/Broad Chronos Gene Effect values were not treated as numerically equivalent, the Sanger validation and cross-cohort synthesis were based on rank correlation rather than absolute-scale error. Target-wise correlation operates across organoids for each gene; within-organoid correlation instead operates across the 20 genes for each organoid. Averaging target-wise correlations does not test within-organoid gene ranking. The original analysis hierarchy, inferential units, resampling procedures, and multiplicity rules are summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S9</xref>; the retrospective within-organoid endpoints are defined in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S17–S19</xref>.</p><p>Resampling units followed the available biological grouping. Development and locked 2D holdout uncertainty used 2000 PatientID-cluster bootstrap replicates, retaining all models from a sampled patient group together. Broad-94 used 5000 model-level bootstrap replicates within OncotreeLineage strata because PatientID was unavailable in the original evaluation records; the later partial-donor sensitivities are reported separately in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.3</xref>. Sanger-148 used 5000 donor-cluster bootstrap replicates, retaining all organoids from a sampled donor together. Tiriac tumor-normal comparisons used 5000 case-level bootstrap replicates within the 38-tumor and 11-normal groups. Unless otherwise specified, 95% percentile CIs were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Paired model comparisons used common resampling indices. The standard error used in the development one-standard-error rule was derived from the 2000-replicate PatientID-cluster bootstrap distribution of OOF predictions.</p><p>For permutation analyses, predictions remained fixed and complete 20-target observed-outcome vectors were moved without disrupting the prespecified biological grouping. The locked 2D sensitivity analysis used 2000 one-sided permutations of patient-aggregated outcome vectors within OncotreeLineage strata. Broad-94 used 5000 one-sided permutations of ModelID-level outcome vectors within lineage. Sanger-148 used 5000 two-sided permutations after donor averaging, with donor-level outcome vectors moved within tumor-type/lineage strata and the absolute macro correlation used as the test statistic. Empirical <italic>p</italic>-values used the standard plus-one numerator and denominator correction. Broad and Sanger target-specific permutation <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted separately within their 20-target families using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure.</p><p>In the retrospective cross-cohort synthesis, common-positive direction was assessed with a one-sided exact binomial benchmark (<italic>n</italic> = 20; null probability = 0.50), interpreted descriptively because targets were correlated and the synthesis was retrospective. Target-specific correlations were pooled on the Fisher-z scale using inverse-variance fixed-effect weights derived from cohort-specific bootstrap uncertainty, and the 20 two-sided meta-analytic <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Random-effects estimates and I<sup>2</sup> were descriptive because only two cohorts were available. Target-panel sensitivity used 20,000 target-bootstrap resamples, while cross-target dependence was assessed using 50,000 one-sided simultaneous block permutations at the Broad ModelID and Sanger donor-mean levels. Expression-only-minus-lineage target differences were evaluated separately in Broad and Sanger using one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of these retrospective analyses was interpreted as a new validation cohort.</p><p>In the Tiriac layer, two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests compared patient-level tumor and normal projections for each target. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR adjustment was applied across 20 tests. Cliff’s delta described effect direction. Concordance between the Tiriac tumor target-median vector and the Broad and Sanger target-median prediction vectors was evaluated using two-sided Spearman correlations across 20 targets. We used PCA and SMD measures only as descriptive domain-shift diagnostics, and they did not inform the confirmatory decision.</p><p>A retrospective coverage-threshold sensitivity analysis compared the prespecified 80% rule with stricter 90% and 95% requirements using the archived target-specific present-feature counts. The number of eligible models among the fixed 20 targets was recorded for each external cohort. Only the eligibility requirement was varied; no features were removed, no models were refitted, and no missing-feature handling was changed (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S16</xref>).</p><p>Tests were two-sided unless explicitly prespecified as one-sided. Within each stated 20-target family, FDR q &lt; 0.05 defined the multiplicity-adjusted target-level significance; exact <italic>p</italic>-values, effect sizes, and CIs were reported together where applicable. Exploratory and post hoc analyses retained those labels even when a statistical threshold was crossed, and no analysis result changed the target panel, feature identities, hyperparameters, primary metrics, or previously generated predictions. Analyses were implemented in Python 3.12.13 using NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.2.3, SciPy 1.17.0, scikit-learn 1.8.0, and joblib 1.5.3. Random seeds, environment files, protocols, SHA-256 manifests, and integrity checks were preserved in the archived reproducibility package.</p><sec id="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="3"><title>2.10.1. Retrospective Evaluation of Gene Ranking Within Organoids</title><p>A retrospective secondary analysis evaluated whether the frozen expression-only predictions ranked the 20 genes within individual organoids in agreement with measured CRISPR outcomes. This secondary analysis was defined after the external outcomes were available and was not a new blinded validation. It retained all 20 targets and all 94 Broad and 148 Sanger organoids; Tiriac was excluded because measured dependency outcomes were unavailable. No predictions, models, features, hyperparameters, or targets were changed, and the original target-wise primary analysis was retained.</p><p>For each organoid, we calculated Spearman correlation across its 20 predicted and 20 observed scores, using average ranks for ties, and summarized the correlations by their arithmetic mean. Lower scores denoted stronger measured or predicted dependency. The main comparator assigned every organoid the same per-gene mean of the observed outcomes across all 852 2D training models, with each training model weighted equally. This fixed ranking tested whether expression predictions improved on gene-level average dependency. We also reused the archived lineage-only predictions: the ridge reference in Broad and patient-weighted 2D lineage means in Sanger. No external outcomes were used to fit either comparator (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S17</xref>).</p><p>To examine a short candidate list, we calculated the overlap between the three lowest predicted scores and the three lowest measured scores, divided by three, within each organoid. The cohort mean was expressed as a percentage. Ties at the selection boundary were to be resolved by the fixed target identifiers; none occurred. Expression-minus-comparator differences were calculated within the same organoids for both the full-ranking correlation and top-three overlap (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S18</xref>). These endpoints assess agreement with measured CRISPR score ordering within the selected panel, not cancer selectivity, cross-gene calibration, drug response, or clinical benefit.</p><p>We estimated 95% percentile CIs using 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples: organoid models sampled within observed lineage strata for Broad, and donor clusters sampled with all their organoids retained together for Sanger. The Sanger main estimate remained organoid-weighted. A donor-level sensitivity analysis first averaged the predicted and observed 20-gene vectors within each of 144 donors, then recalculated both endpoints with equal donor weights and a 10,000-replicate donor bootstrap (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S19</xref>). Seeds were 20260928, 20260929, and 20260930 for Broad, Sanger, and donor-mean sensitivity, respectively. All correlations were defined. Intervals were conditional on the frozen models and fixed panel; they did not include model-training or gene-panel selection uncertainty. The secondary comparisons were not adjusted for multiplicity and were interpreted as exploratory.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot10dot2-biology-15-01782" disp-level="3"><title>2.10.2. Retrospective Sensitivity to Missing-Feature Imputation in Tiriac</title><p>A retrospective sensitivity analysis evaluated the effects of alternative missing-feature replacement values on Tiriac projections. This descriptive analysis was not prespecified. The archived code represented absent inputs as NaN and applied the frozen training-median imputer, followed by the stored scaler and Elastic Net estimator. This pipeline reproduced all 1100 archived Tiriac predictions exactly. The reference predictions were generated with training medians and were retained for comparison with the alternative imputation methods. The 39 absent unique features corresponded to 0–8 missing predictors per target, with the same missing-feature pattern across all 55 samples.</p><p>Using the same frozen models, we compared training-median imputation with two alternatives: zero on the log2(TPM + 1) scale before standardization, and the stored training-reference mean for each feature. These means were estimated after median imputation in the 852-model training data and correspond to zero standardized input, up to floating-point rounding. Only absent features were replaced; observed expression values, including measured zeros, were retained. We summarized absolute projection changes, Spearman correlation across the 20 genes within each profile, and top-three set overlap relative to the median-imputed reference. We evaluated sample-level results and case-averaged profiles, including 38 tumor and 11 normal cases. We also repeated the original tumor–normal comparisons using the same 5000 bootstrap resamples (seed 20260830), Mann–Whitney tests, and 20-target FDR adjustment. These are descriptive checks of projection stability, not prediction accuracy. Because the models are linear and the missing-feature pattern is shared, constant replacement values create a common offset per target; preservation of within-target sample ranks and tumor–normal differences is therefore expected algebraically (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S20 and S21</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" disp-level="3"><title>2.10.3. Retrospective Broad Donor Audit and Sensitivity Analyses</title><p>A retrospective metadata audit linked 16 of the 94 models to 15 PatientID values in the supplied DepMap Model.csv and nine additional models to nine source-specific donor identifiers in the archived Sanger exclusion registry. Thus, donor information was available for 25 models, forming 24 source-specific groups, while 69 models remained unresolved. ACH-002883 and ACH-002884 shared PatientID PT-N65Hvq. The DepMap and Sanger donor namespaces could not be fully reconciled, so the 24 groups do not establish 24 independently verified biological donors. No donor identity was inferred from lineage or model-name similarity (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S22</xref>).</p><p>Retrospective sensitivity analyses used the unchanged predictions, outcomes, and 20-gene panel. Each member of the known same-donor pair was omitted in turn. A conditional full-cohort bootstrap grouped the known pair and treated unresolved models as singleton units, yielding 93 resampling groups; this assumption does not establish independence of the 69 unresolved models. In the donor-documented subset, model-level and donor-cluster bootstraps were compared on the same 25 models, and a separate analysis averaged prediction, outcome, and lineage-reference vectors within the 24 source-specific donor groups before evaluation. All analyses used 5000 paired bootstrap replicates within the observed OncotreeLineage strata (seed 20260929), retaining every model from each sampled group. Percentile 95% intervals were calculated at 2.5% and 97.5%. Target-wise correlations were reranked within each resample and averaged across all 20 targets; an undefined target correlation contributed zero, following the archived convention. Organoid weighting was retained except in the donor-mean analysis. Full-cohort and known-subset model-level replays with the same seed provide matched references; they do not replace the original CIs. <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S23 and S24</xref> report the primary target-wise and secondary within-organoid endpoints. These post hoc intervals were not adjusted for multiple sensitivity comparisons, and no new confirmatory permutation or FDR claim was made.</p></sec></sec><sec id="sec2dot11-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.11. Code and Reproducibility Resources</title><p>The study’s reproducibility package is available on Zenodo (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22472622" ext-link-type="uri">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22472622</ext-link>). The package includes custom analysis and figure-generation scripts; frozen cohort, split, target, and feature registries; trained model artifacts; locked predictions; analysis-ready inputs and processed outputs; bootstrap and permutation results; figure source data; software-environment records; and SHA-256 integrity manifests. It also contains the code, inputs, and results for the primary analyses, retrospective within-organoid gene ranking, Tiriac missing-feature imputation sensitivity, and Broad cohort-size and donor sensitivity analyses. Complete original third-party data releases remain available from the repositories identified in the Data Availability Statement.</p></sec></sec><sec id="sec3-biology-15-01782" disp-level="1"><title>3. Results</title><sec id="sec3dot1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>3.1. Selection of the Expression-Only Model in the 2D Development Cohort</title><p>Five input representations—the lineage-only reference and four molecular candidates—were compared in the development partition of 681 models representing 658 patient groups, using identical patient-grouped outer folds. Candidate-level OOF macro target-wise Spearman correlations and paired differences relative to expression-only are shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f002" ref-type="fig">Figure 2</xref>a,b; full candidate- and target-level results are provided in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S10</xref>.</p><fig id="biology-15-01782-f002" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>Figure 2</label><caption><p>Development-cohort omics ablation and selection of the expression-only model. Error bars show 95% percentile confidence intervals from 2000 PatientID-cluster bootstrap replicates. (<bold>b</bold>) Paired differences in macro Spearman correlation between each augmented molecular representation and expression-only. Performance was nearly identical for expression-only (ρ = 0.4071; 95% CI, 0.3893–0.4232), expression + mutation (ρ = 0.4073; 95% CI, 0.3908–0.4235), and all omics + lineage (ρ = 0.4031; 95% CI, 0.3864–0.4184). The lineage-only reference produced a lower macro correlation (ρ = 0.2598; 95% CI, 0.2388–0.2806) and, as prespecified, was not eligible for molecular candidate selection.</p><p>Relative to expression-only, paired PatientID-cluster bootstrap differences were +0.0010 (95% CI, −0.0047 to 0.0066) for expression + copy number, +0.0002 (95% CI, −0.0075 to 0.0079) for expression + mutation, and −0.0039 (95% CI, −0.0123 to 0.0043) for all omics + lineage (<xref rid="biology-15-01782-f002" ref-type="fig">Figure 2</xref>b). All three intervals included zero, providing no evidence that adding copy-number, mutation, or combined omic and lineage information produced a reliable improvement in development performance.</p><p>The expression-only candidate remained within one bootstrap standard error of the highest-scoring molecular candidate and showed the greatest mean feature-set Jaccard stability across outer folds (0.565 versus 0.550–0.554 for the other molecular candidates). The prespecified one-standard-error rule therefore selected expression-only as the final molecular representation.</p></sec><sec id="sec3dot2-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>3.2. Locked 2D Holdout Performance and Deployment Model Finalization</title><p>After model selection was locked, the expression-only model, target-specific 300-feature sets, and final Elastic Net hyperparameters were applied once to the locked 2D holdout of 171 models representing 165 patient groups. Panel-wide, paired-contrast, target-level, and deployment-finalization results are shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f003" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>a–d; detailed numerical results are provided in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S11</xref>.</p><fig id="biology-15-01782-f003" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>Figure 3</label><caption><p>Locked two-dimensional holdout performance and deployment-model finalization. The holdout-minus-development difference was +0.0023 (95% CI, −0.0372 to 0.0361). The interval included zero, indicating no detectable difference within this preselected panel. This comparison does not remove the dependence introduced by historical target selection.</p><p>The lineage-only holdout reference yielded a macro correlation of 0.2969 (95% CI, 0.2529–0.3368). The expression-only-minus-lineage-only difference was +0.1125 (95% CI, 0.0765–0.1472). The patient-aggregated macro correlation was 0.4133, and the within-lineage permutation analysis across 165 patient groups yielded <italic>p</italic> = 0.00050. These prespecified checks supported rank information beyond lineage composition within the preselected panel. They do not establish independence from historical target selection.</p><p>All 20 locked-holdout target correlations were positive and ranged from 0.170 to 0.550 (<xref rid="biology-15-01782-f003" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>c; <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S11</xref>). The highest values were observed for <italic>EP300</italic> (ρ = 0.550), <italic>CDK6</italic> (ρ = 0.532), and <italic>TSC2</italic> (ρ = 0.525), whereas the lowest were observed for <italic>RAF1</italic> (ρ = 0.170), <italic>MAPK1</italic> (ρ = 0.197), and <italic>BRAF</italic> (ρ = 0.341). Absolute error, R<sup>2</sup>, and calibration measures remained secondary diagnostics and did not alter the rank-based primary assessment.</p><p>Following the one-time holdout evaluation, the selected model was refitted on all 852 2D models while the representation, 20-target panel, 300 target-specific feature identities, hyperparameters, and primary metric remained fixed (<xref rid="biology-15-01782-f003" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>d). All 20 deployment models converged. The 6000 target-feature assignments represented 3845 unique expression features. The final lock, strict audit, and independent replay passed 18/18, 41/41, and 50/50 checks, respectively, with a maximum prediction-reproduction difference of 0.0 (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S11</xref>).</p><p>Because the historical target panel had been selected using all 852 2D models, these holdout results provide internal confirmation conditional on that selection. They do not provide an unbiased estimate of generalization for the complete analysis pipeline. The independent 3D validation assessed transfer to new organoid samples only for the same preselected panel.</p></sec><sec id="sec3dot3-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>3.3. All 300 locked expression features were available for every target, yielding 100% feature coverage. The 94 × 20 prediction matrix was written and SHA-256-sealed before alignment with the observed 3D Gene Effect outcomes. Because Broad-94 had been accessible in earlier methodological work, this analysis remained an exploratory 3D transfer assessment rather than an independent external validation. This subset is not a representative replacement for Broad-94; changes relative to the full cohort can reflect sample and lineage composition as well as grouping. Paired within-subset model-versus-cluster intervals and secondary ranking sensitivities are provided in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S23 and S24</xref>. Incomplete donor ascertainment prevents these analyses from verifying full-cohort independence or providing a fully donor-adjusted effective sample size.</p></sec><sec id="sec3dot4-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>3.4. Blinded Independent External Validation in Sanger-148 Organoids</title><p>The outcome-blinded Sanger eligibility pool comprised 162 organoids from 157 donors with both RNA-seq profiles and quality-controlled CRISPR screening records. Of the 3845 unique locked expression features used across the 20 target models, 3790 were measured in the Sanger matrix; target-specific coverage ranged from 291 to 300 of 300 features (97.0–100%). The 148 × 20 blind prediction matrix and the associated manifests were SHA-256 sealed before CRISPR LFC outcomes were accessed, and all 11 prespecified pre-outcome seal checks passed. Panel-wide validation, target-level results, and robustness analyses are summarized in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f005" ref-type="fig">Figure 5</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S13</xref>.</p><fig id="biology-15-01782-f005" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>Figure 5</label><caption><p>Blinded independent external validation in Sanger-148 organoids. (<bold>a</bold>) Cohort construction and tumor-type composition. Fourteen organoids were excluded from 162 eligible organoids representing 157 donors, leaving 148 organoids from 144 donors. (<bold>d</bold>) Robustness and tumor-type subgroup estimates.
