Our biobank also includes rare models with complex genotypes, such as five COAD/READ-MSS models that all carry <italic>APC</italic>, <italic>TP53</italic>, <italic>KRAS</italic> and <italic>SMAD4</italic> mutations or one with <italic>APC</italic>, <italic>TP53</italic>, <italic>KRAS</italic> and <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations together with a <italic>PTEN</italic> deletion, which will enable studies investigating acquisition of mutations during multi-step carcinogenesis<sup><xref rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr">27</xref>,<xref rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr">28</xref></sup>. Our biobank includes 94 <italic>KRAS</italic>-altered organoids, including specific variant alleles that varied in frequency by tumour type, consistent with patient tumours<sup><xref rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr">29</xref></sup>, thereby enabling the study of this clinically important molecular cohort (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5</xref>).</p><p id="Par21">We used our WGS data to uncover the landscape of mutational signatures available in the Catalog of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) database<sup><xref rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr">30</xref></sup> in organoids, providing insights into disease aetiology and patient clinical history (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6b</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">3</xref>). For example, all MSI models had signatures related to DNA mismatch repair deficiency (SBS15, SBS44, SBS26, SBS20, SBS6 and/or the recently described SBS_MSI_M). SBS88, caused by the bacteria-produced mutagen colibactin<sup><xref rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr">31</xref>,<xref rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr">32</xref></sup>, was detected in 10 COAD/READ-MSS organoids, including those from three early-onset cases, representing 27% of samples from patients with COAD/READ who were diagnosed before the age of 50. Notably, 9 out of 10 SBS88-positive organoids originated from distal (<italic>n</italic> = 4) or rectal (<italic>n</italic> = 5) tumours<sup><xref rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr">33</xref></sup>. We identified six organoids with SBS3, a signature linked to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), some of which overlapped with models detected as HRD by CHORD, which integrates multiple types of somatic mutations to detect HRD<sup><xref rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr">34</xref></sup> (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5</xref>). We detected SBS35, associated with previous platinum treatment, in organoids from donors treated with this chemotherapeutic agent (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">3c</xref>). The high mutational load of cancer cell lines, coupled with the absence of matched normal samples for germline filtering, complicates accurate detection of mutational signatures<sup><xref rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr">35</xref></sup>. By contrast, organoid cultures offer a promising model for studying signature biology, capturing aspects of disease aetiology including genetic factors and clinically relevant exposures.</p><p id="Par22">RNA-seq of the organoids was performed, enabling us to classify the COAD/READ models into two of the most validated and clinically relevant transcriptional subtypes: consensus molecular subtypes<sup><xref rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr">36</xref></sup> (CMS 1–4) and colorectal cancer intrinsic subtypes (CRIS A–E)<sup><xref rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref></sup> (Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">3</xref>). CMS and CRIS classifications showed strong concordance in colorectal cancer organoids and were associated with distinct genomic and anatomical features, with CRIS providing more precise correlations with specific molecular alterations (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6c</xref>).</p><p id="Par23">Whole-genome and transcriptomic profiling showed that organoids maintained stable ploidy, mutational landscapes and transcriptional profiles over up to six months of culture and multiple freeze–thaw cycles (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7</xref> and <xref rid="MOESM1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Supplementary Information</xref>). Long-term culture caused slightly greater—but still modest—genetic drift than repeated freeze–thaw cycles. These results demonstrate that organoids largely preserve genomic integrity over time<sup><xref rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>,<xref rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr">39</xref></sup>, supporting their use as robust and renewable tumour models.</p><fig id="Fig12" position="float"><?disp-level 2?><label>Extended Data Fig. 7</label><caption><title>Organoid genomic and transcriptomic features are stable following prolonged culturing or multiple freeze-thaw cycles.</title><p>Evolution of <bold>a</bold>. ploidy, <bold>b</bold>. number of mutations per megabase (Mb), <bold>c</bold>. number of structural variants (SVs), and <bold>d</bold>. percentage of the genome with somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs) along time-points for four organoids. <bold>e</bold>. This study is one of the most comprehensive genomic analyses of organoids performed to date, both in terms of number of models and depth of characterization. To facilitate accessibility of these data, we have made them available through the Cell Model Passports database<sup><xref rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr">40</xref></sup> (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk/" ext-link-type="uri">https://cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk/</ext-link>).</p></sec><sec id="Sec6" disp-level="1"><title>Mapping cancer dependencies in organoids</title><p id="Par25">Dependency catalogues from pharmacological and genetic screens, including the Cancer Dependency Map, have advanced target discovery and patient stratification. Yet existing cell models do not capture the full tumour diversity (for example, in ESCA), and inter-tumour heterogeneity limits genotype–dependency associations. High mutational burden and lack of matched germline data further complicate linking dependencies to genomic features. Systematic dependency mapping in organoids could address these gaps. However, CRISPR screens in 3D cultures remain limited<sup><xref rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr">41</xref>–<xref rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr">44</xref></sup>, as the increased complexity of screening in 3D cultures across tissue histologies is constrained in scale. To overcome this, we established a scalable platform to map dependencies across our organoid biobank.</p><p id="Par26">Organoids were screened using a 5% basement membrane extract-2 (BME-2) suspension culture, which simplifies handling while preserving genetic and phenotypic stability<sup><xref rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref></sup>. Screening was conducted using the minimal genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 library<sup><xref rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr">41</xref></sup> (MinLibCas9), alongside the larger Human CRISPR Library Yusa v.1.1 (refs. <sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup>) (hereafter, Yusa v1.1) for a subset of models (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8a</xref>). MinLibCas9 required fewer cells than Yusa v1.1 and, combined with suspension culture, increased efficiency of dependency mapping in organoids to enable systematic screening.</p><fig id="Fig13" position="float"><?disp-level 2?><label>Extended Data Fig. 8</label><caption><title>CRISPR-Cas9 screening quality control metrics.</title><p><bold>a</bold>. Overlap of single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) in the Human CRISPR-Cas9 Libraries Yusa v.1.1 (v1.1) and the Minimal Genome-Wide (MinLibCas9). Only genes with at least two shared sgRNAs were included in the analysis. <bold>b</bold>. Pearson correlation between two independent batches of Cas9-expressing organoids. Normalised gene log fold changes (LFCs) values are shown for screens performed in three independent organoid cultures. <bold>c</bold>. Using the BAGEL2 method<sup><xref rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr">45</xref></sup>, we identified a median of 1,440 fitness genes in each organoid (range 297–2,160; Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4a</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">5</xref>), fewer than reported in cell lines (median = 2,507 for 930 cell lines<sup><xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup>). The number of fitness genes was inversely proportional to the log fold change (LFC) standard deviation and other quality control metrics (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4b</xref>, Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8g,h</xref> and Supplementary Tables <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">4</xref> and <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">6</xref>), indicating that greater variability in gene depletion negatively affects fitness gene identification. We applied rigorous quality control criteria to screens, including replicate concordance, clear discrimination of reference essential versus non-essential genes (area under receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) = 0.97 and area under precision-recall curve (AUPR) = 0.973) and good effect size (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4c,d</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">4</xref>), with results comparable to cell lines<sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup> (AUROC = 0.92 and AUPR = 0.9). Our results demonstrate the feasibility of constructing organoid dependency maps, with the potential to uncover new biology.</p><fig id="Fig4" position="float"><?disp-level 2?><label>Fig. 4</label><caption><title>Multi-omic analysis for context-specific organoid dependencies.</title><p><bold>a</bold>,<bold>b</bold>, Number of fitness genes identified (<bold>a</bold>) and gene knockout scaled LFC values (<bold>b</bold>) for 162 organoids coloured by cancer type. <bold>c</bold>,<bold>d</bold>, AUROC (<bold>c</bold>) and AUPR (<bold>d</bold>) obtained after classifying predefined essential and non-essential genes using CRISPRcleanR normalized and corrected LFCs. <bold>e</bold>, Genetic constraint annotation for gene sets, including reference essential and non-essential genes, core fitness genes identified in cell lines (Core Cl), core fitness genes identified in organoids (Core Org), and genes analysed in biomarker analyses restricted to colorectal (COAD/READ, <italic>n</italic> = 85), oesophageal (ESCA, <italic>n</italic> = 59) or all gastrointestinal organoids (GI; <italic>n</italic> = 151). <bold>f</bold>, Mean LFC values of differentially dependent genes for all gastrointestinal organoids, grouped by genetic constraint buckets. All CRISPR screens were performed with a minimum of <italic>n</italic> = 2 technical replicates.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" id="d33e2054" xlink:href="41586_2026_10830_Fig4_HTML.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/60aa/13581617/0ae6f5036fb9/41586_2026_10830_Fig4_HTML.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1224?><?original-width 1600?><?scaled-height 1224?><?scaled-width 1600?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="41586_2026_10830_Fig4_HTML.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/60aa/13581617/274280000fd0/41586_2026_10830_Fig4_HTML.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig></sec><sec id="Sec7" disp-level="1"><title>Organoid core fitness genes</title><p id="Par28">We applied the Adaptive Daisy Model (ADaM) to define core fitness genes in organoids, and compared these with those in cell lines<sup><xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup>. This identified 654 shared core fitness genes and 97 that were unique to organoids (Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">4</xref>). Gene set enrichment analysis of organoid-specific core fitness genes highlighted strong associations with steroid biosynthesis (most significant: Biological Process—steroid biosynthetic process, <italic>P</italic> value = 1.38 × 10<sup>−6</sup>; most enriched: Biological Process—isopentenyl diphosphate biosynthetic process, enrichment fold change = 667.5, Fisher’s exact test), potentially linked with a role for cholesterol in regulating intestinal stem cells and tumourgenesis<sup><xref rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr">46</xref></sup> (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9a</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">4</xref>).</p><fig id="Fig14" position="float"><?disp-level 2?><label>Extended Data Fig. 9</label><caption><title>Organoid-specific core fitness genes and gene-biomarker associations.</title><p><bold>a</bold>. Pathways enriched in gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of 97 organoid-specific core fitness genes. Essential, non-essential and genes untested in organoids owing to single guide RNA (sgRNA) selection were excluded, and compared with pan-cancer core fitness genes from cell lines. Dot size indicates the number of genes per pathway (gene names displayed), while colour represents the FDR-adjusted p-value after Fisher’s exact test. Only pathways with FDR &lt; 10% are shown. BP: biological processes; KEGG: KEGG pathways; H: hallmarks. <bold>b</bold>. Annotation of organoid-specific core essential genes based on genetic constraint, phenotypic effect in mouse knock-outs and tissue specificity of gene expression. Light green indicates highly constrained with severe knockout phenotypes (new core fitness genes); red indicates low constraint with normal knockout phenotypes (cancer organoid selective core fitness genes). <bold>c</bold>. Scaled log fold change (LFC) values of example genes per category in cell lines (n = 930) and in organoids (n = 154). <bold>d</bold>. Volcano plot of statistically significant gene-biomarker associations. Dot colour indicates association significance (A &gt; B &gt; C), while shape corresponds to cancer type. Dashed lines indicate p-value cutoffs. <bold>e</bold>. Log fold change (LFC) profile of WRN with corresponding biomarker associations in colorectal adenocarcinoma (COAD/READ) organoid (n = 85). <bold>f</bold>. Same as panel e for MDM2. Only organoids with Nutlin-3a log IC<sub>50</sub> values are shown (n = 49). <bold>g</bold>. All box plots display the median, first and third quartiles (boxes), and whiskers are 1.5x the interquartile range from the first and third quartiles.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" id="d33e3546" xlink:href="41586_2026_10830_Fig14_ESM.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/60aa/13581617/f3ee35ed46a2/41586_2026_10830_Fig14_ESM.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1260?><?original-width 1600?><?scaled-height 1260?><?scaled-width 1600?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="41586_2026_10830_Fig14_ESM.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/60aa/13581617/07e8ed5b88e2/41586_2026_10830_Fig14_ESM.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig><p id="Par29">Genetic constraint, derived from population-scale human genome sequencing, reflects the degree to which a gene is intolerant to heterozygous variation and provides an orthogonal method to identify disease-linked or functionally important (essential) genes<sup><xref rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr">47</xref>,<xref rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr">48</xref></sup>. Core fitness genes experimentally derived from CRISPR–Cas9 screens in cell lines<sup><xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup> and organoids (this study) were enriched for genetically constrained genes (high categories), as were reference lists of essential genes (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4e</xref>). By additionally excluding genes commonly essential in cell lines (area under the curve (AUC) method), we refined our list to include 18 of 97 organoid-specific core fitness genes and annotated them with mouse knockout phenotypes and GTEx tissue-specific expression (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9b</xref>). Genes with low constraint and normal mouse knockout phenotype, such as isopentenyl diphosphate delta isomerase 1 (<italic>IDI1</italic>), required for isoprenoid synthesis and involved in cholesterol production, may reflect cancer organoid selective fitness dependencies. Conversely, genes under high genetic constraint and with severe knockout phenotypes represent candidate core fitness genes identified in organoids—for example, <italic>ITGB1</italic> (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9b,c</xref>). Together, this integrative approach combining experimental data from organoids with genetic constraint from human populations identifies core fitness genes.</p></sec><sec id="Sec8" disp-level="1"><title>Genomic and clinical dependencies</title><p id="Par30">The number of gastrointestinal tract (COAD/READ, ESCA, PAAD and STAD, <italic>n</italic> = 151) and specifically COAD/READ (<italic>n</italic> = 85) and ESCA (<italic>n</italic> = 59) organoids screened with CRISPR, and their genomic deep characterization, enabled analyses to interpret differential gene dependencies. To focus on context-specific effects, we excluded core fitness genes, curated essential and non-essential genes, non-expressed genes, and genes whose depletion was restricted to or absent from a single organoid. For the remaining genes, we performed differential dependency analysis comparing LFC values between organoids where a gene was essential or non-essential based on BAGEL2 scores (minimum of two organoids per group). This approach identified 7,086, 5,103 and 4,082 differentially dependent genes in gastrointestinal, COAD/READ and ESCA organoids, respectively (Fisher’s exact test, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value &lt; 0.05; Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">7</xref>).</p><p id="Par31">Annotation by genetic constraint showed a distribution across cancer types, in contrast to essential genes (enriched for high constraint) and non-essential genes (enriched for low constraint) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4e</xref>). However, within these differential dependencies, genes with higher genetic constraint tended towards stronger fitness effects (lower mean LFC), as illustrated in gastrointestinal organoids (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4f</xref>). These observations reveal a broad landscape of differential gene dependencies in organoids and constrained genes tend to show greater dependency penetrance across organoids.</p><p id="Par32">To gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of these differential dependencies, we used linear regression models to link gene fitness effects with our curated genomic, patient and clinical features. From this analysis, we identified 1,841 significant gene–biomarker associations (based on false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted <italic>P</italic> values and effect size; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9d</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">8</xref>), distributed across categories of genetic constraint (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4f</xref>, labelled A, B or C depending on strength of statistical association). In COAD/READ, we observed dependency on <italic>WRN</italic> associated with a <italic>RNF43</italic> mutation (effect size = −0.747, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.01), <italic>RPL22</italic> or <italic>SETD1B</italic> mutations (effect size = −0.641, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.027) and mutational signature SBS44 (effect size = −0.823, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.0009), consistent with MSI status due to deficient DNA mismatch repair (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9e</xref>) and showcasing the value of integrating multi-omics biomarkers. Notably, four MSI organoids were not <italic>WRN</italic>-dependent, and lacked expanded TA dinucleotide repeats associated with deficient DNA mismatch repair and underlying <italic>WRN</italic> dependency and inhibitor sensitivity<sup><xref rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr">49</xref></sup>, showing the utility of a large biobank to sub-stratify responses.</p><p id="Par33">We also identified MDM2 dependency for <italic>TP53</italic>-wild-type (effect size = 0.463, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.001) and unexpectedly for <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>G12D</italic></sup> COAD/READ organoids (effect size = −0.576, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.01), of which 4 out of 5 were <italic>TP53</italic>-wild-type. <italic>HRAS</italic> gain-of-function events (effect size = −0.829, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.0019) partially mirrored <italic>MDM2</italic> gain-of-function events (effect size = −0.566, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 0.0039), and all of them correlating with sensitivity to nutlin-3a (an MDM2 inhibitor, PCC = 0.49) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9f</xref>). For ESCA, <italic>CCNE1</italic> amplification, which occurs in 7% of patients<sup><xref rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr">50</xref></sup>, was associated with dependency on CCNE1 (effect size = −0.645, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 3.65 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9g</xref>). Across gastrointestinal organoids, <italic>INTS6L</italic> expression correlates with <italic>INTS6</italic> dependency (effect size = 2.229, adjusted <italic>P</italic> value = 5.28 × 10<sup>−15</sup>) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9h</xref>), as previously described in cell lines<sup><xref rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr">51</xref></sup>. This rich landscape of dependency–biomarker associations illustrates the value of integrating genomic, transcriptomic and clinical features, and highlights novel hypotheses for functional investigation. Some biomarker-linked differential dependencies map to genes under low genetic constraint (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4f</xref>), which may render them suitable candidate therapeutic targets.</p></sec><sec id="Sec9" disp-level="1"><title>EGFR dependency varies by <italic>KRAS</italic> allele</title><p id="Par34">The EGFR–RAS–MAPK signalling pathway is frequently dysregulated in COAD/READ and is targeted by US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved inhibitors of EGFR and KRAS, with an expanding pipeline of RAS agents in development that differ in variant allele specificity, isoform selectivity and mechanism of action<sup><xref rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr">52</xref></sup>. Yet responses remain variable, highlighting the need to define the biological contexts in which specific KRAS inhibitors will confer the greatest therapeutic benefit. Our biobank provides a platform to tackle these questions. In our cohort of 85 COAD/READ organoids with CRISPR data, dependency on this pathway was heterogeneous. <italic>KRAS</italic>-mutant organoids had significantly greater dependency on KRAS than <italic>KRAS</italic> wild-type organoids, whereas <italic>KRAS</italic> wild-type models had greater dependency on EGFR and PTPN11, influenced by alterations in other pathway components such as BRAF (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a</xref>). Notably, KRAS dependency varied by allele, with G12X variant organoids (in which X denotes any amino acid substition) having the greatest dependency (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a</xref>). Compared with other <italic>KRAS</italic>-mutant organoids, G12X models also showed increased EGFR and PTPN11 dependency.</p><fig id="Fig5" position="float"><?disp-level 2?><label>Fig. 5</label><caption><title>EGFR–RAS–MAPK pathway and pre- and post-treatment specific dependencies.</title><p><bold>a</bold>, CRISPR–Cas9 gene knockout dependency values (LFCs) for <italic>KRAS</italic>, <italic>EGFR</italic> and <italic>PTPN11</italic> for COAD/READ (<italic>n</italic> = 85) organoids. Given the diversity of the cohort, we tested pan-RAS, KRAS-specific and variant-specific inhibitors, as well as an EGFR inhibitor and a dual EGFR–ERBB2 inhibitor. All organoids were highly sensitive to the pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors RMC-6236 (mean half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC<sub>50</sub>) = 0.042 μM) and RMC-7977 (mean IC<sub>50</sub> = 0.023 μM) (PCC = 0.89 for organoid IC<sub>50</sub> values; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10b</xref>). By contrast, the activities of the pan-KRAS(OFF) inhibitor BI-2865 and the KRAS degrader ACBI3 were similar, but showed overall lower potency (mean IC<sub>50</sub> ≥ 10 μM for both; PCC = 0.86 for organoid IC<sub>50</sub> values; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10c</xref>). The G12C allele-specific inhibitor sotorasib selectively targeted <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>G12C</italic></sup> organoids (<italic>P</italic> value = 0.044; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10d</xref>), whereas MRTX1133 (G12D allele-selective) inhibited G12D but also affected non-G12D organoids (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10e</xref>). Overall, we observe variable sensitivity to RAS inhibitors with different modes of action.</p><fig id="Fig15" position="float"><?disp-level 2?><label>Extended Data Fig. 10</label><caption><title>CRISPR-Cas9 and drug sensitivity data.</title><p><bold>a</bold>. Error bars in panels f and g represent the mean ± standard deviation of three technical replicates; experiments were performed in biological duplicates.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" id="d33e3613" xlink:href="41586_2026_10830_Fig15_ESM.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/60aa/13581617/c724cbb0a019/41586_2026_10830_Fig15_ESM.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 959?><?original-width 1600?><?scaled-height 959?><?scaled-width 1600?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="41586_2026_10830_Fig15_ESM.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/60aa/13581617/684ca778905e/41586_2026_10830_Fig15_ESM.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig><p id="Par36">Organoids with high CRISPR-derived EGFR dependency were amongst the most sensitive to the EGFR inhibitors afatinib and gefitinib. Notably, <italic>KRAS</italic> wild-type and <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>G12X</italic></sup> organoids had greater sensitivity compared to <italic>KRAS</italic> non-G12 variants (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5b</xref>). Upon combined EGFR and KRAS inhibition, only a subset of <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>G12X</italic></sup>-mutant organoids exhibited pronounced loss of viability (combined maximal effect (<italic>E</italic><sub>max</sub>) &gt; 85%) and synergy (Bliss &gt; 0.25), including when using the pan-KRAS(OFF) inhibitor BI-2865 (Syn/Eff in Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10a,f</xref>), in part owing to potent monotherapy activities. Finally, a <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>Q61H</italic></sup> variant organoid was unresponsive to EGFR inhibition by either CRISPR or small molecules (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5b</xref>). We further confirmed this by showing that EGF withdrawal from the culture medium did not reduce viability in Q61H organoids, unlike in G12X or wild-type organoids (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5c</xref>). Collectively, the biobank and dependency map yield clinically relevant functional insights into the EGFR–KRAS–MAPK pathway, revealing substantial heterogeneity in responses to RAS and EGFR inhibition and showing that EGFR dependency varies across organoids with distinct <italic>KRAS</italic> variant alleles<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec10" disp-level="1"><title>Dependencies in patient-matched organoids</title><p id="Par37">Derivation and interrogation of patient-matched samples pre- and post-treatment can inform on tumour evolution, mechanisms of resistance and approaches to target treatment-refractory cells. Patients with ESCA have a poor prognosis and few treatment options, particularly in advanced disease. We therefore compared the CRISPR–Cas9 dependency profiles for paired ESCA organoids from a 69-year-old man with stage III disease derived from a laparoscopic biopsy (HCM-SANG-0299-C15) before chemotherapy (epirubicin plus capecitabine plus cisplatin) and following surgical resection at the time of relapse (HCM-SANG-0299-C15-B). Both organoids retained a <italic>KRAS</italic> amplification, whereas a <italic>MYC</italic> amplification in the pre-treatment was absent in the post-treatment organoid (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">3b</xref>), implying clonal evolution under the selective pressure of chemotherapy. Although the overall dependency profiles of the matched organoids were similar, MYC dependency was reduced in the post-treatment organoid, consistent with loss of <italic>MYC</italic> amplification (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5d</xref>).</p><p id="Par38">Curation of differential dependencies post-treatment identified several druggable targets, including a reduced dependency on KRAS and DNMT1 and increased dependency on the proteasome core subunit PSMB5 (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5d</xref>), which we validated experimentally. The post-treatment organoid had reduced sensitivity to two pan-RAS inhibitors (RMC-6236 and RMC-7977) and two DNMT1 inhibitors (5-azacytidine and decitabine), and increased sensitivity to two proteosome inhibitors (bortezomib and ixazomib), consistent with predictions from CRISPR experiments (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5e</xref>). There was no difference in <italic>TOP2A</italic> dependency (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5d</xref>) or sensitivity to the TOP2A inhibitor etoposide in the matched samples (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10g</xref>), indicating that differential effects are likely to be target-specific. The organoid derived from the pre-treatment sample also exhibited increased sensitivity to epirubicin and cisplatin versus the post-treatment sample, aligning with clinical relapse (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10g</xref>). Our biobank captured the functional impact of treatment driven tumour evolution, selecting for cancer driver events and conferring differential dependencies that can be unmasked through CRISPR screening and that are candidates for drug repositioning.</p></sec><sec id="Sec11" disp-level="1"><title>Discussion</title><p id="Par39">Reductionist models are central to cancer biology and drug discovery. However, cancer heterogeneity strongly influences prognosis and treatment response, creating a need for larger, more representative model collections to advance precision medicine. Our comprehensive, highly annotated biobank complements 2D cell lines and is designed to catalyse discovery. To maximize access, models are deposited in public repositories and datasets are available via the Cell Model Passport<sup><xref rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr">40</xref></sup> and DepMap Miner (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://dataminer.depmap.sanger.ac.uk/" ext-link-type="uri">https://dataminer.depmap.sanger.ac.uk/</ext-link>) portals.</p><p id="Par40">This study is distinctive for the number of highly annotated organoids and the open availability of detailed genomic, patient and clinical data for each organoid<sup><xref rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr">10</xref></sup>. Future biobanking would benefit from deeper tumour annotation, including histology, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and matched stromal and immune cultures<sup><xref rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr">54</xref></sup>. We used tissue-specific, standardized conditions to generate a molecularly diverse biobank and enable cross-model comparisons. Tailored culture conditions may enrich specific molecular subtypes and alter gene dependencies<sup><xref rid="CR55" ref-type="bibr">55</xref></sup>, and xenotransplantation provides an in vivo context to assess microenvironmental effects.</p><p id="Par41">Genome-wide CRISPR screens in tumour organoids are rare<sup><xref rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr">42</xref>,<xref rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr">56</xref></sup>, yet we map dependencies across a diverse biobank and achieved cell line-level quality despite the added complexity of 3D culture. Distinguishing cancer-selective dependencies from core fitness genes may inform therapeutic index, although matched normal cells are rarely available. To strengthen interpretation, we integrated population-scale genetic constraint data<sup><xref rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr">48</xref></sup>, providing orthogonal support for core fitness genes and indirect evidence of target tolerability.</p><p id="Par42">Our organoid dependency map identified novel and clinically relevant vulnerabilities. We found allele-specific differences in KRAS and EGFR dependencies, with <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>G12X</italic></sup> variants showing greater reliance on KRAS and upstream EGFR signalling. This supports a model<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref>,<xref rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr">57</xref></sup> in which G12X tumours remain responsive to upstream receptor activation, unlike signalling-independent Q61X variants, with therapeutic implications for targeting <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>G12X</italic></sup> cancers, and has been proposed to underlie the enrichment of <italic>KRAS</italic><sup><italic>Q61X</italic></sup> mutations as secondary resistance events to EGFR inhibitors in colorectal cancer. Additionally, by generating and dependency mapping patient-matched organoids before and after treatment, we traced tumour evolution under therapeutic pressure and uncovered new hypotheses for intervention in treatment-refractory ESCA. In summary, we provide a preview of a cancer dependency map across a diverse cohort of highly annotated organoid cultures, with potential to enhance and extend existing efforts as a tool for discovery.</p><p id="Par43">Large-scale sequencing efforts<sup><xref rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr">58</xref>,<xref rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr">59</xref></sup> defined tumour mutational landscapes and transformed understanding of cancer biology. A next frontier in precision oncology is to move beyond descriptive genomics towards multi-scale, integrative functional maps that enable mechanistic modelling of disease, including virtual cell frameworks<sup><xref rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr">60</xref>,<xref rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr">61</xref></sup>. This will require systematic modelling and perturbation across representative tumour cohorts integrated with patient data. Our organoid biobank and dependency map mark a major step towards building functionally informed maps of human cancer.</p></sec><sec id="Sec12" disp-level="1"><title>Methods</title><sec id="Sec13" disp-level="2"><title>Ethical approval and sample collection</title><p id="Par44">All necessary ethical approvals to conduct this work and to ensure that the derived organoids could be used for academic and commercial purposes were obtained from each participating clinical site for the collection of patient samples as well as for the Wellcome Sanger Institute for organoid derivation (IRAS ID:203519; REC 16/LO/1110). Further details are provided in <xref rid="MOESM1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Supplementary Information</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec14" disp-level="2"><title>Availability of Organoid Biobank</title><p id="Par45">Organoids have ethical approval for use in academic and commercial purposes. Models are being distributed by American Type Tissue Culture (ATCC) as part of the HCMI collection (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.atcc.org/hcmi" ext-link-type="uri">https://www.atcc.org/hcmi</ext-link>) and EMD Millipore. Repository details and model availability are provided in Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">2</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec15" disp-level="2"><title>Organoid derivation</title><p id="Par46">Detailed protocols for organoid derivation, cryopreservation and routine culturing are published on protocols.io and include embedded demonstration videos and workflow diagrams<sup><xref rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr">62</xref>–<xref rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr">64</xref></sup>. Tumour samples were washed 3 times with PBS, minced, and either cryopreserved after centrifugation (800<italic>g</italic>, 2 min)<sup><xref rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr">63</xref></sup> or enzymatically digested for 1–2 h at 37 °C. The suspension was filtered (100 μm), centrifuged and washed to remove debris and digestion buffer<sup><xref rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr">62</xref></sup>. Isolated cells were embedded in approximately 15 μl droplets of extracellular matrix (80:20 basement membrane extract (BME):medium; 6.4–9.6 mg ml<sup>−1</sup> protein; Cultrex BME Type 2 Select 3532-001-02) and plated in pre-warmed 6-well plates following established protocols<sup><xref rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr">64</xref></sup>. After polymerization (15–20 min, 37 °C), 2 ml of organoid medium prepared using established recipes<sup><xref rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>,<xref rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr">65</xref>–<xref rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr">67</xref></sup> was added, supplemented with antibiotics and 1 μl ml<sup>−1</sup> ROCK inhibitor (Y-27632, Staratech Scientific S1049-SEL-5mg).</p><p id="Par47">After expansion to ≥25 million cells, 25 cryovials were banked and pellets collected for sequencing. Post-thaw viability was confirmed by re-culturing for four passages with freeze–thaw quality control assessment.</p></sec><sec id="Sec16" disp-level="2"><title>Organoid culture</title><p id="Par48">Organoids were maintained either in 80% BME-2 droplets or in 5% BME-2 suspension culture<sup><xref rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref></sup>. In the 80% BME-2 culture, organoids were cultured as described above. For the 5% suspension method, cancer organoids were suspended in a medium/extracellular matrix (ECM) dilution. For example, combining 10 ml of medium with 500 μl of BME-2 achieved the desired concentration, and organoids were then cultured in ultra-low-adherent flasks or plates.</p><p id="Par49">For passaging, the medium, cells and ECM were collected and centrifuged at 800<italic>g</italic> for 2 min. After discarding the supernatant, organoids were dissociated using TrypLE (Gibco 12604013), an enzymatic reagent. The suspension was incubated for 10–60 min, allowing dissociation into small clumps. The cells were then pelleted and replated as described<sup><xref rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr">64</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec17" disp-level="2"><title>Model identifiers</title><p id="Par50">All models presented in this study have a sanger_ID starting with ‘WTSI’, corresponding to the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute. Additionally, if a model is shared with the HCMI, it also has an HCMI ID starting with ‘HCM’. When both IDs are available, the HCMI nomenclature is used as the sample_ID. The equivalences are shown in Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">2</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec18" disp-level="2"><title>Whole-genome sequencing and analysis</title><sec id="Sec19" disp-level="3"><title>Sequencing and alignment</title><p id="Par51">DNA extracted from snap-frozen tumour tissues, snap-frozen organoid cell pellets, blood or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded normal tissues samples were prepared for WGS. Whole genome paired-end sequencing reads (150 bp) were generated using the Illumina HiSeq X Ten platform with an average coverage of 38×, comparable to coverage used for PCAWG. Reads were aligned using the BWA-MEM (v0.7.17) tool<sup><xref rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr">68</xref></sup>. PCR duplicates, unmapped and non-uniquely mapped reads were filtered out before downstream analysis.</p></sec><sec id="Sec20" disp-level="3"><title>SNV and indel calling</title><p id="Par52">Somatic SNVs and short indels were identified using cgpCaVEMan<sup><xref rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr">69</xref></sup> and cgpPindel<sup><xref rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr">70</xref></sup>, respectively. Germline variants and artefacts were filtered using matched normal samples and a panel of normals, with further post-processing using cgpCaVEManPostProcessing (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/cancerit" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/cancerit</ext-link>). Variant allele frequencies (VAFs) were estimated using vafCorrect (v2.4.0)<sup><xref rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr">71</xref></sup>, and variants with VAF &gt; 0.05 were retained. Further details in <xref rid="MOESM1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Supplementary Information</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec21" disp-level="3"><title>Structural variant and copy number calling</title><p id="Par53">Copy number and allele-specific information were derived using AMBER (v3.5)<sup><xref rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr">72</xref></sup> and COBALT (v1.11)<sup><xref rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr">72</xref></sup>. Somatic and germline SNVs and indels were identified using SAGE (v2.8) and SnpEff (v5.0)<sup><xref rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr">73</xref></sup>. Somatic SVs were called using GRIDSS2 (v2.12.0)<sup><xref rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr">74</xref></sup>, annotated with RepeatMasker (v4.1.2)<sup><xref rid="CR75" ref-type="bibr">75</xref></sup> and kraken2 (v2.1.2)<sup><xref rid="CR76" ref-type="bibr">76</xref></sup>, and filtered with GRIPSS (v1.9)<sup><xref rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr">77</xref></sup>. Subsequently, this information was integrated to calculate the microsatellite status, tumour purity, ploidy, WGD and SCNAs using PURPLE (v2.54)<sup><xref rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr">72</xref></sup>. SCNAs were converted into discrete copy number states. SAGE, GRIPSS, AMBER, COBALT and PURPLE were developed by the Hartwig Medical Foundation (HMF) (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools</ext-link>). Further details in <xref rid="MOESM1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Supplementary Information</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec22" disp-level="3"><title>Cancer driver event annotation</title><p id="Par54">We compiled a list of 783 cancer driver genes, derived as the union of two complementary gene sets from the IntOGen<sup><xref rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr">78</xref></sup> and COSMIC<sup><xref rid="CR79" ref-type="bibr">79</xref></sup> databases, as previously reported<sup><xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup>. Each gene was annotated by its mechanism of action as either activating (Act, for oncogenes), loss-of-function (LoF, for tumour suppressor genes), ambiguous (with evidence of both mechanisms), or fusion. The complete list of cancer driver genes is in <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk/downloads" ext-link-type="uri">https://cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk/downloads</ext-link>.</p><p id="Par55">We collated individual putative cancer driver mutations (for example, frameshift, nonsense, stop-lost, exonic splicing silencer, missense or in-frame mutations) among SNVs and indels within these cancer driver genes from four data sources: IntOGen (including Cancer Genome Interpreter and BoostDM)<sup><xref rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr">78</xref></sup>, MSKCC<sup><xref rid="CR80" ref-type="bibr">80</xref></sup>, and cancer predisposition variants, that were identified by overlap with a reference set of pathogenic germline variants with matching effect<sup><xref rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr">81</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec23" disp-level="3"><title>Loss of heterozygosity</title><p id="Par56">We considered a tumour suppressor gene or an ambiguous gene to have loss of heterozygosity if the DNA copy number (CN) of the minor allele was &lt;0.5 and the difference between the round ploidy and the round total CN was &gt;0 (there was no amplification in the non-mutated allele) or if the VAF of a loss-of-function mutation was &gt;0.85.</p></sec><sec id="Sec24" disp-level="3"><title>Biallelic alterations</title><p id="Par57">Biallelic alterations included all cases with loss of heterozygosity, as well as homozygous deletions, SV disruptions or instances where each allele was affected by a different loss-of-function mutation.</p></sec><sec id="Sec25" disp-level="3"><title>Multiplicity, CCF and clonal mutations</title><p id="Par58">SNVs were intersected with segment SCNAs using the GRanges and findOverlaps functions from the GenomicRanges R package (v1.56.1) to obtain information on the major allele, minor allele, and total tumour CN for each SNV, along with the VAF and tumour purity. The multiplicity (the number of chromosomal copies harbouring a given mutation) and CCF (the proportion of cancer cells carrying a specific mutation within a tumour sample) were then calculated according to the formulas in Steele et al.<sup><xref rid="CR82" ref-type="bibr">82</xref></sup> and Dentro et al.<sup><xref rid="CR83" ref-type="bibr">83</xref></sup>. Clonal mutations, defined as genetic alterations present in all cancer cells within a tumour, were identified as those with a CCF &gt; 0.75.</p></sec><sec id="Sec26" disp-level="3"><title>CN correlation between paired organoids and tumours</title><p id="Par59">SCNA segment data was divided into 100 kb bins across the genome, and the CN for each segment was calculated as the mean CN of all positions within the 100,000 bp window. Positions listed in the ENCODE blacklist<sup><xref rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr">84</xref></sup> (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/Boyle-Lab/Blacklist" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/Boyle-Lab/Blacklist</ext-link>) were excluded from this analysis. Pearson correlations were then computed using the mean CN for each segment between paired organoid and tumour samples.</p></sec><sec id="Sec27" disp-level="3"><title>Focal amplifications</title><p id="Par60">Focal amplifications were defined as the presence of at least two genomic segments, each exceeding 100 kb in size, with a log<sub>2</sub>(CN/ploidy) value &gt; 6.</p></sec><sec id="Sec28" disp-level="3"><title>Signature analysis</title><p id="Par61">Mutational signatures were extracted using SigProfilerExtractor (v1.2.2)<sup><xref rid="CR85" ref-type="bibr">85</xref></sup> for the tumour and organoid samples from each tumour type separately. COAD/READ-MSI samples were analysed separately from COAD/READ-MSS samples. STAD samples were not analysed due to insufficient sample size. The resulting matrix file was used as an input for SigprofilerAssignment (v0.2.5)<sup><xref rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr">30</xref></sup> to assign known COSMIC v3.4 signatures within single base substitution (SBS). De novo signatures were further refitted using the COMICv3.4 and an additional set of novel CRC and MSI specific signatures identified and validated in Mutographs project<sup><xref rid="CR86" ref-type="bibr">86</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par62">For data visualization, COSMIC mutational signatures representing less than 10% of mutations within each sample were categorized as ‘Others’ and excluded from calculations of both the proportion of models with that mutational signature and the proportion of mutations representing each signature by cancer type. SBS5 and SBS40a were collapsed into a single category, based on the hypothesis that these signatures arise from a combination of correlated mutational processes<sup><xref rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr">87</xref>,<xref rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr">88</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec29" disp-level="3"><title>Homologous recombination deficiency</title><p id="Par63">Homologous recombination deficiency was assessed using CHORD (v2.0.3)<sup><xref rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr">34</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec30" disp-level="3"><title>Complex genomic rearrangements</title><p id="Par64">Chromothripsis and other complex genomic rearrangements were detected using ShatterSeek (v1.1)<sup><xref rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr">26</xref></sup>, as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR89" ref-type="bibr">89</xref></sup>.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec31" disp-level="2"><title>RNA-seq and analysis</title><p id="Par65">Paired-end transcriptome reads (75 bp) were quality filtered and mapped to GRCh38 (ensemble build 98) using STAR (v2.5.0c)<sup><xref rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr">90</xref></sup> with a standard set of parameters (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/cancerit/cgpRna" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/cancerit/cgpRna</ext-link>). Resulting bam files were processed to get the per gene read count and transcripts per million (TPM) data using RSEM (v1.3.3)<sup><xref rid="CR91" ref-type="bibr">91</xref></sup>. TPM values were used for the downstream analysis.</p><sec id="Sec32" disp-level="3"><title>CMS/CRIS subtypes</title><p id="Par66">Consensus molecular subtypes (CMS) and colorectal cancer intrinsic subtypes (CRIS) subtypes were inferred for COAD/READ organoids with CMSCaller<sup><xref rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr">36</xref>,<xref rid="CR92" ref-type="bibr">92</xref></sup> using RSEM expected count data.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec33" disp-level="2"><title>CRISPR–Cas9 screening</title><p id="Par67">Detailed protocols including process diagrams and example data for generating Cas9-expressing organoid cultures and CRISPR–Cas9 library transduction in organoid are published on protocols.io<sup><xref rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr">93</xref>,<xref rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr">94</xref></sup>. Stable Cas9-expressing organoids were generated using lentiCas9-Blast (Addgene 52962) with polybrene (8 μg ml<sup>−1</sup>). Following overnight incubation, medium was replaced with complete medium containing Y-27632 (2.5 μM), and blasticidin (Invivogen, ant-bl-1, 10 mg ml<sup>−1</sup>) selection was applied 120 h after transduction. Cas9 activity was measured using a fluorescent reporter assay (Addgene 67982 and 67981)<sup><xref rid="CR95" ref-type="bibr">95</xref></sup>. Only organoid lines with activity of 75% or more were selected for single guide RNA (sgRNA) library transduction.</p><p id="Par68">Two genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 sgRNA libraries were used. The Human CRISPR Library Yusa v.1.1 (ref. <sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref></sup>), containing 100,086 sgRNAs that target 18,009 genes (with 5–10 sgRNAs per gene) and 1,004 non-targeting sgRNAs; and the Minimal Genome-Wide Human CRISPR–Cas9 Library (MinLibCas9, Addgene 164896)<sup><xref rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr">41</xref></sup>, which includes a selected sgRNA primarily drawn from Yusa v1.1 comprising 37,522 sgRNAs that target 18,761 genes (with 2 optimal sgRNAs per gene) and 200 non-targeting sgRNAs (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8a</xref>). Lentiviral volume required for multiplicity of infection of 0.3 was determined by titration, and transduction efficiency assessed by BFP flow cytometry.</p><p id="Par69">A total of 12.5 × 10<sup>8</sup> (Yusa v1.1) or 3.3 × 10<sup>7</sup> (MinLibCas9) cells were transduced in triplicate using the same batch of Cas9-transduced organoids. No significant batch effects were observed across independent batches of Cas9-expressing organoid lines (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8b</xref>). Cells were infected with the lentiviral-packaged whole-genome sgRNA library (for 100× coverage), in medium containing polybrene (8 μg ml<sup>−1</sup>), and Y-27632 (2.5 μM). Following overnight incubation, cells were plated in fresh medium in a 5% suspension. Transduction efficiency (target of 30%) was confirmed on day 6. Screens were maintained under puromycin selection (Invivogen, ant-pr-1, 10 mg ml<sup>−1</sup>) for a further 16 days (21 days in screen in total). A final selection efficiency of at least 60% was required for the screen to pass. At the end of the screen approximately 2.5 × 10<sup>7</sup> cells were collected, pelleted, and stored at −80 °C for downstream processing.</p></sec><sec id="Sec34" disp-level="2"><title>CRISPR screen data processing</title><p id="Par70">CRISPR screens performed using the Yusa v1.1 (ref. <sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref></sup>) and MinLibCas9 (ref. <sup><xref rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr">41</xref></sup>) libraries were harmonized by restricting analyses to shared sgRNAs, enabling integrated downstream processing. Quality control procedures, adapted from established cell line screening pipelines<sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref></sup>, were applied to assess replicate concordance, sgRNA representation and classifier performance in distinguishing essential from non-essential genes. Low-quality replicates and organoids failing predefined quality control criteria were excluded prior to further analysis. Read counts were normalized and corrected for copy-number effects using CRISPRcleanR (v3.0.1)<sup><xref rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr">96</xref></sup>, followed by batch correction across libraries<sup><xref rid="CR97" ref-type="bibr">97</xref></sup>. Gene-level fitness effects were estimated using BAGEL (v2)<sup><xref rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr">45</xref></sup> with curated reference gene sets, and LFC values were scaled relative to essential and non-essential controls to facilitate cross-organoid comparability. Full details of sgRNA selection, quality control thresholds, normalization, batch correction, statistical procedures and final selection of models are provided in the <xref rid="MOESM1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Supplementary Information</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec35" disp-level="2"><title>CRISPR screen processed data analysis</title><sec id="Sec36" disp-level="3"><title>Analysis of organoid core fitness genes</title><p id="Par71">We applied ADaM implemented in the CoRe R package (v1.0.0) (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/DepMap-Analytics/CoRe" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/DepMap-Analytics/CoRe</ext-link>)<sup><xref rid="CR98" ref-type="bibr">98</xref></sup> using the same curated reference essential gene set as previously mentioned<sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref></sup> to calculate false-positive rates. This analysis identified 751 core essential genes (Supplementary table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">4</xref>). Although we used all organoids together as input, only three cancer types were included (PAAD and STAD organoids were excluded), so the resulting core fitness genes do not represent a pan-cancer set.</p><p id="Par72">We compared core fitness genes in organoids with those identified in cell lines<sup><xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref></sup> and observed an overlap of 654 genes, with 97 genes identified as organoid-specific (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9</xref>). We performed a Fisher’s exact test on these organoid-specific core fitness genes to perform pathway enrichment analysis, using Gene Ontology Biological Processes, KEGG pathways<sup><xref rid="CR99" ref-type="bibr">99</xref></sup> and Hallmarks<sup><xref rid="CR100" ref-type="bibr">100</xref></sup> obtained from the msigdbr R package (v7.5.1)<sup><xref rid="CR101" ref-type="bibr">101</xref></sup>. For this analysis, PanCancer common essential genes identified using the AUC method were excluded<sup><xref rid="CR98" ref-type="bibr">98</xref></sup>. For visualization, when multiple pathways shared the same set of organoid-specific core fitness genes, only the pathway with the most significant <italic>P</italic> value was displayed.</p></sec><sec id="Sec37" disp-level="3"><title>Differential dependency analysis in all gastrointestinal, COAD/READ and ESCA organoids</title><p id="Par73">We conducted an analysis to identify genes with the greatest dependency variability across organoids within each cancer type and to highlight context-specific dependencies. The analysis proceeded as follows:</p><list list-type="order"><list-item><p id="Par74">Gene filtering based on consistent depletion/non-depletion. Using binary dependency matrices generated by BAGEL2 for each cancer type, we excluded genes that were only considered depleted in a single organoid and not depleted in only one organoid.</p></list-item><list-item><p id="Par75">Exclusion of core fitness and control genes. Genes previously classified as pan-cancer core fitness genes in cell line datasets, the 751 organoid-specific core fitness genes identified in this study, as well as control sets of essential and non-essential genes, were removed to ensure a focus on genes with differential dependency profiles.</p></list-item><list-item><p id="Par76">Expression thresholding. Genes with a mean expression level of log<sub>2</sub>(TPM + 1) &lt; 0.1 in each cancer type (considered ‘not expressed’) were also excluded from the analysis.</p></list-item></list><p id="Par77">Following these filtering steps, for each remaining gene, we calculated the difference in LFCs (delta LFC) between organoids where the gene was depleted and those where it was not and tested the statistical significance with a Fisher’s exact test. Only genes with a FDR-adjusted <italic>P</italic> value &lt; 0.05 were considered differentially dependent (7,086 for gastrointestinal, 5,103 for COAD/READ and 4,082 for ESCA; Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="supplementary-material">7</xref>).</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec38" disp-level="2"><title>Biomarker analysis</title><p id="Par78">To identify molecular and clinical features associated with context-specific gene dependencies, we performed a systematic biomarker analysis across gastrointestinal, COAD/READ and ESCA organoids. Candidate dependencies were selected from the differential dependency analysis based on recurrence criteria and evaluated against a curated set of genomic, transcriptomic and clinical features, including driver mutations and specific variants, copy number alterations, structural events, mutational signatures, gene expression, pathway activity scores, and composite loss- and gain-of-function events. Associations between gene fitness effects and features were tested using linear regression models incorporating relevant technical and biological covariates, with significance assessed using likelihood-ratio tests and multiple testing correction. Significant associations were prioritized based on adjusted <italic>P</italic> value and effect size and classified into tiers reflecting strength of association. Full details of feature selection, model specification, statistical thresholds and classification criteria are provided in the <xref rid="MOESM1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Supplementary Information</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec39" disp-level="2"><title>High-throughput drug screens</title><p id="Par79">For high-throughput screening, organoids were dissociated into single cells, counted and seeded in 5% BME-2 suspension cultures at model-specific optimized densities. After 96 h to allow organoid re-formation, assay plates were prepared with a 50% BME-2:organoid medium base layer, and organoids were transferred into 384-well plates using Multidrop Combi (Thermo Scientific) dispensers. Twenty-four hours later, compounds were dispensed using an Echo555 (Labcyte), and cells were treated for 72 h. Viability was measured using CellTiter-Glo 2.0 (Promega).</p><p id="Par80">Two independent high-throughput screening projects were conducted. The first project used a full 7 × 7 concentration matrix (49 measurements) for each drug combination, and the second used a reduced 25 measurement concentration matrix encompassing the same concentration range. Compounds were tested in biological duplicates in the first project and single replicates in the second project, with higher technical replication for agents included in multiple combinations like afatinib (also tested as monotherapies).</p><p id="Par81">Raw viability data were analysed independently for each project. Data were normalized per plate using negative (untreated, DMSO) and positive (MG-132, staurosporine, blank) controls. Dose-response curves were fitted using a non-linear mixed-effects model to estimate IC<sub>50</sub> and AUC values using the gdscIC50 R package (v1.7.3)<sup><xref rid="CR102" ref-type="bibr">102</xref></sup>. For combination treatments, the maximum combination effect (combo_MaxE) was defined as the second-highest measured inhibition. Bliss excess was calculated as the difference between observed combination inhibition and the predicted Bliss additivity of the corresponding monotherapies. The results presented are the mean values across both projects.</p></sec><sec id="Sec40" disp-level="2"><title>Validation drug sensitivity testing</title><p id="Par82">For validation drug sensitivity testing, organoids were dissociated into single cells, resuspended in organoid medium, and seeded into 96-well plates over a 50% BME-2:organoid medium base layer (2,000–5,000 cells per well, depending on the model). For monotherapy treatments, nine drug concentrations spanning a 256-fold range were added four days after plating, in technical triplicates. For combination treatments, five concentrations of KRAS inhibitors (sotorasib or MRTX1133) across a 256-fold range were tested with two fixed concentrations of EGFR and ERBB2 inhibitors (afatinib and gefitinib), also in triplicate. Viability was quantified using CellTiter-Glo 2.0 at 72 h post-treatment for monotherapies and at 0, 3, 6 and 9 days for combinations. Dose-response curves were fitted using GraphPad Prism, with three technical and two biological replicates per condition.</p></sec><sec id="Sec41" disp-level="2"><title>EGF depletion from the medium</title><p id="Par83">Organoids were dissociated into single cells, resuspended in organoid culture medium either supplemented with or deprived of EGF, and seeded into 96-well plates over a 50:50 medium-to-ECM layer. The bottom ECM-containing layer was prepared with the same EGF condition as the overlaid medium. Cell viability was quantified using CellTiter-Glo 2.0 seven days after seeding.</p></sec><sec id="Sec42" disp-level="2"><title>Reporting summary</title><p id="Par84">Further information on research design is available in the <xref rid="MOESM2" ref-type="supplementary-material">Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary</xref> linked to this article.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec43" disp-level="1"><title>Online content</title><p id="Par85">Any methods, additional references, Nature Portfolio reporting summaries, source data, extended data, supplementary information, acknowledgements, peer review information; details of author contributions and competing interests; and statements of data and code availability are available at <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="10.1038/s41586-026-10830-y" ext-link-type="doi">https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10830-y</ext-link>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec45" disp-level="1"><title>Supplementary information</title>
