To view a copy of this licence, visit <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/">http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/</ext-link>.</license-p></license></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pmc-pdf" xlink:href="41586_2026_Article_10843.pdf"><?pdf-name 41586_2026_Article_10843.pdf?><?pdf-size 34725285?><?pdf-md5 fd71a5e47255a27b7dcc14934c1ca616?><?pdf-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?pdf-cloudpmc-urn urn:app:6170/13581591/fd71a5e47255/41586_2026_Article_10843.pdf?></self-uri><abstract id="Abs1"><p id="Par1">Despite advances in precision oncology, effective personalized treatments are still lacking for most patients with cancer<sup><xref rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr">1</xref></sup>. The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) accelerates this field by systematically identifying cancer vulnerabilities in diverse preclinical models. Data from over 1,300 cell lines have led to the discovery of new therapeutic strategies across multiple tumour types<sup><xref rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr">2</xref></sup>. However, mapping cancer vulnerabilities using traditional cell lines has limitations, including insufficient cancer subtype representation and the impact of culture conditions on perturbation responses. Here we perform 147 genome-scale CRISPR screens and multi-omic characterizations of next-generation (NextGen) cancer models (organoids and spheroids) across 10 cancer types. This strategy enables the expansion of DepMap to cover new genomic and molecular subtypes and to identify new biomarker-associated vulnerabilities. These new models also preserve transcriptional programs that are silenced in traditional cell lines and facilitate the discovery of specific gene dependencies associated with these programs. Comparisons of traditional and NextGen cancer models enable further identification of distinct effects of growth format and culture medium on gene essentiality. The integrated dataset combines data from both model types to offer a valuable, expansive resource for exploring cancer vulnerabilities and is accessible via the DepMap portal.</p></abstract><abstract id="Abs2" abstract-type="web-summary"><p id="Par2">Integration of genome-scale CRISPR screening data from traditional cell lines and next-generation cancer models expands the representation of tumour subtypes and genomic alterations in The Cancer Dependency Map.</p></abstract><kwd-group kwd-group-type="npg-subject"><title>Subject terms</title><kwd>Cancer genomics</kwd><kwd>Cancer models</kwd></kwd-group><custom-meta-group><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-qastatus</meta-name><meta-value>0</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-live</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-embargo</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-released</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-open-access</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-olf</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-manuscript</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-legally-suppressed</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-pdf</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-supplement</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-pdf-only</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-suppress-copyright</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-real-version</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-scanned-article</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-preprint</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-in-epmc</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-license-ref</meta-name><meta-value>CC BY-NC-ND</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>issue-copyright-statement</meta-name><meta-value>© Springer Nature Limited 2026</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta></front><body><sec id="Sec1"><title>Main</title><p id="Par3">Advances in understanding cancer genomes have led to mutation-tailored therapies that have improved outcomes in cancers such as chronic myeloid leukaemia and melanoma<sup><xref rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref></sup>. However, despite this progress, most patients still lack targeted treatments customized to the molecular makeup of their tumours. DepMap has accelerated personalized cancer medicine by identifying therapeutic targets through genomic profiling and functional screening of cancer models<sup><xref rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>,<xref rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr">4</xref></sup>. Having profiled over 1,300 models, DepMap has uncovered multiple targets that have advanced to clinical trials, but current limitations—including underrepresentation of many cancer subtypes and a reliance on monolayer cultures with serum-containing media—constrain its scope<sup><xref rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr">5</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par4">Three-dimensional (3D) patient-derived models such as organoids and spheroids<sup><xref rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr">6</xref></sup>, termed NextGen models, have emerged as a complement to conventional cell lines. Their specialized culture conditions support the propagation of diverse, underrepresented cancer subtypes and may better recapitulate key features of the tumour microenvironment that are lost in traditional two-dimensional (2D) cultures<sup><xref rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>,<xref rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par5">Here we profile NextGen models via genome-scale CRISPR screens, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), and compare and integrate these data with traditional cell line data. The NextGen models expand tumour subtype coverage in DepMap and preserve tumour-relevant gene expression programs that are silenced in traditional cell lines, which enables the discovery of new biomarker-linked dependencies. A comparison of 2D adherent and 3D organoid models further identifies dependencies shaped by culture environment, a result that highlights the advantages of the integrated traditional and NextGen dataset.</p></sec><sec id="Sec2"><title>Overview of models and data generation</title><p id="Par6">We collected 314 NextGen models comprising 237 carcinoma organoids and 77 central nervous system (CNS) tumour spheroids<sup><xref rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>–<xref rid="CR11" ref-type="bibr">11</xref></sup> (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1a,b</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">1a,b</xref>) and generated WGS and RNA-seq profiles from 291 and 309 models, respectively. WGS confirmed expected recurrent genomic alterations, including the following changes: <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> mutations and chromosome 18q loss in colorectal models; <italic toggle="yes">TERT</italic> promoter mutations in CNS models; and <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> mutations and chromosome 9p loss in pancreas models (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">1a,b</xref>). NextGen models also captured mutations not represented in traditional models, such as <italic toggle="yes">NRAS</italic> in colorectal cancer (4.4% prevalence)<sup><xref rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref></sup> and <italic toggle="yes">ESR1</italic> in breast cancer (7% prevalence)<sup><xref rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref></sup>, and expanded prostate cancer representation with previously underrepresented alterations (<italic toggle="yes">SPOP</italic>,<italic toggle="yes"> RB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CTNNB1</italic>; Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1c,d</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">1a,b</xref>).<fig id="Fig1" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 1</label><caption><title>Multiomics and functional profiling of NextGen cancer models.</title><p><bold>a</bold>, Illustration of NextGen model profiling in DepMap. The combination of multiomic characterization and functional genomic profiling at DepMap is extended to NextGen models. The colour code for individual cancer lineages shown here is used in <bold>b</bold>–<bold>e</bold>. <bold>b</bold>, Lineage composition of the NextGen models profiled for each of the assay types. <bold>c</bold>, Comparison of alteration frequencies per lineage for selected genes across TCGA tumours, NextGen models and traditional cell lines. The intensity of the colour represents the proportion of tumours or models with the indicated genomic alteration. Red frames indicate that values are sourced from publications describing a similar tumour dataset<sup><xref rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>,<xref rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr">58</xref>–<xref rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr">60</xref></sup> but not from the same TCGA dataset<sup><xref rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr">13</xref></sup> used in other parts of this study. <bold>d</bold>, Oncoprint of NextGen models with mutations and CN alterations of driver genes that were not represented in the traditional DepMap models of their respective lineages. <bold>e</bold>, Celligner embedding of gene expression for tumour samples and NextGen cancer models. <bold>f</bold>, Lineage prediction based on nearest neighbour (NN) tumour samples in Celligner. Oeso–stm, oesophagus–stomach. For each of the NextGen and traditional models, the lineages of the 25 nearest neighbour tumour samples (<italic toggle="yes">y</italic> axis) were plotted for each of the annotated lineages of the models (<italic toggle="yes">x</italic> axis). <bold>g</bold>, Distributions of mean dependency log fold changes (naive gene effect) of nonessential (blue) and common essential (maroon) genes. <bold>h</bold>,<bold>i</bold>, Illustration of data integration steps across screens using Chronos (<bold>h</bold>) with a plot of Avana and Humagne data shown for pre-Chronos and post-Chronos processing (<bold>i</bold>). Schematic in <bold>a</bold> created in BioRender; Vazquez, F. <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://biorender.com/fd5u98k" ext-link-type="uri">https://biorender.com/fd5u98k</ext-link> (2026).</p><p><xref rid="MOESM8" ref-type="media">Source data</xref></p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d33e932" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="41586_2026_10843_Fig1_HTML.webp"><?image-name 41586_2026_10843_Fig1_HTML.webp?><?image-size 225466?><?image-md5 e2b189f888784e3823ac033e18cd2d1d?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 1566?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 1566?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/e2b189f88878/41586_2026_10843_Fig1_HTML.webp?><?thumb-name 41586_2026_10843_Fig1_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 16048?><?thumb-md5 92b2199701598f7ff1dbdbedf87085db?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 196?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/92b219970159/41586_2026_10843_Fig1_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par7">We assessed the fidelity of NextGen models in recapitulating tumour transcriptional cell states using Celligner (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1e</xref>), which jointly embeds gene expression data from tumour samples (acquired from TCGA<sup><xref rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr">13</xref></sup>, TARGET and Treehouse (referred to as TCGA-plus) and from MET500<sup><xref rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr">14</xref></sup>; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 13,104) and cancer models<sup><xref rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr">15</xref></sup>. Analyses of 300 NextGen models, 532 traditional cell lines and 266 patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models<sup><xref rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr">16</xref></sup> enabled us to infer the lineage for each model on the basis of 25 nearest neighbour tumour samples.</p><p id="Par8">Celligner-based lineage inference matched annotated lineage for 69% of NextGen models, outperforming PDX models (60%) and traditional cell lines (35%) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1f</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2a,b</xref>). The lower accuracy of traditional cell lines was partly due to their enrichment in an ‘undifferentiated cluster’ associated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and loss of lineage-specific gene expression<sup><xref rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr">15</xref></sup>. In detail, &gt;25% of the traditional models fell into this cluster compared with &lt;2% of NextGen, PDX and tumour samples (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2c</xref>).</p><p id="Par9">NextGen models substantially outperformed traditional cell lines for CNS tumours (93% versus 11%) and oesophagus–stomach tumours (83% versus 24%; Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1f</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2a,b,d</xref>). This result is consistent with previous reports of marked transcriptional divergence between traditional CNS models and corresponding tumours<sup><xref rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>,<xref rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr">17</xref></sup>. Prostate cancer was an exception, for which traditional cell lines (4 out of 7 correct) outperformed NextGen models (0 out of 12; Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1f</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2a,b</xref>). This result probably reflects the derivation of prostate organoids from castration-resistant or neuroendocrine tumours and their known transcriptional heterogeneity<sup><xref rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>,<xref rid="CR18" ref-type="bibr">18</xref></sup>. Pancreas lineage prediction was challenging owing to its proximity to oesophagus–stomach samples in Celligner (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1e</xref>) and the scarcity of pancreas tumour samples. All Celligner data, including 414 additional Human Cell Model Initiative (HCMI) models<sup><xref rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>,<xref rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr">20</xref></sup>, are accessible through the Celligner portal (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://depmap.org/portal/celligner/" ext-link-type="uri">https://depmap.org/portal/celligner/</ext-link>) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2e</xref>).</p><p id="Par10">We performed genome-scale CRISPR screens on 147 NextGen models using the Humagne enAsCas12a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) library<sup><xref rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr">21</xref></sup> (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">3</xref>). Screen quality was comparable between NextGen models and traditional cell lines screened using spCas9 (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1,351) or enAsCas12a (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 36) sgRNA libraries. Moreover, both showed clear separation of non-essential and essential sgRNA score distributions and similar receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and null-normalized mean difference (NNMD) scores (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1g</xref> and Extended Data Fig.<xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig"> 4a,b</xref>).</p><p id="Par11">CNS models were screened as spheroids or on matrix-coated plates (termed ‘coat’ hereafter) and organoids were screened in Matrigel domes or in coat conditions, all in serum-free media (Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="media">1</xref>). Gene expression and essentiality profiles were nearly identical across CNS growth formats (Pearson’s <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.996 and 0.990, respectively), and organoid gene dependencies also strongly agreed between the two conditions (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.984; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">4c–h</xref>). These results suggest that growth format does not significantly affect CRISPR screen outcomes under serum-free conditions. This finding is in contrast to a previous study that used serum-containing media<sup><xref rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr">22</xref></sup>—a discrepancy that may be attributable to differences in medium composition and the comparison strategy used. All models were profiled for WGS, RNA-seq and CRISPR under identical conditions.</p><p id="Par12">To integrate data across models and libraries, we used Chronos<sup><xref rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref></sup>, which corrects for copy number (CN) effects, screen quality and library-specific batch effects (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1h,i</xref>). Because all NextGen models used the Humagne library, library-specific batch effects were confounded with organoid model effects. We therefore pre-trained Chronos on all traditional and NextGen CNS models before applying the pretrained parameters to organoids. The integrated dataset—encompassing WGS, RNA-seq and CRISPR data and growth-format annotations—is available through the DepMap portal (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://DepMap.org/portal" ext-link-type="uri">https://DepMap.org/portal</ext-link>)<sup><xref rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec3"><title>Biomarker-associated dependencies</title><p id="Par13">To identify therapeutic targets in the NextGen CRISPR dataset, we classified genes into five dependency profile classes: non-dependency, weakly selective, strongly selective, high variance and pan-dependency<sup><xref rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr">25</xref></sup> (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5a</xref>). Focusing on the three strong dependency classes, we analysed three representative dependency–biomarker associations—expression addictions, paralogue dependencies and dependencies associated with oncogene gain-of-function (GOF) or tumour suppressor gene (TSG) loss-of-function (LOF)—to identify gene dependencies that were predictable by cellular genetic or molecular features.</p><p id="Par14">Expression addiction, in which gene essentiality correlates with increased levels of its own expression (common for oncogenes and lineage-defining transcription factors<sup><xref rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>,<xref rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>–<xref rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr">27</xref></sup>), was identified for 51 strong dependencies (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &lt; −0.3, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.005). These included 14 oncogenes (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 6.21 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, one-sided Fisher’s exact test) and 21 transcription factors (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 3.09 × 10<sup>−14</sup>; Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2a,b</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM4" ref-type="media">2</xref>). Among these were <italic toggle="yes">HNRNPH1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PROX1</italic>, both implicated in brain tumours<sup><xref rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr">28</xref>,<xref rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr">29</xref></sup> (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5b</xref>). The dependency–expression correlation was stronger for both genes in NextGen models, and both displayed increased expression in brain tumours relative to normal tissue (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5c</xref>). <italic toggle="yes">HNRNPH1</italic> also exhibited elevated expression in biliary tract cancers, as did <italic toggle="yes">PROX1</italic> in colorectal cancers, which may represent tumour-specific vulnerabilities.<fig id="Fig2" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 2</label><caption><title>Biomarker-associated vulnerabilities identified in NextGen models.</title><p><bold>a</bold>–<bold>c</bold>, Expression addiction. Dependency–expression correlation on the same genes was scored (<bold>a</bold>; significance thresholds, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 0.005; two-tailed Pearson’s correlation, <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = –0.3; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 146 (model), 3,786 (gene)). Red label lines indicate that further analysis was carried out. Oncogenes and transcription factor (TF)-encoding genes are enriched in expression addictions (<bold>b</bold>). <italic toggle="yes">HNRNPH1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ESR1</italic> show strong expression addiction in NextGen and traditional models, respectively (<bold>c</bold>). In <bold>c</bold>, <bold>e</bold> and <bold>g</bold>, model lineages are indicated using the colour code in <bold>c</bold>. In <bold>c</bold>, <bold>e</bold> and <bold>h</bold>, regression lines with 95% confidence intervals are displayed. <bold>d</bold>,<bold>e</bold>, Paralogue dependencies were assessed by correlating gene dependency with paralogue expression (<bold>d</bold>; significance thresholds, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 0.005; two-tailed Pearson’s correlation, <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.3; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 146 (model), 3,787 (paralogue pair)). Several points are labelled as dependency gene/paralogue gene. <italic toggle="yes">ENO1</italic> dependency in <italic toggle="yes">ENO2</italic>-low models is more common in NextGen models (<bold>e</bold>). <bold>f</bold>,<bold>g</bold>, Dependencies associated with oncogene GOF or TSG LOF. In <bold>f</bold>, blue points are associations not driven by lineage bias (dark grey, associations driven by lineage bias; light grey, not significant, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> ≥ 0.05 (two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>test) or Δmean dependency ≥ –0.3; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 147). and <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 428 and 169 for altered and unaltered, respectively (traditional). <bold>h</bold>,<bold>i</bold>, <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> CN amplification correlates with enhanced <italic toggle="yes">SCD</italic> dependency (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 9.89 × 10<sup>–4</sup>, two-tailed Pearson’s correlation; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 147) (<bold>h</bold>). <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> CN-amplified oesophagus–stomach organoids show enhanced sensitivity to SCD inhibitors (<bold>i</bold>). <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 6.2 × 10<sup>–6</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P </italic>= 1.7 × 10<sup>–5</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P </italic>= 1.2 × 10<sup>–4</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P </italic>= 2.2 × 10<sup>–4</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P </italic>= 9.5 × 10<sup>–6</sup> for 0.14, 0.41, 1.2, 3.4 and 10 μM, respectively (A939572); <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 4.0 × 10<sup>–6</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P </italic>= 4.4 × 10<sup>–6</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 2.0 × 10<sup>–5</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P </italic>= 6.3 × 10<sup>–5</sup>, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 3.4 × 10<sup>–4</sup> for 0.14, 0.41, 1.2, 3.4 and 10 μM, respectively (CAY-10566). <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> amplified versus neutral; Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2c</xref>). This result is consistent with insufficient <italic toggle="yes">ESR1</italic> expression in breast organoids (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5d</xref>) and previous reports of its progressive loss in organoid culture<sup><xref rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr">30</xref>,<xref rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr">31</xref></sup>. Similarly, <italic toggle="yes">ERBB2</italic> addiction was absent in organoids, with only 3 out of 146 NextGen models expressing <italic toggle="yes">ERBB2</italic> at levels to cause its dependency (log<sub>2</sub>[transcripts per million (TPM) + 1] &gt; 7.5; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5b,d</xref>). These findings indicate that there are differences between NextGen and traditional models in their dependencies on oncogenes.</p><p id="Par16">Paralogue dependencies arise when the loss of a gene increases reliance on its paralogue<sup><xref rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr">26</xref>,<xref rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>,<xref rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr">33</xref></sup>. We evaluated all paralogue pairs with &gt;25% identity and identified 106 strong dependencies linked to reduced paralogue expression (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &gt; 0.3, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.005; Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2d</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM4" ref-type="media">2</xref>). Several were stronger in NextGen models, including <italic toggle="yes">ENO1</italic> dependency linked to low <italic toggle="yes">ENO2</italic> expression, than in traditional models (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.455 versus <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.233, respectively; Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2e</xref>). <italic toggle="yes">ENO2</italic>, a neuron-specific enolase<sup><xref rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr">34</xref></sup>, showed lineage-appropriate expression only in NextGen models (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2e</xref>). Its reduced expression in colorectal and prostate cancers relative to normal tissue (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5c</xref>) suggests that ENO1 inhibition could selectively target these tumours. Previous work has also linked <italic toggle="yes">ENO1</italic> CN deletion to <italic toggle="yes">ENO2</italic> dependency in glioblastoma (GBM)<sup><xref rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr">35</xref></sup>, which indicates that there is mutual paralogue dependency. Conversely, some relationships were weaker in NextGen models. These included <italic toggle="yes">ELMO2</italic> dependency tied to low <italic toggle="yes">ELMO3</italic> expression (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = –0.110 (NextGen) versus <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.545 (traditional); Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5e</xref>), which suggests that there are different requirements for ELMO2-mediated cytoskeletal rearrangement across model types.</p><p id="Par17">To find dependencies related to oncogene GOF and TSG LOF, we analysed 6 oncogenes and 13 TSGs with sufficient NextGen model representation (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> ≥ 5, with at least one hotspot mutation model) and compared dependency scores between altered and unaltered models. After removing associations driven by lineage bias, we identified 83 genetic alteration–dependency pairs with significant dependency enrichment (Δmean dependency &lt; −0.3, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05) in altered models, including the expected <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> dependency enrichment in <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> GOF models (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2f,g</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM4" ref-type="media">2</xref>).</p><p id="Par18">This analysis also revealed an association between <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> GOF and dependency on stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD), a key enzyme in de novo lipogenesis (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2f,g</xref>). This link has been reported in the context of radiosensitizing lung tumours with <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> mutations<sup><xref rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr">36</xref></sup>. In our data, this association was most robust in oesophagus–stomach organoids with <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> CN amplification (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2h</xref>). Pharmacological validation with SCD inhibitors confirmed that <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic>-amplified oesophageal adenocarcinoma organoids were significantly more sensitive to both the compounds tested (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2i</xref>), which suggests that SCD inhibitors could target these cancers via a mechanism orthogonal to KRAS inhibitors. The <italic toggle="yes">SCD</italic> dependency–<italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> GOF link was stronger in NextGen than traditional models (Δmean dependency = –0.442 versus –0.241, respectively; Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2g</xref>), which suggests that the lipid-rich, serum-containing conditions of traditional cell culture mask this dependency by reducing reliance on de novo lipogenesis.</p><p id="Par19">Collectively, these three classes of biomarker-associated dependencies highlight the utility of NextGen models to uncover therapeutically relevant vulnerabilities missed by traditional cell lines.</p></sec><sec id="Sec4"><title>Dependencies tied to GBM gene expression</title><p id="Par20">We next explored transcriptional differences between NextGen and traditional models, with the aim of gaining insight into distinct dependency profiles. To that end, we characterized their differentially activated biological programs using 41 gene expression meta-programs (MPs), as identified in a previous study<sup><xref rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref></sup>. These MPs represent recurrent gene expression modules that account for intratumour heterogeneity (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3a</xref>) and largely reflect environmentally driven gene expression changes. We therefore reasoned that the distinct culture conditions of NextGen and traditional models would lead to differential MP activation. To evaluate this hypothesis, we quantified MP activity by comparing NextGen (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 76) and traditional (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 97) CNS models and organoids (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 229) with lineage-matched traditional cell lines (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 451), and each organoid lineage against its traditional counterpart. Substantial variations in MP activity were observed between NextGen and traditional CNS models and between organoids and traditional cell lines (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3a</xref>). Notably, NextGen CNS models exhibited significantly increased expression of five MPs associated with neural lineages (Δexpression score &gt; 0.79, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 2 × 10<sup>−21</sup>, two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>test), which prompted additional investigations.<fig id="Fig3" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 3</label><caption><title>Identification of vulnerabilities linked to the glial state of GBM.</title><p><bold>a</bold>, Mean difference in 41 gene expression MP scores between NextGen and traditional CNS (top) and carcinoma (bottom) models. The colour indicates the score difference. The point size reflects significance (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> values; two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>test). <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 76 and 97 (CNS–brain); 229 and 451 (all organoid models); 86 and 78 (oesophagus–stomach); 44 and 54 (pancreas); 34 and 86 (colorectal); 28 and 70 (breast); 13 and 66 (ovary); 12 and 7 (prostate) for NextGen and traditional models, respectively. HMG, high-mobility group; MES, mesenchymal; MHC, major histocompatibility complex; NPC, neural progenitor cells; OPCs, oligodendrocyte-progenitor cells; Haemato, haematological; RBCs, red blood cells. <bold>b</bold>, Celligner uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of GBM tumour and models, with the latter classified into glial and mesenchymal groups. <bold>c</bold>, Differential gene expression between glial (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 67) and mesenchymal (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 54) GBM models (highlighted genes exhibited |log<sub>2</sub>[fold change]| &gt; 1 values, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.001, two-tailed Student’s <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test). <bold>d</bold>, Differential gene dependencies between glial (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 36) and mesenchymal (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 60) GBM models. Vulnerabilities enriched in glial GBM models are highlighted in maroon and blue. <bold>e</bold>, <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency in glial, mesenchymal and non-glial NextGen models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 115). Here and in <bold>g</bold>, significance was scored using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests. <bold>f</bold>, Correlation of <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency with gene CNs across GBM models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 95). Significant associations (|<italic toggle="yes">r</italic>| &gt; −0.3, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.005; large points) and genes on chromosome 7p (maroon) and chromosome 9p21.3 (blue) are highlighted. <bold>g</bold>, <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency in glial and mesenchymal GBM models stratified by <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> CN. For glial models, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 36 (all), 25 (<italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss) and 11 (neutral); for mesenchymal models, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 55 (all), 44 (<italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss) and 11 (neutral). <bold>h</bold>, Heatmap of CDK4/6 inhibitor GR<sub>AOC</sub> metrics in seven glial GBM models, with <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> status and <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency. ***<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 7.1 × 10<sup>–</sup><sup>4</sup>, *<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.021 and <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.051 (not significant (NS)) for abemaciclib, palbociclib and ribociclib, respectively (<italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> neutral versus loss; two-tailed Student’s <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test). <bold>i</bold>, Response curves illustrating S phase cell cycle fractions across indicated concentrations of the CDK4/6 inhibitors.</p><p><xref rid="MOESM10" ref-type="media">Source data</xref></p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d33e1729" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="41586_2026_10843_Fig3_HTML.webp"><?image-name 41586_2026_10843_Fig3_HTML.webp?><?image-size 217684?><?image-md5 fb423f62334d30c3ac5110da2fef3dba?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 1604?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 1604?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/fb423f62334d/41586_2026_10843_Fig3_HTML.webp?><?thumb-name 41586_2026_10843_Fig3_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 15323?><?thumb-md5 6654af474b1de277d65758bed1bd7048?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 201?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/6654af474b1d/41586_2026_10843_Fig3_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par21">Focusing on GBM, Celligner revealed that most NextGen GBM models (90.0%) clustered with the majority of GBM tumours (93.1%), whereas most traditional GBM cell lines (87.3%) grouped separately with only 4.2% of tumours (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3b</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6a</xref>). Differential gene expression analyses indicated that the former cluster expressed glial or classical markers (<italic toggle="yes">SOX2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">OLIG1</italic>)<sup><xref rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref></sup>, whereas the latter expressed mesenchymal markers (<italic toggle="yes">VEGFC</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">IGFBP6</italic>)<sup><xref rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>,<xref rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr">40</xref></sup> (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6b</xref>), which led us to label them ‘glial’ and ‘mesenchymal’, respectively. All five neural-lineage-specific MPs were significantly increased in glial models relative to mesenchymal models (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 2 × 10<sup>−15</sup>), reaching levels comparable to GBM tumours (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6c,d</xref>). A companion study<sup><xref rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref></sup> confirmed that traditional culture conditions induced the expression of mesenchymal markers and suppressed glial markers in a NextGen GBM model. This result demonstrates that culture conditions drive cell-state changes.</p><p id="Par22">Next, we explored vulnerabilities tied to glial gene expression. We identified an enrichment of <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency in glial compared with mesenchymal models (Δdependency = –0.44, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.013) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3d,e</xref>). Although this dependency ranked second in effect size, it fell short of the multiple-testing significance threshold (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 0.28), which may be due to the small sample size of glial GBMs (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 36) analysed. Comparisons with other NextGen models confirmed that this enrichment was driven by the glial state rather than serum-free media (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3e</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6e</xref>). Encouraged by the clinical impact of CDK4 and CDK6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors on treatment outcomes, we pursued <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency and its associated biomarker.</p><p id="Par23">Although no recurrent GBM mutations correlated closely with <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6f</xref>), significant associations were found with CNs of genes, including those on chromosome 9p21.3 (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3f</xref>). Of these genes, <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic>—which encodes p16INK4A and is the most frequently deleted gene in GBM<sup><xref rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr">41</xref></sup>—exhibited the third strongest correlation with <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency across adult GBM models (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.520, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 4.12 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) and the strongest in glial GBM models specifically (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.640, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 0.0340; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6g</xref>). Given the established role of <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> in CDK6-mediated cell cycle control, we postulated that <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> CN loss is a biomarker for <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency in glial GBM.</p><p id="Par24">Validation with individual sgRNAs confirmed that <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> knockout caused greater viability loss than <italic toggle="yes">CDK4</italic> knockout in two glial GBM models with <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6h,i</xref>). This result is consistent with the reported exclusive <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency in GBM stem cells with <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2</italic><italic toggle="yes">B</italic> loss<sup><xref rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr">42</xref></sup>. Glial models with <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss were also significantly more sensitive to <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> depletion than mesenchymal models with the same deletion (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3g</xref>). This finding indicates that glial gene expression and <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss independently contribute to <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency.</p><p id="Par25">To pharmacologically validate this association, we profiled seven glial GBM models—five with <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> CN loss and two CN neutral—against three CDK4/6 inhibitors (abemaciclib, palbociclib and ribociclib) using the dye drop method<sup><xref rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr">43</xref></sup>. <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> CN-loss models were more sensitive (mean growth rate AOC (GR<sub>AOC</sub>) = 0.35, 0.25 and 0.15, respectively) to all three inhibitors than CN-neutral models (GR<sub>AOC</sub> = 0.06, –0.03 and –0.07, respectively), with significant differences for abemaciclib (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 7.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) and palbociclib (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.021) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3h</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6j</xref>). CN-loss models also displayed reductions in the S phase fraction at doses that did not affect CN-neutral models (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3i</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6k</xref>), which—together with a previous report on CRISPR-mediated <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> depletion<sup><xref rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr">44</xref></sup>—provides support for a causal role of <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss in enhancing CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity.</p><p id="Par26">In summary, <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic> loss increases <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency and CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity in glial GBM. Given that 92% of glial and classical GBM tumours exhibit homozygous 9p21.3 deletion<sup><xref rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr">45</xref></sup>, these findings indicate that CDK6 inhibition is a relevant therapeutic strategy. These results also underscore the value of NextGen CNS models in uncovering clinically relevant vulnerabilities because they preserve tumour transcriptional states.</p></sec><sec id="Sec5"><title>Mucinous differentiation program in organoids</title><p id="Par27">We proceeded to examine genetic vulnerabilities linked to programs that are preserved in organoids. Out of 41 gene expression MPs, 5 exhibited significant differential expression between the organoid and lineage-matched traditional models (|Δexpression score| &gt; 0.5, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 1 × 10<sup>−30</sup>; Figs. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3a</xref> and <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4a</xref>). In detail, stress, secreted II, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)-classical, cilia and glutathione were increased, whereas cell cycle G1/S was reduced in organoids. The PDAC-classical program displayed the largest difference (|Δexpression score| = 2.30, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 3.86 × 10<sup>−45</sup>), which spurred further investigation.</p><p id="Par28">Although first described in the classical subtype of PDAC<sup><xref rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr">46</xref></sup>, this program is recognized across cancer types with aberrant mucin production<sup><xref rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref></sup>. GeneTEA overrepresentation analysis<sup><xref rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr">47</xref></sup> showed strong enrichment for terms related to epithelial differentiation, mucous membrane and gastrointestinal tissues (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7a</xref>), thereby linking this program to the common developmental path of mucosal gastrointestinal epithelium<sup><xref rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr">48</xref></sup>. We therefore termed it the PDAC-classical and mucinous differentiation (MUC) program (PDAC-classical/MUC).</p><p id="Par29">This program was highly expressed (mean score &gt;1.9) across gastrointestinal tumours (pancreas, oesophagus–stomach and colorectal) but low (&lt;0.5) in non-gastrointestinal tumours (breast, ovary and prostate) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7b</xref>). This gastrointestinal-specific pattern was preserved in 3D organoids (mean score &gt;3.0 in gastrointestinal; &lt;0.6 in non-gastrointestinal), but not in traditional cell lines, which showed low-to-moderate (&lt;1.6) expression across all lineages (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4b,c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7c</xref>). This result extends previous findings that organoids maintain the classical gene expression profile in PDACs<sup><xref rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref></sup>. Furthermore, the results demonstrated that the PDAC-classical/MUC program is broadly preserved across gastrointestinal organoid lineages but suppressed in traditional cell lines.<fig id="Fig4" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 4</label><caption><title>PDAC-classical/MUC program and WNT dependency link revealed in organoids.</title><p><bold>a</bold>, Differences in MP scores between NextGen organoids and traditional cell lines. Bold text (WLS, MESD, FZD5, LGR4 and TCF7L2) indicates factors with increased dependency in high PDAC-classical/MUC models.
