Although ESCCs are overrepresented in traditional oesophagus–stomach models, removing them did not eliminate the significant reduction in program expression in traditional cell lines (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> &lt; 2.1 × 10<sup>−13</sup>, two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>test; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7e</xref>). PDAC-classical/MUC scores correlated strongly with previously defined classical subtype scores<sup><xref rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr">46</xref></sup> (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.969) and were predominantly high in pancreas, oesophagus–stomach and colorectal tumours, with high levels (&gt;3) also appearing in some lung and cervix tumours (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7f,g</xref>). Scores did not correlate with tumour purity (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = 0.061 to –0.193 across lineages; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7h</xref>), and cells with high PDAC-classical/MUC expression were significantly enriched in colon tumours compared with normal tissues<sup><xref rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref></sup>. This result supports the relevance of the PDAC-classical/MUC program to gastrointestinal cancers.</p><p id="Par31">To identify dependencies associated with this program, we correlated PDAC-classical/MUC scores with dependency scores of strong dependency genes (3 strong dependency classes in organoids; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3,521). The top correlated dependencies were enriched for canonical WNT signalling regulators, including <italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic> (ranked first; <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = −0.544), <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic> (second; <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = −0.507), <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic> (fifth; <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = −0.454), <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> (seventh; <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = −0.435) and <italic toggle="yes">LGR4</italic> (21st; <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> = −0.354) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4d,e</xref>). This association held when restricting the analysis to organoids grown with R-spondin 1 and WNT3A (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7i</xref>), which indicated that it was not driven solely by the presence of WNT activators in culture media. Notably, other WNT regulators (for example, <italic toggle="yes">CTNNB1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BCL9L</italic>) did not correlate significantly (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4d</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7j</xref>), which suggests that the association is limited to selective WNT signalling components.</p><p id="Par32">A similar WNT pathway dependency is known in traditional PDAC models with <italic toggle="yes">RNF43</italic> LOF<sup><xref rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr">49</xref></sup>. However, in organoids, these dependencies correlated with the PDAC-classical/MUC transcriptional state irrespective of <italic toggle="yes">RNF43</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CTNNB1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">AXIN2</italic> mutations (Extended Data Figs. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7k</xref> and <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8a,b</xref>). All 19 organoids strongly dependent on the five listed WNT regulators (average Chronos dependency score &lt; –1) were PDAC-classical/MUC-high (expression score &gt; 2.8), including those with and without WNT-activating genetic alterations (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8b</xref>). This result suggests that enhanced WNT dependency is driven by the transcriptional cell state rather than genetic alterations.</p><p id="Par33">These findings extend previous work on the loss of WNT3A and R-spondin dependence during PDAC organoid niche-adaptation<sup><xref rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr">50</xref></sup> by linking specific WNT signalling dependencies to a conserved mucinous differentiation program active across multiple gastrointestinal tumour types. The expression of this program in a subset of lung and cervix tumours suggests a shared WNT-associated vulnerability in these rare, poor-prognosis cancers<sup><xref rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr">51</xref>,<xref rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr">52</xref></sup>. Notably, <italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> dependencies were significantly weaker in lineage-matched 2D models (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> &lt; 4 × 10<sup>−12</sup> for all; Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4f,g</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8c</xref>), which provides further support that the PDAC-classical/MUC program, maintained only in organoids, drives these dependencies.</p></sec><sec id="Sec6"><title>Culture conditions and screen outcomes</title><p id="Par34">To better understand the combined dataset of NextGen and traditional models, we studied differences in gene essentiality between NextGen 3D organoids and traditional 2D models. We compared 3D organoids grown in Matrigel domes with serum-free media (containing EGF and FGF10) to lineage-matched 2D adherent models cultured directly on plastic with serum-containing media (referred to as 3D (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 94) and 2D (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 433) models, respectively). We maintained consistent culture conditions in each cohort to elucidate the effects of these conditions.</p><p id="Par35">Examination of dependencies on frequently mutated oncogenes and TSGs (mutated in &gt;1% in TCGA<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup>) revealed increased <italic toggle="yes">CDK4</italic> dependency in 2D models (mean 3D dependency score = –0.26, mean 2D dependency score = –0.83, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 9.54 × 10<sup>−21</sup>; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8d,e</xref>), which probably reflects greater reliance on this cell cycle driver in these fast-growing models. Similarly, <italic toggle="yes">MDM2</italic> dependency was enriched in 2D models (mean 3D dependency score = –0.27, mean 2D dependency score = –0.54, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 4.23 × 10<sup>−12</sup>; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8d,e</xref>), which held for <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> wild-type (WT) models (mean 3D dependency score = –0.54, mean 2D dependency score = –1.09, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 8.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup>). This result suggests that 2D culture conditions trigger p53 activation, an effect exposed by reduced MDM2-mediated p53 degradation.</p><p id="Par36">Summarizing pathway-level differences in gene dependencies<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup> revealed that most 2D models (65.6%) showed positive mean dependency scores for p53 pathway TSGs (<italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>) compared with only 21.3% of 3D models (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8f,g</xref>). This result further suggests that the p53 pathway is more growth-suppressive in 2D than 3D culture conditions. Conversely, knockout of a TSG did not generally cause a stronger growth benefit in 3D organoids than in 2D models, a result that is in contrast to a previous study analysing serum-containing spheroid cultures<sup><xref rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr">22</xref></sup> (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8d,f</xref>).</p><p id="Par37">To broadly compare gene essentialities, we calculated the difference in mean dependency scores between 3D and 2D models for every gene (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 16,691; excluding common essential genes), and identified gene sets (Hallmark and KEGG gene sets from MSigDB; <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05) that were significantly overrepresented at the extremes of this difference (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a,b</xref>). Clustering these gene sets by component overlap (&gt;0.3; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8h</xref>) merged two sets (adhesion and cytoskeleton (adhesion–cytoskeleton), and cell cycle), whereas five others (lipid metabolism, mTORC1, oxidative phosphorylation, UV response and systemic lupus erythematosus) remained separate.<fig id="Fig5" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 5</label><caption><title>Comparing 2D and 3D dependencies to disentangle the effects of culture conditions.</title><p><bold>a</bold>,<bold>b</bold>, Gene sets enriched for differential dependencies between 3D and 2D models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 94 (3D) and 433 (2D)). Odds ratios for the 9 significant gene sets (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05) overrepresented in the 200 outlier genes were plotted, clustered and coloured by gene overlap (&gt;0.3; <bold>a</bold>). Mean dependency differences and their significance for individual genes (two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>test; gene <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3,521), coloured by the gene set clusters from <bold>a</bold> were also plotted (<bold>b</bold>). <bold>c</bold>–<bold>e</bold>, Minipool screens were performed to elucidate the differing effects of growth format and culture medium. A minipool screen (250 test genes) was designed (<bold>c</bold>) to separate the effects of growth format (plastic versus dome) and culture medium (RPMI–FBS versus OPAC) on gene essentiality. The screens identified genes for which dependencies are primarily altered by growth format (<bold>d</bold>) or culture medium (<bold>e</bold>), with red dashed lines indicating significance threshold (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 0.05, two-sided linear regression <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test) and the point colours indicating gene classes in the minipool library (bottom). Screen <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 11 (dome), 7 (plastic), 9 (OPAC), 9 (RPMI–FBS). <bold>f</bold>,<bold>g</bold>, Comparisons across growth formats and culture media. <bold>f</bold>, Different gene classes represented in the minipool library are highlighted. Integrin and actin regulation classes exhibited significant variance across growth formats. <bold>g</bold>, By contrast, lipid metabolism class were affected by culture medium (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05, two-tailed <italic toggle="yes">F</italic>-test; gene <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 200). <bold>h</bold>, Differential effects on integrin and cholesterol homeostasis dependencies assessed by viability after test gene knockout. Values are the mean ± s.d. (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3). <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> values calculated using two-tailed two-way ANOVA. R–F, RPMI–FBS. <bold>i</bold>, Colocalization of integrin chains (green) with FAK (red) in KP3 cells under plastic or dome growth conditions (both in RPMI–FBS). Nuclei (blue) and actin (white) are also shown. Representative images from three independent experiments are displayed. Scale bar, 20 μm.</p><p><xref rid="MOESM12" ref-type="media">Source data</xref></p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d33e2467" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="41586_2026_10843_Fig5_HTML.webp"><?image-name 41586_2026_10843_Fig5_HTML.webp?><?image-size 243640?><?image-md5 52d1d5fc2ce5df7f5936be1a7d6d2abb?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 1615?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 1615?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/52d1d5fc2ce5/41586_2026_10843_Fig5_HTML.webp?><?thumb-name 41586_2026_10843_Fig5_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 15715?><?thumb-md5 79dec8a74ecf5a7e0f757e7dad5758ec?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 200?><?thumb-scaled-width 199?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/79dec8a74ecf/41586_2026_10843_Fig5_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par38">We focused on the adhesion–cytoskeleton and lipid metabolism gene sets owing to their probable connection to the physical and metabolic culture environments, respectively. The 3D versus 2D growth format difference plausibly affects cell–cell and cell–extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions and associated dependencies<sup><xref rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr">54</xref></sup>. By contrast, differential lipid content in media—2D models use lipid-rich RPMI supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), whereas organoid media contain only linoleic and linolenic acids and lack cholesterol—probably influences lipid-metabolism dependencies.</p><p id="Par39">Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5c</xref>, Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9a</xref> and Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM5" ref-type="media">3</xref>). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9b</xref>).</p><p id="Par40">After applying Chronos to the minipool screen data (which correlated well with genome-wide data, <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &gt; 0.59; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9c</xref>), we used linear regression to distinguish growth-format and culture-medium effects. This analysis identified seven genes for which dependencies were altered by growth formats (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05), including three integrin subunits (<italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ITGA3</italic>) and two actin regulators (<italic toggle="yes">NCKAP1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PTK2</italic>; Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5d</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9d</xref>). Eight genes also exhibited dependency changes across different media, three of which regulate lipid metabolism (<italic toggle="yes">SPTLC1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SPTLC2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SQLE</italic>; Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5e</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9e</xref>).</p><p id="Par41">A global analysis of the minipool screen results across the nine functional gene classes did not reveal collective enhancement or impairment of dependencies between different growth formats and media, except for a minor enhancement (Δdependency = 0.09) in the actin regulation class under RPMI–FBS conditions compared with OPAC (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9f,g</xref>). To capture opposing effects in gene classes (for example, <italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic> dependency increases whereas <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic> decreases in dome culture), we analysed the variance in dependency score differences between conditions (dome versus plastic and OPAC versus RPMI–FBS). Growth format had significantly larger effects on integrin (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 7.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) and actin regulation genes (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 7.2 × 10<sup>−14</sup>), whereas culture medium significantly affected lipid metabolism genes (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 1.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>; Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5f,g</xref>). These data demonstrate functional class-specific effects of growth format and medium.</p><p id="Par42">To validate these findings, we knocked out <italic toggle="yes">ITB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSMO1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">SQLE</italic> in KP3 and HS766T pancreas models under 2D plastic (with RPMI–FBS) and 3D dome (with RPMI–FBS or OPAC) cultures. Cholesterol biosynthesis gene dependencies (<italic toggle="yes">MSMO1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SQLE</italic>) varied by medium, whereas integrin subunit dependencies (<italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic>) were sensitive to growth format (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5h</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10a</xref>). Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed that integrin β1 (encoded by <italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic>) colocalized with FAK in 3D but not 2D cultures, whereas integrin αV (encoded by <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic>) showed enhanced FAK colocalization in 2D relative to 3D cultures, which was partially due to reduced cell surface expression in 3D (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5i</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10b–e</xref>). These findings align with their differential roles in cell–ECM interactions across different growth formats<sup><xref rid="CR55" ref-type="bibr">55</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par43">Notably, neither growth format nor medium significantly affected dependencies on the WNT signalling regulators <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic> (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5f</xref>), which were essential only in organoids with high PDAC-classical/MUC program levels (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4f,g</xref>). This result probably reflects stable maintenance of the PDAC-classical/MUC program in organoids rather than its rapid induction by the short-term shift in culture conditions. This result is in contrast to integrin, actin and lipid metabolism dependencies, which seem to be more responsive to acute changes in growth conditions. Together, these findings highlight how dependencies on specific cellular processes vary with culture environment and underscore the importance of selecting appropriate model systems for the biological question being pursued.</p></sec><sec id="Sec7" sec-type="discussion"><title>Discussion</title><p id="Par44">We generated a comprehensive CRISPR viability dataset for NextGen cancer models—carcinoma organoids and CNS spheroids—and integrated them with traditional cell line data. Incorporating these NextGen models substantially expands the representation of tumour subtypes and genomic alterations in DepMap (Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1a–f</xref>). We view both traditional cell lines and NextGen models as valuable and complementary resources for advancing our understanding of cancer dependencies.</p><p id="Par45">NextGen models preserve key tumour-relevant transcriptional programs that are lost in traditional cell lines. These include the PDAC-classical/MUC program in gastrointestinal cancer organoids (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4b,c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7c</xref>) and neural-lineage-specific programs and a glial state in GBM spheroids (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3b</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6a–d</xref>). The maintenance of these programs correlated with selective dependencies, which highlights the utility of the NextGen models in identifying certain transcriptional-state-specific vulnerabilities missed by the traditional models.</p><p id="Par46">Our data also revealed that oncogenic signalling roles differ significantly between model types. WNT signalling is required for organoids with a PDAC-classical/MUC program but is largely dispensable in traditional models (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4</xref>). By contrast, dependencies on <italic toggle="yes">ESR1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ERBB2</italic> were exclusive to traditional cell lines (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5b,d</xref>), which probably stem from reduced expression of these oncogenes in the organoids (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5d</xref>) owing to composition differences in the media. Together, these findings demonstrate that multiple oncogenic signalling pathways are highly context-dependent, which reinforces the fact that cellular microenvironments substantially shape requirements for these pathways<sup><xref rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr">56</xref>,<xref rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr">57</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par47">We further demonstrated that growth format (3D Matrigel dome versus 2D monolayer) and medium (serum-free OPAC versus serum-containing RPMI) differentially affect gene essentiality (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5</xref>). Dependencies on integrin and actin genes were sensitive to growth format, whereas lipid metabolism dependencies were influenced by medium, a result that revealed gene class-specific effects. This finding highlights the distinct advantages and disadvantages of NextGen and traditional models and underscore the need to understand the limitations of each model type when studying dependencies.</p><p id="Par48">In summary, the current work enhances DepMap by incorporating NextGen models and integrating their data with traditional cell line data. As more NextGen models are profiled, the expanded DepMap will accelerate the discovery of vulnerabilities across a broader range of cancers, which will enable identification of therapeutic strategies tailored not only to tumour genotypes but also to transcriptional states.</p></sec><sec id="Sec8" sec-type="materials|methods"><title>Methods</title><sec id="Sec9"><title>Source and culture conditions of NextGen cancer models</title><p id="Par49">The source of each of the NextGen models is provided in Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="media">1</xref>. In brief, breast cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratories of A.V.L., S.O. and D.L.S. Most of the NextGen CNS tumour models were derived by the laboratory of K.L.L. Colorectal and oesophagus–stomach cancer organoid models were derived by staff at the Cancer Cell Line Factory at the Broad Institute. Ovarian and uterus cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratory of S.J.H. Pancreas cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratories of A.J.A. and S.R. Prostate cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratory of H.B. and the laboratory of Y. Chen. Additional models derived by the HCMI were obtained via the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Models were confirmed for the absence of mycoplasma contamination (Mycoplasma PCR Detection kit; ABM, G238) and authenticated by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling (LabCorp) before expansion. These procedures were repeated monthly during expansion and screening.</p><p id="Par50">Organoid media were prepared using the recommendations provided for each of the models (Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="media">1</xref>). The conditioned media were prepared by culturing WNT3A-producing L cells (L Wnt-3A; ATCC, CRL-2647) and R-spondin-1-producing 293T cells (Cultrex R-spondin 1 (RSPO1) cells; Trevigen, 3710-001-K) in DMEM with 10% serum. After reaching 80% confluency, cells were washed once with PBS and incubated with Advanced DMEM–F12 medium (Thermo Fisher, 12634028) containing 100 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 1% 100× Glutamax (Ad+++) for another week. The conditioned medium from this culture was then collected, filtered and stored at –80 °C before being used for organoid cultures. All organoids were grown initially as domes composed of 75% growth-factor-reduced, Phenol Red-free Matrigel (50 μl per dome; Corning, 356231) in the recommended medium diluted 1:1 with Ad+++. The screening of organoids was conducted either in Matrigel dome cultures or in adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates (see the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’ below).</p><p id="Par51">The NextGen CNS models were grown in tumour stem medium, the composition of which is described in Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="media">1</xref>. The conditioned medium was collected routinely during expansion and preserved for subsequent cultures. Cells were seeded in a mixture of 30% conditioned medium and 70% fresh medium. Some of the models were tested for their ability to grow on a Matrigel-coated plate. In brief, cells were plated in 1% Matrigel-coated flasks and cells attached to the coating were carried forward as adherent models. Models that failed to attach to coated plates were grown as spheroids in ultra-low attachment (ULA) vessels (Corning, 3814). Models that were initially derived as adherent cultures on laminin-coated plates were maintained in the same conditions. To coat plates, Matrigel or laminin (Corning, 354232) was diluted in ice-cold PBS at a concentration of 1%. This solution was then added to culture vessels at approximately one-half the recommended volume of medium for a given vessel (for example, 5 ml solution in a T75 flask). Flasks were incubated at 37 °C overnight, and the solution was aspirated immediately before plating the cells. The growth format of each model is listed in Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM3" ref-type="media">1</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec10"><title>Preparation of samples for WGS and RNA-seq</title><p id="Par52">To generate pellets from the organoids, the medium was first aspirated and then the Matrigel domes were scraped and transferred to a 20× volume of pre-warmed TrypLE (Thermo Fisher, 12604021) with 10 µM ROCK inhibitor (Peprotech, 129830-38-2). This mixture was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. Subsequently, the cells were pelleted by centrifugation, resuspended in a mixture of medium and Matrigel and seeded at a density of 50,000 cells per dome. After 1 week of growth, cell pellets were collected without ROCK inhibitor for WGS and RNA-seq.</p><p id="Par53">For the NextGen CNS tumour models, cells were seeded and propagated for 7–14 days, depending on their growth, and dissociated with TrypLE for 5 min at 37 °C. Following dissociation, the cells were counted, and the pellets of 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells were collected and submitted for WGS and RNA-seq.</p></sec><sec id="Sec11"><title>WGS analysis</title><p id="Par54">WGS for all the DepMap NextGen models was conducted at the Broad Institute Genomics Platform using the PCR-free human WGS procedure. In brief, libraries were constructed and sequenced at 30× coverage on either an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 or NovaSeq X system, with the use of 150 base-pair paired-end reads. The FASTQ files from sequencing were de-multiplexed, aggregated and aligned using the DRAGEN germline pipeline to create BAM files.</p></sec><sec id="Sec12"><title>Mutation calling from WGS</title><p id="Par55">The mutation calls from the WGS results were generated using Mutect2 (ref. <sup><xref rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr">61</xref></sup>), annotated and filtered downstream. The detailed strategies are described in a publicly shared document (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://storage.googleapis.com/shared-portal-files/Tools/25Q3_Mutation_Pipeline_Documentation.pdf" ext-link-type="uri">https://storage.googleapis.com/shared-portal-files/Tools/25Q3_Mutation_Pipeline_Documentation.pdf</ext-link>). In short, variants were aligned to the GRCh38.p14 human genome assembly (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000001405.40/" ext-link-type="uri">https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000001405.40/</ext-link>) and mutation calling was conducted with the following parameters: default format of VCF and HG38; Gatk_docker: broadinstitute/gatk:4.2.6.1; M2_extra_args:–genotype-germline-sites true–genotype-pon-sites true for getting access to germline calls; Filter_funcotations to False PoN: gs://gatk-best-practices/somatic-hg38/1000g_pon.hg38.vcf.gz; Run_funcotator to True; Run_orientation_bias_mixture_model_filter to True. The pipeline was run such that no bait sets were needed.</p></sec><sec id="Sec13"><title>CN calling from WGS</title><p id="Par56">Relative CN data were generated from the WGS data by running the GATK CN pipeline aligned to hg38 (ref. <sup><xref rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr">62</xref></sup>). Absolute CN data from WGS or whole-exome sequencing were generated using PureCN<sup><xref rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr">63</xref></sup>. Arm-level CN values were calculated using PureCN segment-level CN as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr">64</xref></sup>. Gene-level amplifications were defined as having a relative CN (log<sub>2</sub>[relative to ploidy + 1]) greater than 3, and deletions were defined as having a relative CN less than 0.25.</p></sec><sec id="Sec14"><title>RNA-seq</title><p id="Par57">RNA-seq for all the DepMap NextGen models was conducted at the Broad Institute Genomics Platform. In brief, poly-A RNAs were captured with oligo-dT beads, from which libraries (450–550 bp insert size) were prepared using a strand-specific Illumina TruSeq library preparation protocol. These libraries were sequenced to 100 million paired reads on either an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 or NovaSeq X system, with the use of 151 bp paired-end reads. The FASTQ files from sequencing were processed using the DRAGEN RNA-seq pipeline to create BAM files.</p></sec><sec id="Sec15"><title>Source of traditional cell lines</title><p id="Par58">The traditional cell lines used were obtained from DepMap, and the original source can be found on the DepMap portal (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://DepMap.org/portal" ext-link-type="uri">https://DepMap.org/portal</ext-link>). These included several commonly misidentified cell lines registered by the International Cell Line Authentication Committee (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://iclac.org/databases/cross-contaminations/" ext-link-type="uri">https://iclac.org/databases/cross-contaminations/</ext-link>). We reasoned that even though these cell lines are commonly misidentified, their inclusion in the DepMap dataset would be advantageous for comprehensiveness, provided they were confidently identified and authenticated. Accordingly, we performed STR profiling on the cell lines that are frequently misidentified. After confirming their identities, we decided to profile these lines and include their data in DepMap. Mycoplasma testing and STR profiling were performed after receiving the cell lines and every 3 months of culture period thereafter using a Mycoplasma PCR Detection kit (G238, ABM). Cells were grown in RPMI 1640 (Corning, 10-040-CV) supplemented with 2 mM glutamine, 50 U ml<sup>–1</sup> penicillin, 50 U ml<sup>–1</sup> streptomycin (Gibco, 10378016) and 10% FBS (MilliporeSigma, F4135) and incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO<sub>2</sub>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec16"><title>Lineage prediction with Celligner</title><p id="Par59">To predict the lineage of cancer models (NextGen and traditional) using Celligner, the 25 nearest neighbour tumours from the TCGA, TARGET and Met500 datasets (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 13,104) were identified for each model in Celligner’s aligned gene expression space according to pairwise Euclidean distance. For each lineage of the models, we computed the lineage representation among the neighbouring tumours as a global measure of model–tumour lineage similarity. To obtain per-model lineage predictions, we classified each model by the most frequent lineage found among its nearest neighbour tumours.</p><p id="Par60">Models that fell into the ‘undifferentiated cluster’ were excluded in a part of the analysis shown in Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2a</xref>, as this cluster was highly enriched with adherent models from various lineages that exhibited loss of lineage-specific gene expression patterns, which made it difficult to predict lineages of the models in this cluster. The undifferentiated cluster was defined by applying the following criteria to the 79 clusters identified using Celligner: (1) number of DepMap models in the cluster &gt; number of tumour samples in the cluster; and (2) average Hallmark epithelial mesenchymal transition ssGSEA enrichment score among the DepMap models in the cluster &gt; 0.</p><p id="Par61">This procedure identified four clusters with Celligner (clusters 28, 59, 62 and 67), which were collectively designated as the undifferentiated cluster.</p></sec><sec id="Sec17"><title>Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids</title><p id="Par62">After initial expansion and collection of viable stocks and pellets (used for fingerprinting and omics profiling; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">3</xref>), the organoids were tested for blasticidin sensitivity to identify the minimal concentration of blasticidin that gives less than 1% viability of uninfected cells in 10–14 days. Fourteen organoid models were screened as adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates, whereas the rest of the organoids were screened in 3D Matrigel dome cultures. To select the culture conditions for organoid screens, each of the organoid models was subjected to a growth format assay by seeding 50,000 cells into a well of a 24-well non-tissue-culture-treated plate (Corning, 351147) either as a Matrigel dome (75% Matrigel, 50 μl per dome) or on top of a Matrigel coat, referred to as either dome or coat format, respectively. The coated wells were prepared by first adding 1% Matrigel in ice-cold PBS to 50% of the standard filling volume of the well and allowing it to solidify by incubating overnight at 37 °C. Before cell plating, the PBS–Matrigel mixture was aspirated, leaving the Matrigel coat behind, and the cell suspension was added on top of the coat. The growth of cells in the dome and coat formats was compared after 1 week of culture via a viability assay with CellTiter-Glo 3D (3D CTG; Promega, G9683). Models with at least 30% viability on coat relative to dome format were propagated and screened in the coat format. This process enabled us to screen these models in a similar manner to traditional adherent cell lines, but with a thin layer of matrix support, thus decreasing the amount of required Matrigel by approximately tenfold.</p><p id="Par63">Subsequently, all organoids were infected with lentivirus expressing enAsCas12a (Addgene, 136476). For this infection, 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells were exposed to the lentivirus in a 24-well ULA plate (Corning, 3473) in the presence of 8 µg ml<sup>–1</sup> polybrene and 10 µM ROCK inhibitor. After 18 h, the cells were collected by centrifugation and washed once with PBS to remove the virus, and cells were then plated in Matrigel domes at 5 × 10<sup>4</sup> cells per dome. At 24 h after seeding the cells in the Matrigel domes, the medium was replaced with selection medium containing blasticidin at 30 µg ml<sup>–1</sup>. A 3D CTG assay was carried out 10–14 days after infection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to measure the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus. Cells were maintained at a constant blasticidin (as determined using a blasticidin sensitivity assay) concentration throughout the screening process.</p><p id="Par64">Cas12a activity assessment was conducted as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr">65</xref></sup> (a detailed protocol is available as ‘Cas9/Cas12a Activity Assay’ at the Broad Institute Genetic Perturbation Platform (GPP) web portal: <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols" ext-link-type="uri">https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols</ext-link>) using two different types of lentivirus, both of which express GFP, a sgRNA (or sgRNAs) against GFP and the puromycin-resistance gene. One type of these virus expresses two GFP-targeting sgRNA sequences optimized for enAsCas12a (pRDA_221; Addgene, 169142), whereas the other virus type expresses a GFP-targeting sgRNA sequence optimized for spCas9 (pXPR-047; Addgene, 107145), the latter of which served as a negative control. Cells were infected with these two different virus types separately as described above and selected with puromycin for 4 days. GFP expression was measured in the FITC channel by flow cytometry (CytoFLEX LX, Beckman Coulter) 14 days after pRDA_221/pXPR_047 infection with a Zombie Aqua viability stain (BioLegend, 423102) applied to gate out dead cells. Using the non-infection control (NIC) as a negative control, GFP positivity was determined for both the pRDA_221 and pXPR_047 infected cells. Cas activity was calculated using the following formula: (GFP (%) of pXPR_047 – GFP (%) of pRDA_221)/(GFP (%) of pXPR_047).</p><p id="Par65">Cell lines with Cas activity above 70% were selected for screening. However, some lines were screened with activity as low as 44% if they showed sufficiently rapid growth of at least one population doubling per week.</p><p id="Par66">Library titrations were carried out to determine the volume of sgRNA library virus required to achieve an infection efficiency of around 50%. Infections were conducted on 24-well ULA plates, with each well containing 5 × 10<sup>5</sup> cells in 600 µl medium with 4–8 µg ml<sup>–1</sup> polybrene, 10 µM ROCK inhibitor and 50–200 µl library virus. The plate was incubated at 37 °C for 18 h, followed by collection of the cells by centrifugation and a wash with PBS to remove the virus. Cells were subsequently plated in Matrigel domes on a 24-well plate. Puromycin (3 µg ml<sup>–1</sup>) was added 48 h after virus infection. After 4 days of selection, infection efficiency was determined using a 3D CTG cell viability assay.</p><p id="Par67">For the screens, cells were first infected using the same protocol as for library titration, but only with the virus volume selected to give an infection rate of about 50%. The number of cells used for infection was determined such that sufficient number of cells survived puromycin selection to produce at least 500× representation of the library. Before July 2022, the screens were performed using either the C or D versions of the Humagne library (Addgene, 172650 and 172651) at full representation for each library. By contrast, screens after July 2022 were performed in two technical replicates at half representation using a combined C and D library to enable measurement of replicate correlation. After 18 h of incubation with virus in ULA plates, the virus was washed out, and infected cells were plated at 5 × 10<sup>4</sup> cells per dome. To test infection efficiency, we seeded four NIC domes and four infected domes in a 24-well plate (one dome per well). After 24 h, the medium was replaced with the selection medium containing puromycin for the infected plates and half of the domes (two NIC domes and two infected domes) for the infection efficiency assay. Puromycin was washed out and blasticidin treatment was resumed on day 6, when a 3D CTG viability measurement for the infection efficiency assay was conducted to estimate actual screen representation. Screens with less than 200× representation were excluded. The medium was replaced on days 13 and 20, and the samples were passaged on day 9 and optionally on day 17 depending on the confluence of the model, which was determined by visual inspection, each time maintaining minimum target representation. All the cells were collected and frozen as pellets on day 23.</p><p id="Par68">gDNA samples were prepared from the screen pellets using a KingFisher Apex System (Thermo Fisher, 5400940). After preparing gDNA samples, the DNA concentration of each sample was measured using a Qubit4 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher, <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-protein" xlink:href="Q33238">Q33238</ext-link>), and the presence of library DNA was confirmed by performing PCR with a set of library-specific primers. gDNA samples were subsequently submitted for library DNA amplification and sequencing to the GPP at the Broad Institute. PCR and sequencing were performed in accordance with the ‘sgRNA/shRNA/ORF PCR for Illumina Sequencing’ protocol available at the Broad Institute GPP web portal (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols" ext-link-type="uri">https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols</ext-link>). DNA samples were sequenced at a scale matched with the size of the screen: 68 µg gDNA per replicate for screens with 500× representation and 134 µg gDNA per replicate for screens with 1,000× representation.</p></sec><sec id="Sec18"><title>Genome-wide CRISPR screening of NextGen CNS tumours</title><p id="Par69">The pipeline for genome-wide CRISPR screens of the NextGen CNS tumour models was adapted in part from previous work<sup><xref rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr">66</xref></sup> and is composed of the same processes to what is described above in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’ except for the following differences.</p><p id="Par70">CNS models were tested for the growth format and seeding density that resulted in optimal growth rates and for polybrene sensitivity, which was used at a concentration that resulted in &gt;85% survival. For growth testing, cells were plated in both Matrigel-coated and ULA 6-well tissue culture plates. Specifically, cells were seeded in duplicate at densities of 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000 cells per well for both the Matrigel-coated plates and ULA plates. Cells were allowed to grow for 7 days, with a medium change performed at day 3 or 4 as needed. After 7 days, cells from all the conditions were counted and a doubling time was calculated for each condition. The condition that gave the lowest doubling time while maintaining high cell viability was used for the screen. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standardized concentration of 50 µg ml<sup>–1</sup> and 3 µg ml<sup>–1</sup>, respectively. For enAsCas12a transduction, 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells were exposed to lentivirus expressing enAsCas12ain a 24-well ULA plate in the presence of the optimized concentration of polybrene. At 18 h after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and the cells were plated in the optimal growth format at 2× the optimal seeding density. Subsequently, cells were selected with blasticidin. A CellTiter-Glo cell viability assay (CTG; Promega, G7572) was carried out 14 days after infection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to measure the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus.</p><p id="Par71">For library titration, infections were conducted on 24-well ULA plates, with each well containing 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells in 600 µl medium, the optimized concentration of polybrene and 50–200 µl library virus. The volume of virus required for an infection efficiency of about 50% was determined as described above in ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’. Blasticidin treatment was resumed on day 7 instead of day 6 after infection, and a CTG viability measurement for the infection efficiency assay was performed on the same day to estimate actual screen representation. Medium was replaced on days 10 and 17, and the samples were passaged on days 7 and 14, each time maintaining minimum target representation. All cells were collected and frozen as pellets on day 21, from which gDNA samples were prepared, and the library DNA was amplified by PCR and sequenced.</p></sec><sec id="Sec19"><title>Genome-wide CRISPR screens of cancer cell lines</title><p id="Par72">The original source for all the cell lines is available at the DepMap portal (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://DepMap.org/portal" ext-link-type="uri">https://DepMap.org/portal</ext-link>). The CRISPR screens of the traditional cancer cell lines with the spCas9 sgRNA libraries (Avana and KY) were carried out as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr">67</xref>,<xref rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr">68</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par73">For the CRISPR screens of the traditional cancer cell lines with the enAsCas12a sgRNA library (Humagne-CD), the cell lines were first tested for doubling time and cell size. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standard concentration of 40 μg ml<sup>–1</sup> and 2 μg ml<sup>–1</sup>, respectively. To infect adherent cells with lentivirus expressing enAsCas12a (Addgene, 136476), 5 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells were exposed to the virus in a T175 flask (Corning, 354487) in the presence of 4 µg ml<sup>–1</sup> polybrene. For suspension cells, 1.8 × 10<sup>7</sup> cells were exposed to the virus in a 12-well plate (Corning, 3513) in the presence of 4 µg ml<sup>–1</sup> polybrene, which was followed by centrifugation at 930<italic toggle="yes">g</italic>, 37 °C for 2 h. One day after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and cells were then plated at around 50% confluence. Blasticidin was added to the medium 2–3 days after infection. A CTG assay was carried out after 3 days of blasticidin selection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to estimate the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus. Cells were maintained in blasticidin for at least 10 days after transduction and throughout the screening process. After enCas12a transduction and blasticidin selection, enCas12a activity was assessed as described in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’.</p><p id="Par74">Library titrations were performed in 12-well tissue-culture-treated plates, with each well containing 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells in 2 ml medium, 4 μg ml<sup>–1</sup> polybrene and 0, 10, 25, 75, 200 or 500 μl virus. These 12-well plates were spun at 930<italic toggle="yes">g</italic>, 37 °C for 2 h, after which an additional 2 ml medium was added to each well for a final volume of 4 ml per well. After 24 h of infection, the cells in each well of the 12-well infection plate were split into 2 wells of a 6-well plate with 0 and 2 μg ml<sup>–1</sup> puromycin in fresh medium. An optimal seeding density was chosen such that the unselected population reached &lt;70% confluence after selection. After 3 days of selection, infection efficiency for a given virus volume was determined as the ratio of live cells in the puromycin-containing well (2 μg ml<sup>–1</sup>) to the number of live cells in the puromycin non-containing well. A linear regression of the virus volume to the transduction efficiency was performed to estimate the volume of virus required to transduce 50% of the population.</p><p id="Par75">The remaining procedures of the screen were the same as for the procedures described above in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’ except for the following modifications. For library infection, after 24 h of incubation with virus in 12-well plates, the virus was washed out with PBS and infected cells were plated with puromycin at an appropriate seeding density and flask size. After 72 h of selection, puromycin was washed out and blasticidin treatment was resumed. Screens with less than 250× representation or at an infection efficiency of higher than 60% were excluded. Cells were passaged every 3–6 days depending on the confluence of the model, as determined by visual inspection, each time maintaining minimum target representation. All cells were collected and frozen as pellets on day 22–23.</p></sec><sec id="Sec20"><title>Genome-wide CRISPR screening data processing and quality control evaluation</title><p id="Par76">All screens were initially evaluated for sequencing quality and selected to have a mean of at least 185 reads per gene. Naive gene effect scores were calculated by taking the log of the ratio of normalized reads for each gene in screened samples to that of normalized reads for each gene in the corresponding plasmid library. For screens using the two Humagne C and D libraries, the log fold change scores of libraries were averaged together. An ROC-AUC was calculated on the basis of per cent of true positive hits (essential genes with log fold change below –1) for every possible false discovery rate. An NNMD was calculated for each screen by taking the difference between the average log fold changes for essential and non-essential genes and dividing by the standard deviation of the non-essential genes<sup><xref rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr">69</xref></sup>. Screens that had an NNMD greater than –1.25 or a correlation between replicates less than 0.19 were excluded from downstream analyses. Chronos scores were then calculated using the open-source code Chronos (v.2.0.8; <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/broadinstitute/chronos" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/broadinstitute/chronos</ext-link>) as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref></sup> for each type of guide library (Avana spCas9, KY spCas9 or Humagne CD enAsCas12a) independently. To mitigate batch effects between guide libraries, the mean Chronos score per gene in individual libraries was regularized towards the global mean across all libraries. On the DepMap portal, the file ‘ScreenGeneEffect’ contains Chronos gene effect estimates for each individual screen, with library effects corrected out whereas organoid-specific effects are preserved. Beginning with the 26Q1 release, a similar strategy will be used to preserve organoid-specific effects in ‘CRISPRGeneEffect’, which integrates all screens of the same model into a model-indexed table that can be used with portal tools.</p></sec><sec id="Sec21"><title>Comparison of gene expression profiles between spheroid and adherent cultures of the NextGen CNS models</title><p id="Par77">Nine NextGen CNS models were adapted to grow as adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates (coat culture) for 4 weeks or more. RNA samples were collected both before and after adaptation and profiled by RNA-seq using a similar protocol as described above. For these 18 samples (nine models × two conditions (spheroid and coat)), a correlation matrix was calculated based on the expression of the top 10% highly variable genes (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1,919). Subsequently, hierarchical clustering of the correlation matrix was conducted using the hclust and heatmap.2 functions in R (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">4c</xref>). To compare the expression levels of individual genes between the nine samples of spheroid culture and the nine samples of coat culture, the difference in expression levels of all the genes measured in this analysis (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 19,193) were analysed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">4f</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="Sec22"><title>Comparison of gene dependency profiles between different growth formats of NextGen CNS models and organoids</title><p id="Par78">For the NextGen CNS tumour models and organoids, the gene dependency profiles were compared between the two different culture conditions used for each of these model groups. Specifically, for the NextGen CNS models, the dependency scores between spheroid culture (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 14) and coat culture (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 25) and for organoids, and the dependency scores between Matrigel dome culture (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 55) and coat culture (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 14) were compared for every gene assessed in the CRISPR screen of these models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 18,159) using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U</italic>-tests (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">4h</xref>). For the organoids in Matrigel dome cultures, only the models from lineages that have corresponding coat-cultured models (ampulla of Vater, colorectal, oesophagus–stomach, ovary, prostate and uterus) were included in this comparison.</p></sec><sec id="Sec23"><title>Classification of dependency profiles</title><p id="Par79">The classification of dependency profiles (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">5a</xref>) was conducted primarily based on a published strategy<sup><xref rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr">25</xref></sup> using the entire set of the NextGen (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 147) and organoid (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 108) models. First, we identified a negative control set of non-expressed genes per model as having a log<sub>2</sub>[TPM + 1] expression value of less than 0.2. We then inferred the probability that the score represents a true dependency by using an expectation–maximization step until convergence independently in each screen or model. The dependent distribution was derived from the list of essential genes, which was generated from the intersection of previously published lists of essential genes<sup><xref rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr">70</xref>,<xref rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr">71</xref></sup>. The null distribution was determined from non-expressed gene scores for the respective model if the expression data were available, or otherwise from the non-essential gene list inferred from a published study<sup><xref rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr">70</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par80">To identify pan-dependencies, we selected a gene rank threshold <italic toggle="yes">T</italic> based on the dependency rank of all the genes in their 90th percentile least depleted model. The distribution of this 90th percentile rank was bimodal, and <italic toggle="yes">T</italic> was defined as the rank that gives the minimum density between the two peaks. To identify high variance genes, we first selected an expression threshold by analysing the distribution of expression values across all NextGen (or organoid) models, which was bimodal, and selecting the value corresponding to the minimum density between the two modes. Genes with average expression less than this value were designated as lowly expressed. The variance threshold <italic toggle="yes">V</italic> was determined as the 99th percentile variance over lowly expressed genes. To identify strongly selective genes, we computed the product <italic toggle="yes">S</italic> of the skew and kurtosis of the distribution of gene dependencies over all NextGen (or organoid) models for each gene.</p><p id="Par81">Using the scores defined above, we classified the genes in the following order:<list list-type="order"><list-item><p id="Par82">Pan-dependency: ranked in the 90th percentile least depleting line above <italic toggle="yes">T.</italic></p></list-item><list-item><p id="Par83">Strongly selective dependency: <italic toggle="yes">S</italic> &lt; –0.86, has a probability of dependency &gt;0.5 in at least three models, and does not meet criterion (1).</p></list-item><list-item><p id="Par84">High variance dependency: the variance in the dependency score is above <italic toggle="yes">V</italic> and does not meet criteria (1) or (2).</p></list-item><list-item><p id="Par85">Weakly selective dependency: has a probability of dependency &gt;0.5 in at least one model and does not meet criteria (1)–(3).</p></list-item><list-item><p id="Par86">Non-dependency: probability of dependency &lt;0.5 for all models and does not meet criteria (1)–(4).</p></list-item></list></p></sec><sec id="Sec24"><title>Identification of biomarker-associated dependencies</title><p id="Par87">To identify dependencies with expression addiction, we scored the Pearson’s correlation coefficient (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic>) and the significance (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>) of correlation between the expression level (log<sub>2</sub>[TPM + 1]) and dependency (Chronos gene effect) of the same gene across all the NextGen models that were profiled by both RNA-seq and CRISPR screening (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 146) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2a</xref>). This process was conducted for all the genes that have expression data and were classified as strong dependency (strongly selective, high variance or pan-dependency) in the NextGen model CRISPR screen dataset (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3,786). The false discovery rate (or <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> value) was calculated using the Benjamin–Hochberg procedure for this and subsequent analyses unless otherwise indicated. The genes that met the criteria for significance (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &lt; −0.3 and <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.005) were identified as dependencies with expression addiction. For each of the strong dependency genes identified from the NextGen model data, the correlation between expression and dependencies was also computed across the profiling results of the traditional cell lines that have lineage-matched NextGen models and gene expression data (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 572).</p><p id="Par88">Paralogue dependencies were identified by calculating the Pearson’s correlation coefficient and the significance of correlation between the dependency (Chronos gene effect) on a gene and the expression level (log<sub>2</sub>[TPM + 1]) of its paralogue partner (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2d</xref>). We conducted this process for all the strong dependency genes in the NextGen model CRISPR screen dataset (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3,800), comparing their dependency with the expression level of the respective paralogue partners listed on Ensembl genome browser 113 (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.ensembl.org/" ext-link-type="uri">https://www.ensembl.org/</ext-link>). Paralogue pairs were extracted via BioMart query for all human paralogues with valid HGNC symbols. Only gene pairs with at least 25% sequence identity between paralogues and with variance in expression &gt;1 over all the NextGen models were considered for analyses. The dependency gene–paralogue pairs that met the significance criteria (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &lt; –0.3 and <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.005) were identified as paralogue dependencies. Here again, we computed correlations for the same dependency–expression paralogue pairs in the traditional model profiling results (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 572).</p><p id="Par89">To find dependencies that are associated with oncogene GOF or TSG LOF, we first identified models with oncogene GOF as either harbouring a hotspot mutation or CN gain (log<sub>2</sub>[relative to ploidy + 1] &gt; 3) of the oncogene, and TSG LOF as either having a damaging mutation or CN loss (log<sub>2</sub>[relative to ploidy + 1] &lt; 0.25) of the TSG for all the oncogenes and TSGs listed in OncoKB<sup><xref rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr">1</xref></sup> (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.oncokb.org/" ext-link-type="uri">https://www.oncokb.org/</ext-link>). We selected 6 oncogenes and 13 TSGs that had at least 1 model of hotspot mutation and 5 or more models of relevant alteration among the NextGen models with CRISPR screen profiles (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 147). For each of these oncogenes and TSGs, we assessed whether any of the strong dependencies were significantly enriched in the NextGen models with the respective cancer gene alteration (‘altered’) compared with the rest of these models (‘unaltered’) using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests with a threshold of <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05 (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2f</xref>).</p><p id="Par90">To test whether the observed association between the cancer gene alteration and dependency was consistently beyond the effects caused by lineage bias of the cancer gene alteration, we also computed the differences in mean dependency between NextGen screens in each lineage and the remaining NextGen screens, only considering lineages that have at least five models screened. If the dependency difference observed across the two classes of models distinguished by the presence of a cancer gene alteration was outside the range of all dependency differences observed across all lineages, then we deemed the dependency–biomarker relationship to be driven by the cancer gene alteration. Otherwise, the dependency pattern was attributed to lineage effects. The mean dependency scores for the altered and unaltered groups, as well as the significance of these mean dependency scores, were similarly calculated for all these 6 oncogenes and 13 TSGs in the traditional models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 597).</p></sec><sec id="Sec25"><title>SCD inhibitor sensitivity assay in oesophageal adenocarcinoma organoids</title><p id="Par91">To examine whether the increased reliance on <italic toggle="yes">SCD</italic> of oesophageal adenocarcinoma organoids with <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> CN amplification, identified via CRISPR screens, can be reproduced with pharmacological SCD inhibition, we tested two chemical inhibitors of SCD: A939572 and CAY-10566. Specifically, we tested four oesophageal adenocarcinoma models, two with <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> CN amplification (CCLFUPGI0012T and CCLFUPGI0030T) and two with neutral <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> CN (CCLFUPGI0022T and HCMSANG0300C15). On day 0, for each of these four models, 10,000 cells per well were seeded into 120 wells of 96-well ULA plates (Revvity, 6055802) in a slurry culture with 100 μl of 5% Matrigel–OPAC per well. One of the following compounds was added to the culture at the same time as seeding using a D500e Digital Dispenser (Tecan Life Sciences): A939572, CAY-10566 and bortezomib. For each of these compounds, nine different doses with serial dilutions (2 nM to 10 μM, 2.9-fold dilution between the neighbouring doses) and DMSO control were tested in quadruplicate. On day 3, 50 μl fresh medium containing the corresponding concentration of the compounds was added to the culture.</p><p id="Par92">To measure viability of cells following compound treatment, 50 μl 3D CTG assay reagent was added to the culture and mixed by pipetting on day 7. This was followed by an incubation of the plates at room temperature (RT) for 30 min on a digital microplate shaker (Thermo Scientific, 88882006) at 300 rpm. Subsequently, luminescence emission was measured using a CLARIOstar Plus plate reader (BMG LABTECH).</p></sec><sec id="Sec26"><title>Scoring the activity of gene expression MPs</title><p id="Par93">We used a published method<sup><xref rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref></sup> to score the activity of 41 different gene expression MPs in each of the tumour samples and culture models. In brief, MP scores were calculated as the average relative expression of the MP gene set minus the average relative expression of a control gene set; that is,<disp-formula id="Equa"><alternatives><tex-math id="d33e3166"><?equation-image-name d33e3166.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 7b07668a09f456e1f30a1f2004516596?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/7b07668a09f4/d33e3166.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}
