To define the control gene set, all analysed genes were grouped into 25 bins on the basis of their mean expression levels. Subsequently, for every gene in the MP gene set, 100 genes were selected randomly from the same expression bin to constitute the control gene set.</p><p id="Par94">MP expression across different sample types (for example., traditional versus NextGen models, 2D models versus organoids, tumours versus traditional models, tumours versus NextGen models, GBM tumours versus GBM models with specific gene expression subtype, and between different subtypes of oesophagus–stomach tumours) (Figs. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3a</xref> and <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4a,b</xref> and Extended Data Figs. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6d</xref> and <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7d,e</xref>) were compared using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests.</p></sec><sec id="Sec27"><title>NextGen GBM model dependency analyses</title><p id="Par95">To analyse gene expression and associated dependencies in the NextGen GBM models, the transcriptional landscape of GBM models was visualized in a 2D UMAP using Celligner embedding (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3b</xref>). The cohort included 55 traditional and 70 NextGen GBM models, alongside 189 tumour samples from the TCGA-plus and Met500 GBM cohort. Two clusters were identified visually on the UMAP plot on the basis of distinct groupings of data points. Differential gene expression analysis was conducted to compare the transcriptional profiles of the clusters by computing log<sub>2</sub> fold changes to quantify expression differences and performing two-tailed Student’s <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-tests to assess significance for each gene. Significance was determined using adjusted <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> values (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> values), with thresholds applied at <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.001 and |log<sub>2</sub>[fold change]| &gt; 1 (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3c</xref>).</p><p id="Par96">Differential dependency analysis was performed between the glial GBM models (screen <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 36) and either mesenchymal GBM models (screen <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 60) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3d</xref>) or all the other non-glial NextGen models (organoids and non-glial NextGen CNS models; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 115) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6e</xref>). Common essential genes were excluded from the analysis. Significant dependencies (effect size &lt; –0.3, <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> &lt; 0.05 cutoff was also used for Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3d</xref>) were identified and visualized using a volcano plot.</p><p id="Par97">To identify a CN of a gene that can serve as a biomarker to predict <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency, the Pearson’s correlation between <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency and CN of genes (only those in the top 10% high variance of CN in the DepMap GBM models) was calculated and plotted across DepMap GBM models (with CRISPR and CN data; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 95; Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3f</xref>). The correlation between <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency and CN of genes was similarly calculated using only the DepMap GBM models that exhibited the glial pattern of gene expression (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 36; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6g</xref>). Associations with |<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> | &gt; 0.3 and <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05 were considered as significant. We also analysed the difference in <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency between mutant and non-mutant screens for all the hotspot or damaging mutations that have ≥5 mutant cases in the DepMap GBM models (5 mutations met this criterion; Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">6f</xref>) again using the data from the entire DepMap GBM model cohort. None of these mutations was significantly associated with <italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency (all <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &gt; 0.95 by a two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>test).</p></sec><sec id="Sec28"><title><italic toggle="yes">CDK6</italic> dependency validation in patient-derived short-term cultures</title><p id="Par98">We used seven patient-derived (NextGen) GBM models (BT286, BT179, BT145, BT320, BT444, BT224 and BT187) to evaluate their sensitivity to CDK4/6 inhibition. Patient-derived models were maintained at 37 °C and 5% CO<sub>2</sub>. Cells were plated at 500–2,000 cells per well in 60 µl medium in 384-well CellCarrier plates (Perkin Elmer, 6057302) and allowed to adhere for a minimum of 24 h. Cells were then treated with drugs in half-log dilution series with a D300 digital drug dispenser (Hewlett Packard). Palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib (MedChem Express, HY-50767, HY-15777, HY-16297A, respectively) were identity and purity verified by LC–MS and prepared as 10 mM stocks in DMSO. Palbociclib was diluted to 5 mM before dispensing owing to solubility limitations. At the time of drug addition, a time = 0 control plate was fixed. Following 96 h or 120 h in drug, treated plates were fixed.</p><p id="Par99">Plates (both time = 0 and treated plates) were stained, fixed, imaged and analysed according to the Dye Drop or Deep Dye Drop protocols<sup><xref rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr">43</xref></sup>. In brief, for Dye Drop, cells were stained with Hoechst 33342 (1:5,000, Thermo Fisher, 62249) and LIVE/DEAD far red fluorescent dye (LDR, 1:2,000, Thermo Fisher, <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-nucleotide" xlink:href="L10120">L10120</ext-link>), prepared in a 10% solution of OptiPrep (Sigma, D1556) in PBS to displace the growth medium, for 30 min at RT. Cells were then fixed with 4% formaldehyde, prepared in 20% OptiPrep (a denser solution to displace the stain solution and media column), for 30 min at RT. Fix, stain and medium were aspirated and 80 µl PBS was added per well. Plates were then sealed and stored at 4 °C until image acquisition. For Deep Dye Drop, cells were stained with LDR and pulsed with EdU (Lumiprobe, 30540) in a 10% solution of OptiPrep in PBS for 1 h before fixation with 4% formaldehyde, prepared in 20% OptiPrep for 30 min. Wells were aspirated and cells were then permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 (Sigma, T8787) in 10% OptiPrep for 20 min at RT, and EdU was then labelled with cy3-azide (Lumiprobe, C1030) by Click chemistry in 20% OptiPrep for 30 min at RT. Following aspiration, cells were blocked in Odyssey buffer (LI-COR Biosciences, 927-40150) for 1 h at RT, and then stained with anti-phospho histone H3 Alexa 488 (pH3, 1:2,000, Cell Signaling Technologies, 3465S) and Hoechst 33342 (1:5,000) overnight at 4 °C. Cells were washed once with PBST, twice with PBS and sealed for storage at 4 °C until image acquisition. All wash steps were performed with an EL406 washer equipped with a 96-channel head (Biotek).</p><p id="Par100">Images were acquired on an Operetta (Perkin Elmer) with a ×10 objective. Six fields of view were imaged per well. Nuclear segmentation was performed based on Hoechst intensity with Columbus (v.2.7.0, Perkin Elmer). A ring around the nucleus was drawn and the intensity of each marker was measured in the nuclear and ring masks. The intensity in the ring was subtracted from the nuclear intensity to correct for deviations in local background intensities. Cells were classified as live or dead on the basis of LDR signals, cells positive for EdU or pH3 were classified as S phase or M phase, respectively, and the integrated Hoechst intensity was used to measure DNA content and to assign cells doubly negative for EdU and pH3 to the G1 (DNA content = 2<italic toggle="yes">N</italic>) or G2 (DNA content = 4<italic toggle="yes">N</italic>) phases of the cell cycle. Cells negative for EdU with intermediate DNA content were assigned ‘S dropout’. All gating was performed with custom Python scripts that are publicly available (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/datarail/DrugResponse/wiki" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/datarail/DrugResponse/wiki</ext-link>). Live cell counts were used to calculate growth rate inhibition values<sup><xref rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr">72</xref></sup>.</p></sec><sec id="Sec29"><title>PDAC-classical/MUC program expression analyses</title><p id="Par101">To assess the relationship between PDAC-classical/MUC program expression and the classical score (based on a previously defined ‘classical’ gene set<sup><xref rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr">46</xref></sup>) of tumour samples, the classical score was determined using the same strategy as the calculation of the MP expression score described above (in the section ‘Scoring the activity of gene expression MPs’). The relationship between the purity of tumour samples and the level of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression was analysed by compiling the ABSOLUTE tumour purity score of the TCGA tumour samples of pancreas, oesophagus–stomach and colorectal lineages (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 149, 375 and 448, respectively) from previous studies<sup><xref rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr">59</xref>,<xref rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr">73</xref></sup>.</p><p id="Par102">The expression levels of the PDAC-classical/MUC program in various sample types (tumours, NextGen models and traditional cell lines) were also visualized by the colour of the points on the Celligner plots (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4c</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7c</xref>) to show the similarity of the overall gene expression profiles of the models and tumours displaying high expression levels of this program across different lineages (pancreas, oesophagus–stomach and colorectal).</p></sec><sec id="Sec30"><title>Dependencies associated with PDAC-classical/MUC program expression</title><p id="Par103">To identify genetic dependencies associated with the level of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression, the Pearson’s correlation coefficient and the significance of correlation (two-tailed) were calculated between the level of the PDAC-classical/MUC program and the dependency scores of strong dependency genes (strongly selective + high variance + pan-dependency; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3,521) identified from the organoid screen data using all the organoid models with gene expression and CRISPR screen data (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 108 (all organoids), <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 60 (organoids grown with R-spondin 1 and WNT3A); Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4d</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7i</xref>). The enrichment of the MSigDB gene set ‘GOBP WNT signalling pathway’ in the dependencies associated with PDAC-classical/MUC program expression was assessed by gene set enrichment analysis, which was conducted using the open-source code GSEApy (v.1.1.5; <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://pypi.org/project/gseapy/" ext-link-type="uri">https://pypi.org/project/gseapy/</ext-link>) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4d</xref>).</p><p id="Par104">The PDAC-classical/MUC program-associated dependencies on the selective components of the WNT signalling pathway, namely <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic> (plus <italic toggle="yes">LGR4</italic> for some analyses), were investigated further as follows. The dependency on these WNT pathway components were compared between the organoid models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 108) and the traditional cell lines that have lineage-matched organoid models (screen <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 485) using the density plots and two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests (Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4f</xref>). To test whether dependencies on these WNT pathway components observed in organoids (with high levels of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression) is driven by specific mutations, 14 hotspot mutations and 573 damaging mutations that have 2 or more mutant models in the cohort of CRISPR-screened organoids (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 108) were selected. For each of these 587 mutation types, dependencies on the 5 WNT pathway components listed above were compared between the mutant and non-mutant models (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">7k</xref>). For mutations and CN alterations that result in the activation of the WNT pathway, namely, <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> damaging mutation, <italic toggle="yes">CTNNB1</italic> hotspot mutation, <italic toggle="yes">CTNNB1</italic> CN amplification and <italic toggle="yes">RNF43</italic> damaging mutation, dependencies on <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic> were also compared between the organoids that have at least one of these alterations (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 30) and those that do not have any of them (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 78) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8a,b</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="Sec31"><title>Cancer gene dependencies in 3D organoids versus 2D models</title><p id="Par105">To compare dependencies on cancer genes (that is, oncogenes and TSGs) between the 2D models (screen results from traditional adherent models that have lineage-matched 3D organoids; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 433) and organoids (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 94), 90 cancer genes (40 oncogenes and 50 TSGs) with frequent (&gt;1%) mutation rates in the TCGA cohort were selected based on a previous publication<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup>. <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2B</italic> was not included as none of the organoids has a CRISPR screen result for this TSG. The dependencies on each of these cancer genes were compared between the 2D models and 3D organoids. The significance of the difference was assessed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests. For the cancer genes for which mutation (hotspot mutation for the oncogenes and damaging mutation for the TSGs) is annotated in DepMap, the same analysis was conducted after removing the mutant models to see whether the differing dependencies between the 2D models and 3D organoids is attributable to the differing rates of mutation between these two model types (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8d</xref>).</p><p id="Par106">To assess whether 2D models and 3D organoids exhibit difference in dependencies on a group of oncogenes or TSGs in the same signalling pathway, each of the 89 cancer genes frequently mutated in TCGA tumours were classified into one of the ten oncogenic signalling pathways based on the function of the protein they encode<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup>. For the groups of oncogenes and the groups of TSGs that belong to the same pathway (13 groups), mean dependency scores for the genes in the same group were calculated for each model. Subsequently, the mean dependency scores of the 2D models and 3D organoids were compared using two-tailed Mann–Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U-</italic>tests (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">8f</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="Sec32"><title>Differential dependency analysis between 3D organoids and 2D models</title><p id="Par107">To identify functional classes that are enriched for genes exhibiting differing degrees of dependency between 2D models (screen results from traditional adherent models that are lineage-matched with 3D organoids; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 433) and 3D organoids (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 94), we ranked all genes (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 16,691; excluding common essential genes) according to their mean difference in dependency score between organoid models and lineage-matched adherent models. The genes with the 100 most extreme differences in each direction were combined into one set. Gene sets from the Hallmark and KEGG legacy collections, which contain 101–249 member genes that were ranked in this analysis, were tested for enrichment among this set of 200 genes using a hypergeometric test (or one-sided Fisher’s exact test). The gene sets that achieved significance at <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05 were compared for similarity using the overlap coefficient:<disp-formula id="Equb"><alternatives><tex-math id="d33e3638"><?equation-image-name d33e3638.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 223941de395100a94a148d37e9e90b68?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/223941de3951/d33e3638.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

In brief, the lentiviral particles were generated by the co-transfecting the lentiviral plasmid with a packaging plasmid (psPAX2; 12260, Addgene) and VSV-G envelope (pMD2.G; Addgene, 12259) into 293FT cells using PEIpro transfection reagent (Polyplus, 101000033). The medium was replaced 12 h after transfection, and the virus-containing medium was collected after 36–48 h.</p></sec><sec id="Sec34"><title>Library preparation for minipool screens</title><p id="Par110">For the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a,b</xref>). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome, <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://adhesome.org/" ext-link-type="uri">https://adhesome.org/</ext-link>); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">9a</xref>. We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table <xref rid="MOESM5" ref-type="media">3</xref>). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public" ext-link-type="uri">https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public</ext-link>), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening.</p></sec><sec id="Sec35"><title>Minipool screening</title><p id="Par111">Before screening, models were tested for their growth in an alternative medium (1:1 OPAC organoid medium for 2D models and RPMI with 10% FBS for 3D organoids) and with alternative growth format (3D Matrigel dome growth for 2D models and 2D monolayer growth for 3D organoids) for at least two passages. Only the combination of medium type and growth format that enabled a comparable rate of growth with the original conditions (&lt;2-fold difference in the doubling times) and reasonably rapid growth (doubling time &lt;120 h), as well as the original conditions of growth format–culture medium pair, were used for the screening. Moreover, all the models selected for screening were subjected to titrations of library virus and puromycin to determine the dose of virus to achieve optimal infection rates and the concentration of puromycin to kill uninfected cells within 3 days, respectively.</p><p id="Par112">For the screen, selected models were infected with the amount of library virus required for infecting 30% of the cells in accordance with the result of virus titration on day 0. The infected cells were selected with the concentration of puromycin determined in the puromycin titration between day 1 and day 4. On day 4, cells were seeded into up to 4 conditions (2D monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS (RPMI–FBS); plastic culture with 1:1 OPAC; 3D Matrigel dome culture (dome culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS; and dome culture with 1:1 OPAC), depending on how many conditions survived the above-mentioned selection criteria for the respective model. For plastic culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 10 ml of the respective medium and seeded on a Falcon 100 mm TC-treated cell culture dish (Corning, 53003). For dome culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 0.5 m of the medium used for the condition and subsequently mixed with 1.5 ml of Matrigel. Approximately 40 domes, each with 50 µl of Matrigel–cell suspension were placed on a 100 mm TC-treated culture dish, which was followed by the incubation of the plate at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. Subsequently, 10 ml of the culture medium was added before further incubation. We prepared two technical replicates per each condition.</p><p id="Par113">These cultures were maintained until day 14 with refreshment of the medium every 3 days. If the culture showed signs of confluency (coverage of more than 80% of the bottom surface by the cells for monolayer culture on plastic plates and appearance of a dark spot in the middle of the domes for Matrigel dome culture), we passaged the cells instead of replacing the medium while keeping the number of cells after passaging to 2 million cells per dish. Trypsinization (with 0.25% trypsin and 0.1% EDTA (Corning, 25-053-CI)) was used for the passaging of cells in plastic cultures, whereas cells in dome cultures were passaged in accordance with the strategy described above in the section ‘Source and culture conditions of NextGen cancer models’. At day 14, cells were collected by trypsinization and counted. gDNA samples were prepared from these cells and the abundance of individual sgRNA sequences in the genome of these cells were analysed by PCR amplification of the sgRNA sequences, preparation of sequencing libraries from the PCR products and subsequent sequencing of these libraries as described in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening for gDNA isolation and sequencing’.</p></sec><sec id="Sec36"><title>Minipool screen analysis</title><p id="Par114">Minipool screens were evaluated for sequencing quality by having a total read count of at least 500,000 reads across replicates. Gene scores and NNMDs were computed in the same manner as the genome-wide screens. Replicate correlation was computed as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient over log fold changes in all non-control genes. Screens with NNMDs greater than –1.5 and replicate correlations less than 0.2 were excluded from downstream analyses. Screens with a single replicate were retained if their other metrics passed these quality control thresholds. Chronos scores were calculated as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref></sup>, with adjusted hyperparameters (smoothing regularization parameter = 0.3, kernel width = 5) for the smaller library size. Subsequently, we modelled the Chronos score <italic toggle="yes">Y</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">g</italic></sub><sub>,<italic toggle="yes">k</italic></sub> for each gene <italic toggle="yes">g</italic> and screen <italic toggle="yes">k</italic> with the generalized linear regression model:<disp-formula id="Equc"><alternatives><tex-math id="d33e3748"><?equation-image-name d33e3748.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 a65283094d0c7ac6276fb8b7ba402a4b?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/6170/13581591/a65283094d0c/d33e3748.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

The second and third terms capture the growth format effect and medium effect, where <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">d</italic></sub> and <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub> are indicator variables representing the types of growth format (Matrigel dome culture (dome) versus monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic)) and culture medium (serum-free OPAC medium versus serum-containing RPMI–FBS medium), respectively. The fourth term captures interaction effects between these two conditions, and the final term captures model effects to account for multiple screens in the same cell line. Differences in effect sizes across growth format and serum status were extracted as <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">d</italic></sub> and <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub>, respectively. Significance values corresponding to the same coefficients were extracted from the <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> values calculated using two-sided linear regression <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test.</p><p id="Par116">To assess the effects of growth format (or culture medium) on the core functional classes of gene targets included in our minipool library, we calculated the variance in <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">d</italic></sub> (or <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub>) across members of the same class and compared it to the variance in <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">d</italic></sub> (or <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub>) across all non-control genes outside of class. For each gene set, we tested whether the in-class variance was significantly greater than the out-of-class variance using one-tailed <italic toggle="yes">F</italic>-tests.</p></sec><sec id="Sec37"><title>Single-gene validation viability assay</title><p id="Par117">The viability effect (10 days after sgRNA transduction) of CRISPR-mediated knockout of <italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSMO1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SQLE</italic> (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5h</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10a</xref>) was assessed using CTG cell viability assays. Specifically, KP3 and HS766T pancreatic cancer cells, both of which were engineered to express enAsCas12a, were infected with several different types of sgRNA-expressing lentivirus on day 0, which included CRISPR cutting controls (sgCh2 and sgAAVS1), sgRNAs targeting common essential genes (sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11) and sgRNAs against the experimental genes (sgITGB1, sgITGAV, sgMSMO1 and sgSQLE). The infected cells were selected with 2 μg ml<sup>–1</sup> puromycin between day 1 and day 3. On day 3, cells were trypsinized, counted and reseeded without puromycin. For the 2D monolayer culture on a plastic plate (or plastic culture), cells were seeded at 2,000 cells per well in 100 µl RPMI medium with 10% FBS onto an opaque 96-well plate (Corning, 3903). For the 3D Matrigel dome culture (or dome culture), 10,000 cells were resuspended with 50 μl Matrigel and plated as a dome onto a 12-well plate, which was subsequently incubated (Corning, 356231) at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. The Matrigel dome was then covered with 1,200 μl per well of either the RPMI medium with 10% FBS or the 1:1 OPAC medium before further incubation. The medium was replaced every 3 days until day 10. Puromycin (2 μg ml<sup>–1</sup>) was added back to the culture at the first medium replacement.</p><p id="Par118">On day 10, the medium of the plastic-cultured cells was replaced with 100 μl per well of fresh RPMI with 10% FBS, and 40 μl per well of CTG assay reagent was subsequently added. Following incubation at RT for 30 min with constant shaking, luminescence emission was measured using a SpectraMax M5 Multi-Mode microplate reader (Molecular Devices, M5). For the dome-cultured cells, the medium was replaced with 350 μl per well of fresh RPMI with 10% FBS and 350 μl per well of 3D CTG assay reagent was subsequently added. Following incubation at RT for 30 min with constant shaking, the dissolution of Matrigel was confirmed by microscopy. Next, 150 μl of the lysate was transferred to an opaque 96-well plate to measure luminescence emission via a microplate reader. The luminescence signal from each of the experimental wells was normalized using a scale in which the average value of the cutting control wells (six wells; triplicate wells for each of sgCh2 and sgAAVS1) was scored as 0 and the average value for the common essential control wells (nine wells; triplicate wells for each of sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11) was scored as −1. The normalized viability score for each of the experimental wells was plotted. The relative viability scores before normalization were also plotted (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10a</xref>). The experiments were repeated twice. Each of these experiments was conducted with technical replicates (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3).</p></sec><sec id="Sec38"><title>Immunofluorescence and flow cytometry of single-gene validation</title><p id="Par119">For immunostaining of cells grown in either plastic culture or the dome culture conditions, cells were propagated on a Nunc 8-Well Lab-Tek chamber slide (Thermo Fisher, 177402). For plastic culture, the slide was first incubated with 100 μg ml<sup>–1</sup> collagen I (Corning, 354236) and 20 μg ml<sup>−1</sup> laminin (SouthernBiotech, 1415-01) for 60 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, 20,000 cells were seeded with 200 μl RPMI with 10% FBS per well. For dome culture, 30,000 cells were resuspended with 30 μl Matrigel and placed as a dome at the centre of a well of an 8-well chamber slide. After incubating at 37 °C for 30 min to solidify Matrigel, 200 μl RPMI with 10% FBS was added to the well before further incubation. Fixation and staining were performed essentially as previously described<sup><xref rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr">57</xref></sup>. In brief, after 3–5 days of culture, cells were washed twice with PBS before fixation. Plastic-cultured cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT. Dome-cultured cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde and 0.2% glutaraldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT, washed twice with PBS and incubated with 0.2% sodium borohydride for 30 min at 4 °C for the quenching of glutaraldehyde. For both plastic and dome cultures, this fixation procedure was followed by two washes with PBS and two rounds of incubations with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 10 min for the quenching of paraformaldehyde. After permeabilizing the cells with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 min on ice, the slides were incubated with IF buffer (0.1% BSA, 0.2% Triton-X, 0.05% Tween-20 and 0.05% NaN<sub>3</sub> in PBS + 10% normal goat serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 005-000-121)) for 1 h at RT for blocking. For dome culture, slides were additionally incubated with M.O.M. blocking reagent (Vector Laboratories, MKB-2213-1) for 1 h at RT to reduce endogenous mouse IgG staining of Matrigel. Subsequently, the slides were incubated with primary antibody diluted in IF buffer overnight at RT. After washing with TBS-T (0.05% Tween-20 in TBS) 3 times for 10 min each at RT, slides were incubated with secondary antibody diluted in IF buffer for 1 h at RT. This was followed by washing with PBS-T 4 times for 10 min each at RT and then the slides were incubated with PBS containing 1 μg ml<sup>–1</sup> 4′6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; MilliporeSigma, D9452) and Phalloidin-iFluor 647 conjugate (Cayman Chemical, 20555; 1:1,000 dilution) for 30 min at RT for nuclear counterstaining and enhancement of F-actin staining, respectively. For post-fixation, slides were incubated with 1% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 5 min at RT, washed with PBS and incubated with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 5 min. Finally, cover glasses (no. 1.5) were mounted on the slides with ProLong Gold Antifade mountant (Thermo Fisher, <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-protein" xlink:href="P36930">P36930</ext-link>). The following primary and secondary antibodies were used for the staining: anti-FAK (MilliporeSigma, 05-537 (4.47, mouse); 1:200 dilution); anti-FAK (MilliporeSigma, 06-543 (rabbit); 1:200); anti-integrin β1 (BD Pharmingen, 556048 (HUTS-21); 1:50); anti-integrin αV (MilliporeSigma, AB1930; 1:500); goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11001; 1:500); goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11008; 1:500); goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 568 (Thermo Fisher, A-11004; 1:500); and goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 568 (Thermo Fisher, A-11011; 1:500).</p><p id="Par120">Images were acquired using confocal microscopy, which was performed on a Zeiss LSM 710 laser scanning confocal system equipped with Axio Observer (Carl Zeiss). A ×63 objective lens was used for all imaging (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5i</xref> and Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10e</xref>). <italic toggle="yes">Z</italic>-stack images were acquired with a step size of 0.36 μm (for images acquired with ×25, ×40 and ×63 objectives). Images represent maximum intensity projections of five consecutive focal planes. Images were processed using Photoshop (Adobe) for contrast and brightness adjustment, which were applied equally to all the samples from the same experiment.</p><p id="Par121">To quantify colocalization between integrin chains (integrin β1 and integrin αV) and FAK in KP3 cells grown in either plastic or dome cultures, images of integrin staining and FAK staining from the same region were loaded onto Fiji (ImageJ v.1.54p). Subsequently, the regions of interest were manually defined by drawing boundaries around single cells and the intensity correlation quotient (Li’s ICQ)<sup><xref rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr">74</xref></sup> of the two stainings in the region of interest was calculated using the Coloc2 plugin (v.3.1.0) for Fiji. Approximately 20 single cells were analysed per sample (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10b</xref>).</p><p id="Par122">The cell surface expression levels of integrin β1 and integrin αV in cells grown in either plastic or dome conditions were analysed by flow cytometry. For this, KP3 cells were grown in either plastic or dome conditions in RPMI with 10% FBS for 5 days. For collection, cells were first washed with PBS twice. Plastic-cultured cells were subsequently detached from the plate by incubating with 5 mM EDTA–PBS for 10 min at 37 °C and collected. Dome-cultured cells were collected by scraping and centrifugation. The pellets containing cells and Matrigel were resuspended in 5 mM EDTA–PBS and incubated at RT for 30 min with continuous rotation to dissolve Matrigel. Subsequently, cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT, washed twice with PBS and incubated with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 10 min twice for the quenching of paraformaldehyde. The cells were then incubated with 10% normal goat serum–PBS for 1 h at RT for blocking. For primary antibody staining, 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells were incubated at RT for 1 h with one of the following antibodies, all diluted in 10% normal goat serum–PBS: anti-integrin β1 (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank (DSHB), AIIB2; 1:40 dilution); anti-integrin αV (DSHB, P3G8; 1:58); rat IgG1κ isotype control (Thermo Fisher, 14-4301-82; 1:1,000); or mouse IgG1κ isotype control (Thermo Fisher, 14-4714-82; 1:500). This was followed by three washes with PBS for 10 min each at RT with continuous rotation and secondary antibody staining, during which cells were incubated at RT for 1 h with one of the following antibodies, all diluted in 10% normal goat serum–PBS: goat anti-rat IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11006; 1:500); or goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11001; 1:500). The cells were then washed with PBS three times for 10 min each at RT with continuous rotation and analysed by flow cytometry, which was conducted on a CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) (Extended Data Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">10c,d</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="Sec39"><title>Statistical analysis</title><p id="Par123">Statistical analyses were conducted as follows. For Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2a</xref>, Pearson’s correlation between dependency and expression of the same gene across the NextGen models (gene <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3,786 (strong dependency), model <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 146) was calculated for testing the degree and significance of the expression addiction relationship. Genes that met <italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &lt; –0.3 and <italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.005 (two-tailed) were considered significant. Harboring Wnt-activating alterations did not have constant effects on Wnt regulator dependencies: it reduced the dependencies on <italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">LGR4</italic>, but enhanced <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic> dependency. <bold>b</bold>, Mutation-independent association between PDAC-classical/MUC program expression and dependencies on Wnt regulators. The correlation between PDAC-classical/MUC program expression and dependency on the five regulators of Wnt signaling (<italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">LGR4</italic>) as well as their mean dependency scores in the organoid models were plotted, where Wnt-activating genetic alterations were indicated by the color code shown in <bold>a</bold>. All the organoids with strong mean dependency scores on these Wnt regulators (mean Chronos score &lt; −1; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 21) exhibited enhanced PDAC-classical/MUC program expression (expression score &gt; 2.8) regardless of Wnt-activating genetic alterations. Regression lines with 95% confidence intervals are also displayed. <bold>c</bold>, Wnt dependency in the traditional cell lines and organoids. The mean dependency in the organoids (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 108; y-axis) and lineage-matched traditional models (screen <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 485; x-axis) were plotted for all the members of the MSigDB ‘GOBP_WNT_SIGNALING_PATHWAY’ gene set. For the seven members that exhibited significant correlation with the PDAC-classical MP expression (<italic toggle="yes">MESD</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WLS</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FZD5</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">LGR4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MARK2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SOX9</italic>; see Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4d</xref>), the NextGen organoids exhibited stronger dependency than lineage-matched traditional cell lines (mean[NextGen] &gt; mean[traditional]). However, this held true for less than a half of the remaining members of this gene set (198/438 [45.2%]). <bold>d</bold>,<bold>e</bold>, Differential dependencies on frequently mutated oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) between 2D models and 3D organoids. Dependency on frequently mutated (&gt;1% mutation rate in the TCGA cohort<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup>) oncogenes and TSGs (40 oncogenes and 50 TSGs) were compared between the 3D organoids grown in serum-free conditions (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 94) and lineage-matched 2D adherent models cultured directly on plastic plates with serum-containing media (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 433). In <bold>d</bold>, the mean dependency scores in 2D vs 3D models are represented in the x- and y-axes, respectively. Here and in <bold>f</bold>, the color of the points indicates the type of the cancer genes (red: oncogenes, blue: TSGs) and the point sizes indicate the significance of the difference. Only 22 oncogenes and 20 TSGs that exhibited statistically significant (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05) difference of dependency were shown here, while in <bold>c</bold>, the pathways displaying significant and non-significant (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> ≥ 0.05) differences are distinguished by filled and open circles, respectively. We also compared the dependency on each of these cancer genes after removing the mutant (hotspot mutation for oncogenes; damaging mutations for TSGs) models for the respective gene, but it remained significant for all the 42 genes shown here. In <bold>e</bold>, the distribution of dependency in individual models were plotted for two representative cancer genes (<italic toggle="yes">CDK4</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MDM2</italic>), where the lineage was indicated by the point color (see <bold>g</bold> for the legend). For <italic toggle="yes">MDM2</italic>, the dependency distribution in <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> WT models (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 22 [3D organoids], 97 [2D models]) were also plotted (right). Here and in <bold>g</bold>, the statistical significance was assessed by two-tailed Mann-Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U</italic> test. <bold>f</bold>,<bold>g</bold>, A pathway-level summary of the differential dependencies on frequently mutated oncogenes and TSGs. Oncogenes and TSGs analyzed in <bold>a</bold> were classified into the 10 oncogenic signaling pathways in accordance with a previous publication<sup><xref rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref></sup>. For each of these 10 pathways, mean dependency scores on the oncogenes or TSGs that belong to the respective pathway were calculated and these mean scores were compared between 3D (y-axis; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 94) and 2D (x-axis; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 433) models (<bold>f</bold>). The pathway:cancer gene type (oncogene or TSG) pairs with two or more genes were plotted. The mean dependency scores of the individual models were also plotted for the TSGs of the p53 pathway (<bold>g</bold>). <bold>h</bold>, Clustering of the gene sets that are enriched for differential dependencies between 2D models and 3D organoids. In the global comparison of gene dependencies, the nine gene sets with significant overrepresentation (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> &lt; 0.05 by one-sided Fisher’s exact test) of the 200 outlier genes (top 100 genes in either extreme) in the distribution of mean dependency differences (see Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a</xref>) were clustered by the degree of overlap in their component genes. Note that this analysis was conducted not only on the selected cancer genes but on all the genes measured in the screen except for the common essential genes (as opposed to <bold>d</bold>-<bold>g</bold>). The number of member genes within each of these gene sets is: 200 (HALLMARK_OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION), 200 (HALLMARK_MTORC1_SIGNALING), 200 (HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT), 139 (KEGG_SYSTEMIC_LUPUS_ERYTHEMATOSUS), 158 (HALLMARK_FATTY_ACID_METABOLISM), 200 (HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS), 199 (KEGG_FOCAL_ADHESION), 213 (KEGG_REGULATION_OF_ACTIN_CYTOSKELETON), and 158 (HALLMARK_UV_RESPONSE_UP). Two pairs of gene sets exhibited a high-degree of overlap (overlap coefficient &gt; 0.3) with each other and therefore we merged each of them into one gene set: • KEGG_FOCAL_ADHESION and KEGG_REGULATION_OF_ACTIN_CYTOSKELETON (merged and renamed as ‘Adhesion/Cytoskeleton’) • HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT and HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS (‘Cell Cycle’) The remaining five gene sets, HALLMARK_FATTY_ACID_METABOLISM (‘Lipid Metabolism’), HALLMARK_MTORC1_SIGNALING (‘mTORC1’), HALLMARK_OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION (‘OxPhos’), HALLMARK_UV_RESPONSE_UP (‘UV’), and KEGG_SYSTEMIC_LUPUS_ERYTHEMATOSUS (‘SLE’) were not merged with others. Also see Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a,b</xref>.</p><p>
cancer-dependency-rsi/data/papers/PMC13581591.xml:85:<fig id="Fig14" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Extended Data Fig. 9</label><caption><title>CRISPR minipool screens in different growth formats and medium types.</title><p><bold>a</bold>, Composition of test genes in the minipool library (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 250). The library for the minipool screen was designed primarily to evaluate the essentiality of genes that exhibit large differences in the systematic comparison of gene dependencies between 2D models and 3D organoids (see Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5a,b</xref>). These genes include those involved in the regulation of adhesion/cytoskeleton (further divided into “ECM Adhesion”, “Actin Regulation”, “Tight Junction”, “Adherens Junction” and “Integrin” classes) and the control of cholesterol homeostasis (as a part of the “Lipid Metabolism” class). They were categorized into nine core classes that are listed on the left based on the function of the encoded protein. Some of the test genes belong to multiple classes, while others do not belong to any of these classes but are still included in the library based on specific interests. The membership patterns of individual genes across the nine functional classes, along with the count of test genes exhibiting each specific pattern, are shown (top). The number of test genes that belong to each of the nine classes were also plotted (left). <bold>b</bold>, Quality control (QC) test of individual minipool screens. Seven models were subjected to screening with the minipool library under different combinations of growth formats (adherent culture on plastic dishes [plastic] and Matrigel dome culture [dome]) and culture media (RPMI/FBS and OPAC serum-free media). 18 screens passed the criteria for QC, which were total readcounts ≥ 5 ×106 and null-normalized mean difference (NNMD) ≤ −1.5. These QC metrics for individual screens as well as the log fold change (LFC) correlation of replicate samples (where replicate samples were available) are presented. <bold>c</bold>, Correlation between the genome-wide screen results and minipool screen results. The dependency scores from the genome-wide CRISPR screen (x-axis) and minipool screen (y-axis) were plotted for all the genes (nonessential [negative] controls, common essential [positive] controls and test genes) that were targeted by the minipool library for all the five models screened in minipool format under the same conditions as the genome-wide screens. This showed high concordance (<italic toggle="yes">r</italic> &gt; 0.59) between the genome-wide screen result and minipool screen result for all these pairs. <bold>d</bold>,<bold>e</bold>, Impact of the growth format and culture medium on the Chronos gene effect of representative genes measured by the minipool screen. All genes with significant differential dependency across conditions, in addition to <italic toggle="yes">CDK4</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">GPX4</italic>, are shown. In <bold>d</bold>, the Chronos gene effects under the Matrigel dome culture (dome) and adherent culture on a plastic plate (plastic) were plotted for pairs of matched screens (same model type, same culture medium; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 7). Results from cultures with the RPMI/FBS medium and OPAC medium are indicated by the blue and orange points, respectively. In <bold>e</bold>, the Chronos gene effects under cultures with the RPMI/FBS medium (serum-containing) and OPAC medium (serum-free) were plotted for pairs of matched screens (same model type, same growth format; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 5). Results from the dome culture and plastic culture are indicated by the blue and orange points, respectively. In both plots, the results from the same pair are indicated by the connecting line and the red horizontal line indicates the median gene effect score of the sample group. The statistical significance of the difference in the gene effects under dome vs plastic cultures as well as under RPMI/FBS vs OPAC media, assessed by a two-tailed paired <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test, are also indicated. Genes whose dependency was significantly (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> &lt; 0.05) affected by the growth formats (dome vs plastic) or culture media (RPMI/FBS vs OPAC) are indicated by the asterisks. The dependencies on three integrin subunits (<italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ITGA3</italic>) and <italic toggle="yes">NCKAP1</italic>, a regulator of cytoskeletal organization, were specifically influenced by the growth format but not by the culture medium. In contrast, the dependencies on three mediators of lipid metabolism (<italic toggle="yes">SPTLC1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SPTLC2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SQLE</italic>) and <italic toggle="yes">RICTOR</italic>, an oncogene in the PI3K/mTOR pathway, were affected by the culture medium but not by the growth format. The dependency on <italic toggle="yes">PTK2</italic>, a gene encoding FAK—a central mediator of adhesion-dependent signaling, was significantly altered by both growth format and culture medium. Here and in <bold>f</bold>, <bold>g</bold>, the centre line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges. <bold>f</bold>,<bold>g</bold>, The effects of growth formats and culture media on gene dependencies per gene class. Differential dependencies resulting from different growth formats (dome - plastic; <bold>f</bold>) and different culture media (OPAC - RPMI/FBS; <bold>g</bold>), both calculated as coordinates in a linear regression model (see <xref rid="Sec8" ref-type="sec">Methods</xref>), were plotted for each of the nine classes (see <bold>a</bold>) of minipool test genes. None of these gene classes exhibited significant enrichment or depletion of dependencies (relative to the rest of the test genes) upon changes in growth format or culture medium, except for the effect of culture medium on ‘Actin Regulation’ gene dependencies, which were enhanced with the RPMI/FBS medium as compared to the OPAC medium (<italic toggle="yes">q</italic> = 0.0224 by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U</italic> test; indicated by the asterisk). <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 75 (actin regulation), 30 (adherens junction), 53 (cell cycle), 89 (ECM adhesion), 22 (integrin), 20 (lipid metabolism), 20 (PI3K/mTOR signaling), 34 (tight junction) and 29 (WNT signaling).</p><p>
cancer-dependency-rsi/data/papers/PMC13581591.xml:89:<fig id="Fig15" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Extended Data Fig. 10</label><caption><title>Growth formats and culture media respectively influence dependencies on integrins and cholesterol biosynthesis mediators.</title><p><bold>a</bold>, Specific effects of growth format and culture medium on the dependencies on integrin and regulators of cholesterol homeostasis. The KP3-enAsCas12a and HS766T-enAsCas12a cells were infected with lentivirus expressing cutting control sgRNAs (sgCh2 and sgAAVS), sgRNAs against pan-dependency genes (sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11), or sgRNAs for indicated test genes. Following a puromycin selection to eliminate uninfected cells, these cells were propagated under different growth formats (monolayer culture on plastic dishes [plastic] vs Matrigel dome culture [dome]) and culture media (RPMI/FBS or OPAC medium) for seven days and viability scores relative to the average viability of cells transduced with cutting control sgRNAs were scored and plotted. Values = means ± SD (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3). The same experimental results were also presented in Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5h</xref>, where the average viability of cells transduced with cutting control sgRNAs was set as 0, the average viability of cells with knockout (KO) of pan-dependency genes was set as -1 and the viability scores of cells that received sgRNAs against the test genes were plotted on this scale. <italic toggle="yes">P</italic>-values were scored by two-tailed two-way ANOVA test (vs samples with cutting control sgRNAs [sgCh2 and sgAAVS]). <bold>b</bold>, Colocalization of FAK with different integrin chains between plastic and dome growth formats. The KP3 cells were grown under plastic or dome conditions with the RPMI/FBS medium for five days and immunostained for either integrin β<sub>1</sub> and FAK or integrin α<sub>v</sub> and FAK (see Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5i</xref>). Colocalization between integrin subunits and FAK was scored by calculating intensity correlation quotient, or Li’s ICQ<sup><xref rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr">74</xref></sup>, on background-subtracted images. Shown are the aggregated results of two independent experiments. <italic toggle="yes">P</italic>-values were scored by two-tailed Mann-Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U</italic> test. <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 20 (integrin β<sub>1</sub>/FAK staining, plastic), 19 (integrin β<sub>1</sub>/FAK staining, dome), 18 (integrin α<sub>V</sub>/FAK staining, plastic) and 21 (integrin α<sub>V</sub>/FAK staining, dome). <bold>c</bold>,<bold>d</bold>, Flow cytometry analysis of cell-surface integrin β<sub>1</sub>/α<sub>v</sub> expression under different growth formats. The KP3 cells, grown under plastic or dome conditions with the RPMI/FBS medium for 5 days, were stained for integrin β<sub>1</sub> and integrin α<sub>v</sub> without permeabilization and analyzed by flow cytometry to assess the cell-surface expression levels of these integrin chains. The gating strategy for flow cytometry analysis is shown in <bold>c</bold>. Thus, debris and dead cells were first excluded based on forward scatter-area (FSC-A) and side scatter-area (SSC-A) profiles. Subsequently, singlets were identified based on FSC-A and forward scatter-height (FSC-H) profiles. These singlets were then subjected to integrin expression analysis. The cell-surface expression level of integrin α<sub>v</sub>, but not that of integrin β<sub>1</sub>, was reduced to the negative control (isotype-matched IgG) level under the dome growth (<bold>d</bold>). <bold>e</bold>, Differing roles of integrin β<sub>1</sub> and integrin α<sub>v</sub> in controlling the localization of FAK under plastic vs dome culture conditions. KP3-enAsCas12a cells were infected with lentivirus expressing a cutting control sgRNA (sgCh2), or sgRNAs targeting <italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic>. These cells were propagated under plastic or dome conditions with the RPMI/FBS medium for 4 days and immunostained for FAK (red). The nuclei of these cells were also visualized by DAPI staining (blue). In the control (sgCh2) cells, FAK accumulated to the cell periphery under both two culture conditions (dot-or oval-like patterns in plastic culture and uniform membrane staining in dome culture). The knockout (KO) of <italic toggle="yes">ITGB1</italic> prevented this accumulation specifically in the dome but not in plastic culture. In contrast, the KO of <italic toggle="yes">ITGAV</italic> prevented FAK localization to cell periphery only in the plastic but not dome culture. Representative images from three independent experiments are displayed. Bar = 20 μm.</p><p>

We collected 314 NextGen models comprising 237 carcinoma organoids and 77 central nervous system (CNS) tumour spheroids 8 – 11  (Fig.  1a,b  and Extended Data Fig.  1a,b ) and generated WGS and RNA-seq profiles from 291 and 309 models, respectively. WGS confirmed expected recurrent genomic alterations, including the following changes:  TP53  and  APC  mutations and chromosome 18q loss in colorectal models;  TERT  promoter mutations in CNS models; and  TP53  and  KRAS  mutations and chromosome 9p loss in pancreas models (Fig.  1c  and Extended Data Fig.  1a,b ). NextGen models also captured mutations not represented in traditional models, such as  NRAS  in colorectal cancer (4.4% prevalence) 12  and  ESR1  in breast cancer (7% prevalence) 12 , and expanded prostate cancer representation with previously underrepresented alterations ( SPOP ,  RB1 ,  APC  and  CTNNB1 ; Fig.  1c,d  and Extended Data Fig.  1a,b ). To integrate data across models and libraries, we used Chronos 23 , which corrects for copy number (CN) effects, screen quality and library-specific batch effects (Fig.  1h,i ). Because all NextGen models used the Humagne library, library-specific batch effects were confounded with organoid model effects. We therefore pre-trained Chronos on all traditional and NextGen CNS models before applying the pretrained parameters to organoids. The integrated dataset—encompassing WGS, RNA-seq and CRISPR data and growth-format annotations—is available through the DepMap portal ( https://DepMap.org/portal ) 24 .

To broadly compare gene essentialities, we calculated the difference in mean dependency scores between 3D and 2D models for every gene ( n  = 16,691; excluding common essential genes), and identified gene sets (Hallmark and KEGG gene sets from MSigDB;  q  < 0.05) that were significantly overrepresented at the extremes of this difference (Fig.  5a,b ). Clustering these gene sets by component overlap (>0.3; Extended Data Fig.  8h ) merged two sets (adhesion and cytoskeleton (adhesion–cytoskeleton), and cell cycle), whereas five others (lipid metabolism, mTORC1, oxidative phosphorylation, UV response and systemic lupus erythematosus) remained separate. Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig.  5c , Extended Data Fig.  9a  and Supplementary Table  3 ). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig.  9b ).

After applying Chronos to the minipool screen data (which correlated well with genome-wide data,  r  > 0.59; Extended Data Fig.  9c ), we used linear regression to distinguish growth-format and culture-medium effects. This analysis identified seven genes for which dependencies were altered by growth formats ( q  < 0.05), including three integrin subunits ( ITGB1 ,  ITGAV  and  ITGA3 ) and two actin regulators ( NCKAP1  and  PTK2 ; Fig.  5d  and Extended Data Fig.  9d ). Eight genes also exhibited dependency changes across different media, three of which regulate lipid metabolism ( SPTLC1 ,  SPTLC2  and  SQLE ; Fig.  5e  and Extended Data Fig.  9e ).

A global analysis of the minipool screen results across the nine functional gene classes did not reveal collective enhancement or impairment of dependencies between different growth formats and media, except for a minor enhancement (Δdependency = 0.09) in the actin regulation class under RPMI–FBS conditions compared with OPAC (Extended Data Fig.  9f,g ). To capture opposing effects in gene classes (for example,  ITGB1  dependency increases whereas  ITGAV  decreases in dome culture), we analysed the variance in dependency score differences between conditions (dome versus plastic and OPAC versus RPMI–FBS). Growth format had significantly larger effects on integrin ( q  = 7.3 × 10 −5 ) and actin regulation genes ( q  = 7.2 × 10 −14 ), whereas culture medium significantly affected lipid metabolism genes ( q  = 1.5 × 10 −4 ; Fig.  5f,g ). These data demonstrate functional class-specific effects of growth format and medium.

Cas12a activity assessment was conducted as previously described 65  (a detailed protocol is available as ‘Cas9/Cas12a Activity Assay’ at the Broad Institute Genetic Perturbation Platform (GPP) web portal:  https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols ) using two different types of lentivirus, both of which express GFP, a sgRNA (or sgRNAs) against GFP and the puromycin-resistance gene. One type of these virus expresses two GFP-targeting sgRNA sequences optimized for enAsCas12a (pRDA_221; Addgene, 169142), whereas the other virus type expresses a GFP-targeting sgRNA sequence optimized for spCas9 (pXPR-047; Addgene, 107145), the latter of which served as a negative control. Cells were infected with these two different virus types separately as described above and selected with puromycin for 4 days. GFP expression was measured in the FITC channel by flow cytometry (CytoFLEX LX, Beckman Coulter) 14 days after pRDA_221/pXPR_047 infection with a Zombie Aqua viability stain (BioLegend, 423102) applied to gate out dead cells. Using the non-infection control (NIC) as a negative control, GFP positivity was determined for both the pRDA_221 and pXPR_047 infected cells. Cas activity was calculated using the following formula: (GFP (%) of pXPR_047 – GFP (%) of pRDA_221)/(GFP (%) of pXPR_047).

Cell lines with Cas activity above 70% were selected for screening. However, some lines were screened with activity as low as 44% if they showed sufficiently rapid growth of at least one population doubling per week.

For the screens, cells were first infected using the same protocol as for library titration, but only with the virus volume selected to give an infection rate of about 50%. The number of cells used for infection was determined such that sufficient number of cells survived puromycin selection to produce at least 500× representation of the library. Before July 2022, the screens were performed using either the C or D versions of the Humagne library (Addgene, 172650 and 172651) at full representation for each library. By contrast, screens after July 2022 were performed in two technical replicates at half representation using a combined C and D library to enable measurement of replicate correlation. After 18 h of incubation with virus in ULA plates, the virus was washed out, and infected cells were plated at 5 × 10 4  cells per dome. To test infection efficiency, we seeded four NIC domes and four infected domes in a 24-well plate (one dome per well). After 24 h, the medium was replaced with the selection medium containing puromycin for the infected plates and half of the domes (two NIC domes and two infected domes) for the infection efficiency assay. Puromycin was washed out and blasticidin treatment was resumed on day 6, when a 3D CTG viability measurement for the infection efficiency assay was conducted to estimate actual screen representation. Screens with less than 200× representation were excluded. The medium was replaced on days 13 and 20, and the samples were passaged on day 9 and optionally on day 17 depending on the confluence of the model, which was determined by visual inspection, each time maintaining minimum target representation. All the cells were collected and frozen as pellets on day 23.

CNS models were tested for the growth format and seeding density that resulted in optimal growth rates and for polybrene sensitivity, which was used at a concentration that resulted in >85% survival. For growth testing, cells were plated in both Matrigel-coated and ULA 6-well tissue culture plates. Specifically, cells were seeded in duplicate at densities of 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000 cells per well for both the Matrigel-coated plates and ULA plates. Cells were allowed to grow for 7 days, with a medium change performed at day 3 or 4 as needed. After 7 days, cells from all the conditions were counted and a doubling time was calculated for each condition. The condition that gave the lowest doubling time while maintaining high cell viability was used for the screen. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standardized concentration of 50 µg ml –1  and 3 µg ml –1 , respectively. For enAsCas12a transduction, 1.5 × 10 6  cells were exposed to lentivirus expressing enAsCas12ain a 24-well ULA plate in the presence of the optimized concentration of polybrene. At 18 h after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and the cells were plated in the optimal growth format at 2× the optimal seeding density. Subsequently, cells were selected with blasticidin. A CellTiter-Glo cell viability assay (CTG; Promega, G7572) was carried out 14 days after infection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to measure the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus.

Library titrations were performed in 12-well tissue-culture-treated plates, with each well containing 1.5 × 10 6  cells in 2 ml medium, 4 μg ml –1  polybrene and 0, 10, 25, 75, 200 or 500 μl virus. These 12-well plates were spun at 930 g , 37 °C for 2 h, after which an additional 2 ml medium was added to each well for a final volume of 4 ml per well. After 24 h of infection, the cells in each well of the 12-well infection plate were split into 2 wells of a 6-well plate with 0 and 2 μg ml –1  puromycin in fresh medium. An optimal seeding density was chosen such that the unselected population reached <70% confluence after selection. After 3 days of selection, infection efficiency for a given virus volume was determined as the ratio of live cells in the puromycin-containing well (2 μg ml –1 ) to the number of live cells in the puromycin non-containing well. A linear regression of the virus volume to the transduction efficiency was performed to estimate the volume of virus required to transduce 50% of the population.

All screens were initially evaluated for sequencing quality and selected to have a mean of at least 185 reads per gene. Naive gene effect scores were calculated by taking the log of the ratio of normalized reads for each gene in screened samples to that of normalized reads for each gene in the corresponding plasmid library. For screens using the two Humagne C and D libraries, the log fold change scores of libraries were averaged together. An ROC-AUC was calculated on the basis of per cent of true positive hits (essential genes with log fold change below –1) for every possible false discovery rate. An NNMD was calculated for each screen by taking the difference between the average log fold changes for essential and non-essential genes and dividing by the standard deviation of the non-essential genes 69 . Screens that had an NNMD greater than –1.25 or a correlation between replicates less than 0.19 were excluded from downstream analyses. Chronos scores were then calculated using the open-source code Chronos (v.2.0.8;  https://github.com/broadinstitute/chronos ) as previously described 23  for each type of guide library (Avana spCas9, KY spCas9 or Humagne CD enAsCas12a) independently. To mitigate batch effects between guide libraries, the mean Chronos score per gene in individual libraries was regularized towards the global mean across all libraries. On the DepMap portal, the file ‘ScreenGeneEffect’ contains Chronos gene effect estimates for each individual screen, with library effects corrected out whereas organoid-specific effects are preserved. Beginning with the 26Q1 release, a similar strategy will be used to preserve organoid-specific effects in ‘CRISPRGeneEffect’, which integrates all screens of the same model into a model-indexed table that can be used with portal tools.

To identify pan-dependencies, we selected a gene rank threshold  T  based on the dependency rank of all the genes in their 90th percentile least depleted model. The distribution of this 90th percentile rank was bimodal, and  T  was defined as the rank that gives the minimum density between the two peaks. To identify high variance genes, we first selected an expression threshold by analysing the distribution of expression values across all NextGen (or organoid) models, which was bimodal, and selecting the value corresponding to the minimum density between the two modes. Genes with average expression less than this value were designated as lowly expressed. The variance threshold  V  was determined as the 99th percentile variance over lowly expressed genes. To identify strongly selective genes, we computed the product  S  of the skew and kurtosis of the distribution of gene dependencies over all NextGen (or organoid) models for each gene.

To find dependencies that are associated with oncogene GOF or TSG LOF, we first identified models with oncogene GOF as either harbouring a hotspot mutation or CN gain (log 2 [relative to ploidy + 1] > 3) of the oncogene, and TSG LOF as either having a damaging mutation or CN loss (log 2 [relative to ploidy + 1] < 0.25) of the TSG for all the oncogenes and TSGs listed in OncoKB 1  ( https://www.oncokb.org/ ). We selected 6 oncogenes and 13 TSGs that had at least 1 model of hotspot mutation and 5 or more models of relevant alteration among the NextGen models with CRISPR screen profiles ( n  = 147). For each of these oncogenes and TSGs, we assessed whether any of the strong dependencies were significantly enriched in the NextGen models with the respective cancer gene alteration (‘altered’) compared with the rest of these models (‘unaltered’) using two-tailed Mann–Whitney  U- tests with a threshold of  q  < 0.05 (Fig.  2f ).

We used a published method 37  to score the activity of 41 different gene expression MPs in each of the tumour samples and culture models. In brief, MP scores were calculated as the average relative expression of the MP gene set minus the average relative expression of a control gene set; that is, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

To define the control gene set, all analysed genes were grouped into 25 bins on the basis of their mean expression levels. Subsequently, for every gene in the MP gene set, 100 genes were selected randomly from the same expression bin to constitute the control gene set.

The PDAC-classical/MUC program-associated dependencies on the selective components of the WNT signalling pathway, namely  TCF7L2 ,  WLS ,  FZD5  and  MESD  (plus  LGR4  for some analyses), were investigated further as follows. The dependency on these WNT pathway components were compared between the organoid models ( n  = 108) and the traditional cell lines that have lineage-matched organoid models (screen  n  = 485) using the density plots and two-tailed Mann–Whitney  U- tests (Fig.  4f ). To test whether dependencies on these WNT pathway components observed in organoids (with high levels of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression) is driven by specific mutations, 14 hotspot mutations and 573 damaging mutations that have 2 or more mutant models in the cohort of CRISPR-screened organoids ( n  = 108) were selected. For each of these 587 mutation types, dependencies on the 5 WNT pathway components listed above were compared between the mutant and non-mutant models (Extended Data Fig.  7k ). For mutations and CN alterations that result in the activation of the WNT pathway, namely,  APC  damaging mutation,  CTNNB1  hotspot mutation,  CTNNB1  CN amplification and  RNF43  damaging mutation, dependencies on  TCF7L2 ,  WLS ,  FZD5  and  MESD  were also compared between the organoids that have at least one of these alterations ( n  = 30) and those that do not have any of them ( n  = 78) (Extended Data Fig.  8a,b ).

To compare dependencies on cancer genes (that is, oncogenes and TSGs) between the 2D models (screen results from traditional adherent models that have lineage-matched 3D organoids;  n  = 433) and organoids ( n  = 94), 90 cancer genes (40 oncogenes and 50 TSGs) with frequent (>1%) mutation rates in the TCGA cohort were selected based on a previous publication 53 .  CDKN2B  was not included as none of the organoids has a CRISPR screen result for this TSG. The dependencies on each of these cancer genes were compared between the 2D models and 3D organoids. The significance of the difference was assessed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney  U- tests. For the cancer genes for which mutation (hotspot mutation for the oncogenes and damaging mutation for the TSGs) is annotated in DepMap, the same analysis was conducted after removing the mutant models to see whether the differing dependencies between the 2D models and 3D organoids is attributable to the differing rates of mutation between these two model types (Extended Data Fig.  8d ).

To identify functional classes that are enriched for genes exhibiting differing degrees of dependency between 2D models (screen results from traditional adherent models that are lineage-matched with 3D organoids;  n  = 433) and 3D organoids ( n  = 94), we ranked all genes ( n  = 16,691; excluding common essential genes) according to their mean difference in dependency score between organoid models and lineage-matched adherent models. The genes with the 100 most extreme differences in each direction were combined into one set. Gene sets from the Hallmark and KEGG legacy collections, which contain 101–249 member genes that were ranked in this analysis, were tested for enrichment among this set of 200 genes using a hypergeometric test (or one-sided Fisher’s exact test). The gene sets that achieved significance at  q  < 0.05 were compared for similarity using the overlap coefficient: \documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

For the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig.  5a,b ). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome,  https://adhesome.org/ ); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig.  9a . We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table  3 ). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool ( https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public ), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening.

Before screening, models were tested for their growth in an alternative medium (1:1 OPAC organoid medium for 2D models and RPMI with 10% FBS for 3D organoids) and with alternative growth format (3D Matrigel dome growth for 2D models and 2D monolayer growth for 3D organoids) for at least two passages. Only the combination of medium type and growth format that enabled a comparable rate of growth with the original conditions (<2-fold difference in the doubling times) and reasonably rapid growth (doubling time <120 h), as well as the original conditions of growth format–culture medium pair, were used for the screening. Moreover, all the models selected for screening were subjected to titrations of library virus and puromycin to determine the dose of virus to achieve optimal infection rates and the concentration of puromycin to kill uninfected cells within 3 days, respectively.

For the screen, selected models were infected with the amount of library virus required for infecting 30% of the cells in accordance with the result of virus titration on day 0. The infected cells were selected with the concentration of puromycin determined in the puromycin titration between day 1 and day 4. On day 4, cells were seeded into up to 4 conditions (2D monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS (RPMI–FBS); plastic culture with 1:1 OPAC; 3D Matrigel dome culture (dome culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS; and dome culture with 1:1 OPAC), depending on how many conditions survived the above-mentioned selection criteria for the respective model. For plastic culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 10 ml of the respective medium and seeded on a Falcon 100 mm TC-treated cell culture dish (Corning, 53003). For dome culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 0.5 m of the medium used for the condition and subsequently mixed with 1.5 ml of Matrigel. Approximately 40 domes, each with 50 µl of Matrigel–cell suspension were placed on a 100 mm TC-treated culture dish, which was followed by the incubation of the plate at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. Subsequently, 10 ml of the culture medium was added before further incubation. We prepared two technical replicates per each condition.

Minipool screens were evaluated for sequencing quality by having a total read count of at least 500,000 reads across replicates. Gene scores and NNMDs were computed in the same manner as the genome-wide screens. Replicate correlation was computed as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient over log fold changes in all non-control genes. Screens with NNMDs greater than –1.5 and replicate correlations less than 0.2 were excluded from downstream analyses. Screens with a single replicate were retained if their other metrics passed these quality control thresholds. Chronos scores were calculated as previously described 23 , with adjusted hyperparameters (smoothing regularization parameter = 0.3, kernel width = 5) for the smaller library size. Subsequently, we modelled the Chronos score  Y g , k  for each gene  g  and screen  k  with the generalized linear regression model: \documentclass[12pt]{minimal}
