Integrin and actin regulation classes exhibited significant variance across growth formats.  g , By contrast, lipid metabolism class were affected by culture medium ( q  < 0.05, two-tailed  F -test; gene  n  = 200).  h , Differential effects on integrin and cholesterol homeostasis dependencies assessed by viability after test gene knockout. Values are the mean ± s.d. ( n  = 3).  P  values calculated using two-tailed two-way ANOVA. R–F, RPMI–FBS.  i , Colocalization of integrin chains (green) with FAK (red) in KP3 cells under plastic or dome growth conditions (both in RPMI–FBS). Nuclei (blue) and actin (white) are also shown. Representative images from three independent experiments are displayed. Scale bar, 20 μm.

Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig.  5c , Extended Data Fig.  9a  and Supplementary Table  3 ). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig.  9b ).

Differential dependency analysis was performed between the glial GBM models (screen  n  = 36) and either mesenchymal GBM models (screen  n  = 60) (Fig.  3d ) or all the other non-glial NextGen models (organoids and non-glial NextGen CNS models;  n  = 115) (Extended Data Fig.  6e ). Common essential genes were excluded from the analysis. Significant dependencies (effect size < –0.3,  q  < 0.05;  P  < 0.05 cutoff was also used for Fig.  3d ) were identified and visualized using a volcano plot.

To assess the effects of growth format (or culture medium) on the core functional classes of gene targets included in our minipool library, we calculated the variance in  β d  (or  β s ) across members of the same class and compared it to the variance in  β d  (or  β s ) across all non-control genes outside of class. For each gene set, we tested whether the in-class variance was significantly greater than the out-of-class variance using one-tailed  F -tests.

For Fig.  5a , the top 100 genes in either extreme of the distribution of mean dependency differences (3D organoids ( n  = 94) versus lineage-matched 2D models ( n  = 433)) were combined to form a set of 200 genes with differential dependencies. Gene sets from the Hallmark and KEGG legacy collections were tested for enrichment among this set of differential dependency genes using hypergeometric test (or one-sided Fisher’s exact test). The gene sets that achieved significance at  q  < 0.05 were considered as significantly overrepresented in differential dependency genes. These gene sets were tested for the mutual overlap of their constituent genes. Gene sets exhibiting high-degrees of overlap (overlap coefficient > 0.3) were merged with each other (Extended Data Fig.  8h ).

For Fig.  5g , the variances of dependency between different growth formats and different culture media were scored for all nine of the core functional classes of minipool target genes. The variances were compared between in-class genes and out-of-class genes (that is, rest of the 250 test genes in the minipool library) for each of the 9 core functional classes using one-tailed  F -tests. The functional class is considered to be significantly affected by the growth format or culture medium if the corresponding  q  value was less than 0.05. The numbers of genes in each of the 9 core functional classes are as follows: actin regulation,  n  = 75; adherens junction,  n  = 30; cell cycle,  n  = 53; ECM adhesion,  n  = 89; integrin,  n  = 22; lipid metabolism,  n  = 20; PI3K–mTOR signalling,  n  = 20; tight junction,  n  = 34; WNT signalling,  n  = 29.

For Extended Data Fig.  9d,e , for the seven pairs of minipool screens that were conducted with the same model, same medium but different growth format (dome versus plastic), the Chronos dependency scores of all the test genes in the minipool library ( n  = 250) were compared using two-tailed paired  t -tests (d). Similarly, for the five pairs of minipool screens that were conducted with the same model, same format but different culture medium (OPAC versus RPMI–FBS), the Chronos dependency scores of all the test genes in the minipool library were also compared using two-tailed paired  t -tests (e). All genes with significant differential dependencies in either of these comparisons as well as  CDK4  and  GPX4  are shown in the plots.

For Extended Data Fig.  9f,g , effects of growth formats (f) and culture media (g) on gene dependencies (calculated by a linear regression model (see the section ‘Minipool screen analysis’ of the  Methods )) were compared between in-class genes and out-of-class genes (that is, the rest of the 250 test genes in the minipool library) for each of the 9 core functional classes of the minipool library. Significance of the difference was assessed by two-tailed Mann–Whitney  U- test. The numbers of genes in each of the 9 core functional classes are as follows: actin regulation,  n  = 75; adherens junction,  n  = 30; cell cycle,  n  = 53; ECM adhesion,  n  = 89; integrin,  n  = 22; lipid metabolism,  n  = 20; PI3K–mTOR signalling,  n  = 20; tight junction,  n  = 34; and WNT signalling,  n  = 29.

Plasmids generated in this study and the mini-pool library (Supplementary Table  3 ) will be deposited into Addgene.

 Extended Data Fig. 9 CRISPR minipool screens in different growth formats and medium types. a , Composition of test genes in the minipool library ( n  = 250). The library for the minipool screen was designed primarily to evaluate the essentiality of genes that exhibit large differences in the systematic comparison of gene dependencies between 2D models and 3D organoids (see Fig.  5a,b ). These genes include those involved in the regulation of adhesion/cytoskeleton (further divided into “ECM Adhesion”, “Actin Regulation”, “Tight Junction”, “Adherens Junction” and “Integrin” classes) and the control of cholesterol homeostasis (as a part of the “Lipid Metabolism” class). They were categorized into nine core classes that are listed on the left based on the function of the encoded protein. Some of the test genes belong to multiple classes, while others do not belong to any of these classes but are still included in the library based on specific interests. The membership patterns of individual genes across the nine functional classes, along with the count of test genes exhibiting each specific pattern, are shown (top). The number of test genes that belong to each of the nine classes were also plotted (left).  b , Quality control (QC) test of individual minipool screens. Seven models were subjected to screening with the minipool library under different combinations of growth formats (adherent culture on plastic dishes [plastic] and Matrigel dome culture [dome]) and culture media (RPMI/FBS and OPAC serum-free media). 18 screens passed the criteria for QC, which were total readcounts ≥ 5 ×106 and null-normalized mean difference (NNMD) ≤ −1.5. These QC metrics for individual screens as well as the log fold change (LFC) correlation of replicate samples (where replicate samples were available) are presented.  c , Correlation between the genome-wide screen results and minipool screen results. The dependency scores from the genome-wide CRISPR screen (x-axis) and minipool screen (y-axis) were plotted for all the genes (nonessential [negative] controls, common essential [positive] controls and test genes) that were targeted by the minipool library for all the five models screened in minipool format under the same conditions as the genome-wide screens. This showed high concordance ( r  > 0.59) between the genome-wide screen result and minipool screen result for all these pairs.  d , e , Impact of the growth format and culture medium on the Chronos gene effect of representative genes measured by the minipool screen. All genes with significant differential dependency across conditions, in addition to  CDK4  and  GPX4 , are shown. In  d , the Chronos gene effects under the Matrigel dome culture (dome) and adherent culture on a plastic plate (plastic) were plotted for pairs of matched screens (same model type, same culture medium;  n  = 7). Results from cultures with the RPMI/FBS medium and OPAC medium are indicated by the blue and orange points, respectively. In  e , the Chronos gene effects under cultures with the RPMI/FBS medium (serum-containing) and OPAC medium (serum-free) were plotted for pairs of matched screens (same model type, same growth format;  n  = 5). Results from the dome culture and plastic culture are indicated by the blue and orange points, respectively. In both plots, the results from the same pair are indicated by the connecting line and the red horizontal line indicates the median gene effect score of the sample group. The statistical significance of the difference in the gene effects under dome vs plastic cultures as well as under RPMI/FBS vs OPAC media, assessed by a two-tailed paired  t -test, are also indicated. Genes whose dependency was significantly ( P  < 0.05) affected by the growth formats (dome vs plastic) or culture media (RPMI/FBS vs OPAC) are indicated by the asterisks. The dependencies on three integrin subunits ( ITGB1 ,  ITGAV  and  ITGA3 ) and  NCKAP1 , a regulator of cytoskeletal organization, were specifically influenced by the growth format but not by the culture medium. In contrast, the dependencies on three mediators of lipid metabolism ( SPTLC1 ,  SPTLC2  and  SQLE ) and  RICTOR , an oncogene in the PI3K/mTOR pathway, were affected by the culture medium but not by the growth format. The dependency on  PTK2 , a gene encoding FAK—a central mediator of adhesion-dependent signaling, was significantly altered by both growth format and culture medium. Here and in  f ,  g , the centre line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges.  f , g , The effects of growth formats and culture media on gene dependencies per gene class. Differential dependencies resulting from different growth formats (dome - plastic;  f ) and different culture media (OPAC - RPMI/FBS;  g ), both calculated as coordinates in a linear regression model (see  Methods ), were plotted for each of the nine classes (see  a ) of minipool test genes. None of these gene classes exhibited significant enrichment or depletion of dependencies (relative to the rest of the test genes) upon changes in growth format or culture medium, except for the effect of culture medium on ‘Actin Regulation’ gene dependencies, which were enhanced with the RPMI/FBS medium as compared to the OPAC medium ( q  = 0.0224 by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney  U  test; indicated by the asterisk).  n  = 75 (actin regulation), 30 (adherens junction), 53 (cell cycle), 89 (ECM adhesion), 22 (integrin), 20 (lipid metabolism), 20 (PI3K/mTOR signaling), 34 (tight junction) and 29 (WNT signaling).

After matching gene symbols to the table’s `SYMBOL (EntrezID)` labels, the 200-gene selection tail overlaps 26 of the 250 test genes, leaving 224 outside it. Excluding those 26 still does not remove selection of whole pathways, so independent confirmation must remain conditional on the fixed panel.

A panel-wide association is not automatically infeasible at six models. It can be estimated conditional on their measured contrasts; generalizing to new environmental models requires much wider uncertainty. A null estimate would support a useful bound only if that interval is sufficiently narrow.

Identifying genes cancer cells need to survive or grow may help researchers choose experimental targets. Direct testing is difficult and costly in organoids, which are small three-dimensional models grown from patient tumors. Using gene activity measurements from 852 conventional cancer models, we built predictive models for a preselected panel of 20 genes. Our primary evaluation asked whether the models could rank organoids by their dependence on each gene. Performance was weaker in organoids, but a small signal remained in 94 Broad organoids and in 148 Sanger organoids from 144 donors. Predictions for the Sanger organoids were fixed before the measured outcomes were accessed. A separate retrospective analysis examined whether the same predictions could rank the 20 genes within each organoid. This retrospective analysis showed modest improvement over tumor-lineage predictions for the full ranking, while improvement for the three strongest measured dependencies was observed only in Sanger. Pancreatic organoid results remained projections because direct measurements were unavailable. These findings provide limited evidence for ranking genes within the selected panel. They do not establish which experiments will succeed or which treatments will work in patients.

Transferability of transcriptome-based gene-dependency models from two-dimensional cancer models to organoids remains uncertain. Expression-only Elastic Net models for 20 preselected genes were selected using patient-grouped nested cross-validation in 681 models and evaluated in a locked 171-model holdout. Historical target selection used all 852 models, making holdout performance conditional internal confirmation rather than an unbiased generalization estimate. After refitting on all 852 models, frozen models underwent exploratory evaluation in 94 Broad organoids and blinded validation in 148 Sanger organoids from 144 donors. Predictions were sealed before Sanger outcome access. Primary target-wise Spearman correlations, ranking organoids per gene, averaged 0.4094, 0.1518, and 0.1015 in holdout, Broad, and Sanger, respectively. Sanger association exceeded the within-lineage permutation null ( p  = 0.00040), but improvement over lineage-only prediction remained uncertain (difference, 0.0462; 95% confidence interval, −0.0065–0.0986).  CDK6 ,  MDM4 , and  CCNE1  passed false discovery rate correction in Sanger. Retrospective within-organoid gene ranking modestly improved over lineage-only prediction in both cohorts; top-three overlap improved only in Sanger. Pancreatic results remained unvalidated projections. Findings support weak cross-domain rank transfer and limited within-organoid ranking within the selected panel, without establishing genome-wide transferability, causal explanations for attenuation, or prospective experimental or therapeutic utility.

Large-scale functional genomic studies now enable the systematic interrogation of genes required for fitness across cancer models with diverse molecular backgrounds. The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) links molecular profiles of cancer cell lines to functional-screening data, enabling the identification of common and context-specific dependencies [ 3 , 4 ]. Genome-scale loss-of-function screens using clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), collectively termed CRISPR–Cas9, have made systematic gene inactivation feasible in human cells [ 5 , 6 ]. High-resolution libraries have improved discrimination between core-essential genes and context-specific vulnerabilities [ 7 ], whereas copy-number-associated cutting toxicity has motivated correction methods such as CERES [ 8 ]. Large-scale ribonucleic acid (RNA) interference screens have provided complementary maps of dependency and synthetic lethality [ 9 ]. Although Broad and Sanger dependency datasets show broad concordance, gene-effect estimates can vary across screening libraries, experimental protocols, and computational processing [ 10 , 11 ]. Methods such as Chronos seek to improve dependency estimation by accounting for cell-population dynamics [ 12 ]. Nevertheless, genome-scale CRISPR screening remains costly, technically demanding, and sample-intensive, limiting its routine application across newly derived cancer models.

Despite these advances, the extent to which transcriptome-dependency relationships learned in 2D cancer cell lines transfer to independent 3D organoid cohorts remains unresolved. A rigorous assessment requires model selection to be completed without access to 3D outcomes, predictions to be locked before outcome evaluation, and performance to be tested across independently generated CRISPR datasets. Here, we developed target-specific, expression-based Elastic Net models for a fixed panel of 20 genes using 852 pan-cancer 2D models. Candidate molecular representations were compared using patient-grouped nested cross-validation. The selected model was evaluated once in a locked 2D holdout for internal confirmation conditional on historical target selection. Without outcome-guided retraining, the frozen model was then examined exploratorily in Broad organoids and subjected to blinded independent external validation in a non-overlapping Sanger organoid cohort. Target-level findings from the two 3D cohorts were integrated in a retrospective transportability synthesis, and the locked models were subsequently projected onto an independent pancreatic organoid RNA-seq cohort lacking measured CRISPR outcomes. The primary hypothesis concerned ranking organoids by measured dependency for each gene, not ranking genes within an individual organoid. We hypothesized that this between-organoid signal would remain detectable but attenuated in 3D systems. A separate retrospective analysis evaluated gene ranking within individual organoids using the same frozen predictions. This secondary analysis addressed a different prediction task and did not replace the original primary evaluation.

Study design, data sources, and evidence hierarchy. Target-specific Elastic Net models were developed from transcriptomic profiles and CRISPR Gene Effect values in 852 two-dimensional cancer models obtained from DepMap Public 26Q1 and the CCLE. Candidate representations were compared in 681 development models, and the selected expression-only representation was evaluated once on a locked 171-model internal holdout set; the final models were then refitted on all 852 models, keeping the targets, target-specific features, hyperparameters, and primary metric fixed. Historical target selection included the holdout models, so this evaluation provides internal confirmation conditional on the selected panel. Without retraining, these models were applied to 94 Broad NextGen organoids for exploratory evaluation and to 148 Sanger organoids representing 144 donors for blinded independent external validation. Sanger predictions were sealed using the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm before access to CRISPR outcomes. Broad and Sanger target-level results were subsequently combined in a retrospective transportability synthesis. The Tiriac pancreatic RNA-sequencing cohort comprised 55 samples and was used only for secondary projection because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable. The dashed border identifies this non-validation application cohort. The figure depicts the primary workflow; the model specification and prespecified primary metric remained unchanged. The separate retrospective within-organoid ranking analysis is described in  Section 2.10.1  and  Tables S17–S19  and was not a new blinded validation. Colored boxes distinguish the five labeled stages, and arrows indicate their order in the workflow. CCLE, Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia; CRISPR, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats; DepMap, Cancer Dependency Map; RNA, ribonucleic acid; SHA-256, 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm.

In the fourth layer, the Broad-94 and Sanger-148 target-level rank correlations were combined only after the two cohorts had been evaluated separately [ 38 , 39 ]. The retrospective transportability synthesis assessed directional concordance, pooled target-level associations, and between-cohort heterogeneity. It was not treated as a third external validation and did not alter any component of the frozen model. Because Broad/DepMap Chronos Gene Effect and Sanger corrected CRISPR log fold change (LFC) values are assay-specific scales, the synthesis focused on rank transfer rather than absolute numerical equivalence.

The fifth layer applied the same frozen models to 55 RNA-seq samples from the Tiriac pancreatic organoid cohort, accessed through the Genomic Data Commons (GDC) ORGANOID-PANCREATIC project [ 32 ]. The resource comprised 44 tumor samples from 38 independent tumor cases and 11 normal samples from 11 independent normal cases. Because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable, this layer was restricted to secondary transcriptomic projection and expression-domain diagnostics and was not used to estimate predictive accuracy or therapeutic sensitivity. Across all layers, no 3D observation contributed to 2D candidate selection, feature learning, hyperparameter tuning, or deployment coefficient estimation. After access to 3D data, no retraining, recalibration, target or feature reselection, hyperparameter retuning, or replacement of the prespecified primary metric was permitted. The secondary within-organoid endpoints were evaluated retrospectively and did not modify the frozen predictions or original primary results. Detailed cohort construction, preprocessing, modeling, and statistical procedures are provided in  Section 2.2 ,  Section 2.3 ,  Section 2.4 ,  Section 2.5 ,  Section 2.6 ,  Section 2.7 ,  Section 2.8 ,  Section 2.9  and  Section 2.10 , and the archived code, frozen models, locked predictions, and verification records are described in  Section 2.11 .

Predictions from the five outer-test folds were combined to generate out-of-fold (OOF) predictions for all 681 development models. The primary candidate score was the arithmetic mean of the 20 target-specific Spearman correlations, termed the macro target-wise Spearman correlation. We retained target-specific mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R 2 ), calibration intercept, and calibration slope as secondary diagnostics, which did not alter model selection. Stability of the target-specific feature sets across outer folds was summarized using pairwise Jaccard similarity.

Candidate selection used only the development OOF predictions. Uncertainty for each candidate was estimated from 2000 bootstrap resamples of PatientID clusters. The one-standard-error threshold was defined as the highest observed molecular-candidate OOF macro Spearman correlation minus the candidate’s bootstrap standard error. Among molecular candidates meeting this threshold, we selected the least complex representation according to the prespecified order: expression-only, expression + copy number, expression + mutation, and all omics + lineage. Lineage-only was a non-molecular reference and was excluded from this rule.

The locked holdout outcomes were evaluated once after the prediction lock. The primary endpoint was the macro target-wise Spearman correlation. We calculated target-specific Spearman correlation, MAE, RMSE, R 2 , calibration intercept, and calibration slope as secondary diagnostics. We estimated uncertainty in the macro Spearman correlation from 2000 bootstrap resamples of PatientID clusters; we retained all rows belonging to a sampled patient group together, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles defined the 95% confidence interval (CI). The holdout-minus-development difference distribution was obtained by subtracting the development OOF bootstrap value from the holdout bootstrap value within each iteration. No model, feature, hyperparameter, or metric was changed during evaluation. Because historical target-panel selection used all 852 models, this stage provided internal confirmation conditional on that selection. We did not interpret its performance as an unbiased generalization estimate. The patient-cluster bootstrap did not account for uncertainty or optimism arising from historical target selection.

To evaluate information beyond tumor lineage, the lineage-only ridge reference described in  Section 2.4  was refitted in the 681 development models and applied to the same 171 holdout models. The difference in macro Spearman correlation between the selected model and the lineage-only reference was estimated using common PatientID-cluster bootstrap resamples. When more than one model was associated with a patient, observed outcomes and predictions were additionally averaged at the PatientID level. With predictions fixed, complete 20-target outcome vectors were permuted among patient groups within each OncotreeLineage stratum for 2000 iterations. The one-sided empirical  p -value was calculated as (1 + the number of null statistics greater than or equal to the observed statistic)/2001. The patient-aggregated macro Spearman correlation was retained as a sensitivity estimate.

To preserve an auditable prediction-before-outcome sequence in the current run, the prediction matrix and the model, feature, and lock manifests were written and SHA-256 sealed before the observed 3D outcome matrix was extracted. After sealing, only the 20 fixed Gene Effect columns were aligned to the predictions by ModelID. No model component or prespecified primary endpoint was changed after access to the outcome; the retrospective within-organoid endpoints are reported separately in  Section 2.10.1 . Nevertheless, because Broad-94 had been used in prior methodological work, we did not classify the cohort as a previously unseen, blinded independent validation set; instead, we retained it for a retrospective exploratory assessment of 3D transportability.

The primary estimand was the macro target-wise Spearman correlation. We calculated target-specific Spearman correlation, MAE, RMSE, R 2 , calibration intercept, and calibration slope as secondary diagnostics and did not use them to reopen model selection. We estimated macro- and target-specific uncertainty from 5000 model-level bootstrap resamples performed with replacement within OncotreeLineage strata, preserving the observed lineage counts; 95% CIs were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The lineage-only ridge reference was applied to the same 94 organoids, and the expression-only-minus-lineage difference was estimated using paired bootstrap resamples. Target-specific partial Spearman correlations, adjusted for lineage indicators; lineage subgroup estimates for groups containing at least 7 models; and leave-one-lineage-out analyses were retained as secondary sensitivity analyses.

For the panel-wide permutation test, predictions were held fixed, and each organoid’s complete 20-target outcome vector was permuted among model rows within the same OncotreeLineage stratum for 5000 iterations, thereby preserving cross-target dependence and lineage composition. The one-sided empirical  p -value was calculated as (1 + the number of null macro Spearman statistics greater than or equal to the observed statistic)/5001. Target-specific permutation  p -values were adjusted across the 20 targets using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. All Broad resampling procedures used random seed 20260829. As specified in  Table S5 , rank transportability was the primary endpoint. Absolute-scale error, calibration, and lineage sensitivity were secondary diagnostics. Broad results were not used to retrain the model or select targets based on effect direction or statistical significance.

The primary external-validation estimand was the target-specific Spearman correlation between the blinded predictions and Sanger LFC values, followed by the arithmetic mean of the 20 target correlations (macro target-wise Spearman correlation). This primary estimand evaluates the ordering of organoids for a fixed gene and does not assess the ordering of genes within an organoid. Rank correlation was selected because the Sanger-corrected LFC and DepMap/Broad Chronos Gene Effect values are on assay-specific scales and were not assumed to be numerically comparable. Uncertainty was estimated with 5000 donor-cluster bootstrap resamples, retaining all organoids from a sampled donor together; 95% CIs were obtained from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. For the null distribution, repeated organoids were first averaged within donor, predictions were held fixed, and each donor-level 20-target observed-outcome vector was permuted within tumor-type/lineage strata for 5000 iterations. The two-sided empirical  p -value was calculated as (1 + the number of absolute null macro correlations at least as large as the observed absolute macro correlation)/5001. Target-specific permutation  p -values were adjusted across the 20 targets using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure.

A lineage-only comparator, frozen before access to Sanger outcomes and based on patient-weighted 2D lineage means, was applied to the same cohort. We evaluated the expression-only-minus-lineage macro difference using paired donor-cluster bootstrap resamples, and we also calculated partial Spearman correlations adjusted for the primary tumor-type indicators. The influence of repeated donors was examined in two additional analyses: one retained the lexicographically first sample identifier per donor, and the other averaged predictions and outcomes within donor. An independent replay recomputed cohort size, donor count, overlap exclusions, feature coverage, target and prediction order, the complete 2960-pair grid, correlation statistics, bootstrap and permutation results, lineage adjustment, and file hashes; all 22 checks passed. As detailed in  Table S6 , no model, target, feature, hyperparameter, or prespecified primary metric was changed after outcome unlock. The retrospective within-organoid endpoints were evaluated separately using the unchanged predictions.

Directional concordance was defined as a positive Spearman correlation for the same target in both Broad-94 and Sanger-148. The number of common-positive targets was compared with a one-sided exact binomial distribution with  n  = 20 and a null success probability of 0.50. This comparison was interpreted only as a descriptive sign benchmark: dependence among targets limits the binomial interpretation, and the synthesis was defined after the cohort-specific results were known. Agreement in relative target performance was evaluated separately using the two-sided Spearman correlation between the vectors of 20 Broad and 20 Sanger target-specific correlations.

For target-level pooling, each cohort-specific Spearman correlation was transformed to the Fisher-z scale. We derived inverse-variance weights from the cohort-specific uncertainty intervals obtained from the lineage-stratified Broad bootstrap and the donor-clustered Sanger bootstrap. Because Broad donor structure was incompletely ascertained, its original uncertainty weights may overstate precision; the synthesis is conditional on this unresolved model-level independence assumption. A fixed-effects pooled estimate was calculated for each target and then transformed back to the Spearman correlation scale. The resulting two-sided meta-analytic  p -values were adjusted across the 20 targets using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure. Because only two 3D cohorts were available, random-effects estimates and the I 2  heterogeneity statistic were retained as descriptive sensitivity measures and were not used as confirmatory decision criteria.

The panel-wide combined 3D estimate was defined as the arithmetic mean of the 20 fixed-effect target correlations. Sensitivity to target-panel composition was assessed by resampling the 20 locked targets with replacement for 20,000 iterations, then recalculating the combined macro correlation at each iteration. We reported the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as a descriptive 95% interval; this interval characterizes sensitivity to the composition of the fixed target panel and is not a new-patient or new-organoid sampling interval. Attenuation from 2D to 3D was calculated for each target by subtracting the corresponding locked 2D holdout correlation from the Broad or Sanger correlation, with panel-level summaries obtained using the same target-bootstrap structure.

The 20-target median projection vector for Tiriac tumor cases was compared separately with the corresponding median prediction vectors for Broad-94 and Sanger-148. This comparison assessed whether the projected pancreatic target hierarchy was consistent across organoid applications. Concordance was quantified using two-sided Spearman correlations across the 20 targets. Because all compared values were predictions from the same locked model family and Tiriac lacked measured CRISPR outcomes, these correlations were interpreted as secondary evidence of target-ranking consistency rather than independent evidence of predictive accuracy.

Statistical analyses preserved the prespecified role and strongest available biological independence unit of each study layer. In the development, locked 2D holdout, Broad-94, and Sanger-148 analyses, the primary rank-based measure was the Spearman correlation between predicted and observed outcomes for each target and the arithmetic mean of the 20 target correlations (macro target-wise Spearman correlation). MAE, RMSE, R 2 , calibration intercept, and calibration slope were secondary diagnostics in the development, locked-holdout, and Broad analyses and did not reopen model selection. Because Sanger-corrected LFC and DepMap/Broad Chronos Gene Effect values were not treated as numerically equivalent, the Sanger validation and cross-cohort synthesis were based on rank correlation rather than absolute-scale error. Target-wise correlation operates across organoids for each gene; within-organoid correlation instead operates across the 20 genes for each organoid. Averaging target-wise correlations does not test within-organoid gene ranking. The original analysis hierarchy, inferential units, resampling procedures, and multiplicity rules are summarized in  Table S9 ; the retrospective within-organoid endpoints are defined in  Section 2.10.1  and  Tables S17–S19 .

For permutation analyses, predictions remained fixed and complete 20-target observed-outcome vectors were moved without disrupting the prespecified biological grouping. The locked 2D sensitivity analysis used 2000 one-sided permutations of patient-aggregated outcome vectors within OncotreeLineage strata. Broad-94 used 5000 one-sided permutations of ModelID-level outcome vectors within lineage. Sanger-148 used 5000 two-sided permutations after donor averaging, with donor-level outcome vectors moved within tumor-type/lineage strata and the absolute macro correlation used as the test statistic. Empirical  p -values used the standard plus-one numerator and denominator correction. Broad and Sanger target-specific permutation  p -values were adjusted separately within their 20-target families using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure.

In the retrospective cross-cohort synthesis, common-positive direction was assessed with a one-sided exact binomial benchmark ( n  = 20; null probability = 0.50), interpreted descriptively because targets were correlated and the synthesis was retrospective. Target-specific correlations were pooled on the Fisher-z scale using inverse-variance fixed-effect weights derived from cohort-specific bootstrap uncertainty, and the 20 two-sided meta-analytic  p -values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Random-effects estimates and I 2  were descriptive because only two cohorts were available. Target-panel sensitivity used 20,000 target-bootstrap resamples, while cross-target dependence was assessed using 50,000 one-sided simultaneous block permutations at the Broad ModelID and Sanger donor-mean levels. Expression-only-minus-lineage target differences were evaluated separately in Broad and Sanger using one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of these retrospective analyses was interpreted as a new validation cohort.

In the Tiriac layer, two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests compared patient-level tumor and normal projections for each target. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR adjustment was applied across 20 tests. Cliff’s delta described effect direction. Concordance between the Tiriac tumor target-median vector and the Broad and Sanger target-median prediction vectors was evaluated using two-sided Spearman correlations across 20 targets. We used PCA and SMD measures only as descriptive domain-shift diagnostics, and they did not inform the confirmatory decision.

The [review’s three critical failures](/Users/bmarti44/github/bufferright/research/reviews/g1_review_r1_verdict.md:1) require an operational endpoint, separation from selection outcomes, and an audited processing dependency graph.

1. **Preferred: format lability versus external prediction loss.** Retains the scientific connection between controlled environmental measurements and molecular transfer. A correlation between minipool effects and the downloaded Broad group-comparison table is useful development evidence. It cannot clear the independent-transfer gate.

**1. One primary estimand for the preferred route**

Choose **format**, based on its six model supports. The intervention bundle is **plastic culture versus Matrigel-dome culture, holding the recorded medium fixed**. It does not isolate geometry from matrix exposure.

For gene \(g\), define measured format lability:

\[
s_g=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{m=1}^{6}
       \frac{1}{|K_m|}\sum_{k\in K_m}
       \left|Y_{mgk,\mathrm{Dome}}-Y_{mgk,\mathrm{Plastic}}\right|.
\]

Here \(K_m\) contains the observed matched media. ACH-003040’s two medium-specific contrasts receive half its model weight each; every other model contributes one contrast. Each model therefore receives weight \(1/6\).

The target family is the **224 test genes outside the exact 200-gene selection tail**, subsequently restricted only by frozen identifier, assay-coverage and source-estimability rules. This is one selected family, with equal target weights.

For transfer:

- Train a molecular dependency predictor \(f_g\) using conventional models only.
- Reserve conventional reference donors \(R\) disjoint from training donors \(T\).
- Apply the **same fitted predictor** to \(R\) and donor-disjoint Sanger organoids \(C\).
- Evaluate within colorectal, oesophageal, gastric, ovarian and pancreatic groups, with equal prespecified group weights. Required source coverage must be demonstrated before locking these groups.
- Retain one sample/library per donor using an outcome-independent selection hierarchy.

For domain \(D\in\{R,C\}\), define target-specific donor-ordering accuracy:

\[
C_g^D=\frac15\sum_{\ell=1}^{5}
 P\!\left[
 (f_g(X_i)-f_g(X_j))(Y_{ig}-Y_{jg})>0
 \mid i,j\text{ distinct donors in group }\ell
 \right],
\]

with ties receiving half credit. Then define transfer loss:

\[
d_g=C_g^R-C_g^C.
\]

Positive values mean worse ordering in organoids. This compares ordering accuracy without subtracting Chronos from Sanger LFC.

The **single primary parameter** is the finite-panel linear-projection coefficient

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\beta=
\frac{a^\top M_Xd}{a^\top M_Xa},
\qquad a_g=s_g/\operatorname{IQR}(s).
}
\]

\(M_X\) removes the fixed baseline covariates: source dependency mean and SD, source ordering accuracy, signed and absolute Broad selection-table `MeanDifference`, and the library’s functional-class indicators. Use their fixed column space; overlapping classes do not justify adaptive variable selection.

**Interpretation:** additional loss of correct donor ordering per one-IQR increase in measured format lability, conditional on those baselines, this target family and these environmental supports.

The predictor comparison must include lineage-only, genotype-only, S3-style expression Elastic Net, and genotype-plus-expression models, using the same permitted observations. Select the predictor family and tune it entirely within \(T\), then freeze it before evaluating \(R\) and \(C\). Environmental scores enter the explanatory association, not external predictor selection.

This route still needs the individual-level source matrix. Published group means cannot supply \(C_g^R\).

**2. Selection circularity: exact exclusion plus conditional external evaluation**

The downloaded trace supports this reproducible rule:

1. In `organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tests_full.csv`, retain `DropEssential=False`.
2. Sort by signed `MeanDifference`.
3. Take the lowest 100 and highest 100 genes. **Do not substitute an FDR cutoff.**
4. Match the table’s `SYMBOL (EntrezID)` identifiers to library genes.
5. Exclude their intersection with `All test genes=True`.

That removes **26 of 250 test genes**, leaving **224** before other eligibility exclusions. The tail boundaries have no ties.

However, **224 does not mean selection-independent genes**. Whole functional classes were chosen using the same comparison. The [library documentation](/Users/bmarti44/github/bufferright/research/cancer-dependency-rsi/data/raw/broad_figshare/README.txt:1) and enrichment trace make that pathway-level selection explicit.

The remaining protection is therefore:

- Condition the claim on the entire historical panel-selection process and fixed family.
- Use the Broad comparison table only as development information and frozen baseline covariates.
- Obtain the evaluation outcome from Sanger donors excluded from all overlapping Broad environmental, selection, training and reference cohorts.
- Exclude uncertain donor matches from confirmatory eligibility.
- Establish that Sanger evaluation outcomes did not influence any source predictor, selection artifact or environmental-score processing artifact.

This can neutralize **reuse of the selection outcome as confirmation**. It cannot identify a genome-wide, selection-unconditional association. Adjusting for `MeanDifference` alone would not establish independence.

**3. Independent units and achievable precision**

Format supplies **seven contrasts across six models**, at most six independent environmental donors pending crosswalk completion. Medium supplies five contrasts across four models; restricting medium to dome gives four clean supports.

The 224 genes are correlated targets. They are not 224 environmental experiments.

There are two different inferential ambitions:

- **Conditional on the six measured environmental supports:** a panel-wide association is feasible in principle. External donors provide repeated evaluations of a fixed vector of measured lability scores. Cross-target dependence must be retained by resampling complete donor outcome vectors.
- **For latent biological sensitivity or new environmental models:** technical measurement error and environmental-model sampling matter. Neither is resolved by having many genes. With collapsed screen estimates and unaudited replicate uncertainty, the latent-sensitivity coefficient remains unidentified.

A rough precision check illustrates the limitation. If a model-cluster influence SD were \(s_u\), an approximate 95% half-width would be:

\[
t_{.975,5}s_u/\sqrt6\approx1.05s_u
\]

for format, versus \(1.59s_u\) for four-model medium. An influence SD of 0.10 already produces approximately ±0.105 for format, before other uncertainty. These are feasibility illustrations, not calibrated intervals for deliberately selected models.

For external ordering accuracy, under a simple independent-donor null, its SE is approximately \(1/(3\sqrt N)\): about 0.027 at 150 donors. A difference between two equally sized domains has SE around 0.038 per target under those assumptions. Donor pairs are dependent; their quadratic count does not provide quadratic precision.

A shared coefficient can be more precise than individual target losses, but that depends on the **actual joint covariance**, residual lability variation after conditioning, and environmental-score uncertainty.

**Verdict:** a conditional panel-wide parameter is plausible. “Only a bound” is not forced by \(n=6\), and a useful bound is not guaranteed. No actual precision claim is defensible before the eligible donor counts and joint uncertainty are established. A bound on *true biological sensitivity* additionally needs a defensible measurement-error model.

**4. Sanger’s permitted role**

Sanger can provide external evidence for the frozen association after establishing continuous-outcome identities, target coverage, donor crosswalks, library selection and processing provenance. Do not inherit S3’s cohort count as this study’s eligible count.

Its pipeline fits spline corrections using cross-sample LFC means and applies ComBat across libraries. Those operations use outcomes and can alter ranks. If fitted wholly within the external cohort, they do not automatically contaminate Broad training, but they couple external observations and require processing-aware uncertainty or a clearly conditional processed-cohort interpretation. If evaluation outcomes influenced development artifacts, the affected processing must be reconstructed or replaced. [Sanger processing code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Garnett-Lab/SangerOrganoidBiobank/main/scripts/CRISPR_pipeline.R).

The quarantined BAGEL matrix cannot supply this continuous ordering endpoint. Its 930-column schema also does not establish the intended organoid cohort.

Recover the 18 displayed cell identifiers from retained transcripts without reopening values. Map them to donors and targets. Conservatively exclude implicated external donors, record target exposure, and assess whether that exposure influenced family or endpoint choices. Unrecoverable exposure prevents an intact outcome-unseen claim; it does not automatically invalidate the entire resource.

Sanger cannot identify a causal culture contribution to transfer loss. Platform, library, population and processing differences remain alternative explanations.

**5. Falsification, inconclusive and invalid-result rules**

Propose **\(\delta=0.10\) ordering-accuracy loss per lability IQR**.

Its justification is experimental prioritization: ten additional incorrect orderings per 100 donor comparisons materially degrade a ranking tool; a drop from 0.60 accuracy to 0.50 removes its useful discrimination. This is a proposed decision-based margin, not an established clinical threshold. Its utility rationale must be accepted before evaluation and cannot be enlarged to match attainable precision.

Using one prespecified joint 95% interval \([L,U]\):

| Result | Decision |
|---|---|
| \(L>0.10\) | Support the practically meaningful positive association. |
| \(U<0.10\) | Falsify the claim of an association at least this large. |
| Entire interval lies inside \((-0.10,0.10)\) | Support practical equivalence for this conditional parameter. |
| \(U<-0.10\) | Support a practically meaningful association in the opposite direction. |
| \(L\le0.10\le U\) | Inconclusive about the primary meaningful-positive claim. |

A small positive estimate can therefore falsify the meaningful-positive claim. A nonsignificant estimate with a wide interval cannot.

Additional rules:

- Unresolved provenance, donor identity, score direction or joins: **invalid for confirmation**.
- No demonstrated above-chance source prediction: **no established source relationship whose transfer can be assessed**.
- Zero residual lability variation after baseline conditioning: parameter undefined.
- Material dependence on one environmental model or plausible measurement-error assumptions: no robust biological interpretation; report that limitation.
- One primary coefficient receives the confirmatory decision. Target-specific, pathway and medium analyses remain exploratory.

A bound here concerns the usefulness of the **measured lability score** for explaining this transfer endpoint. It does not bound the total causal contribution of culture conditions.

That distinguishes the estimand from S1’s environmental findings, S2’s dependency/biomarker maps and S3’s transfer evaluation. It remains a candidate novelty claim until the outstanding supplement/code audit checks this exact relationship.

**Recommend one fixed, panel-wide association using the six-model format contrast and independently evaluated molecular-prediction loss.** It is potentially G1-passable after resolving data access and preprocessing provenance. **Nothing currently establishes a G1 pass**, and an imprecise null would not rescue the gate.

The [review’s three critical failures](/Users/bmarti44/github/bufferright/research/reviews/g1_review_r1_verdict.md:1) require an operational endpoint, separation from selection outcomes, and an audited processing dependency graph.

1. **Preferred: format lability versus external prediction loss.** Retains the scientific connection between controlled environmental measurements and molecular transfer. Requires individual-level conventional-model data, Sanger continuous outcomes and molecular covariates, and the provenance audit described below.
2. **Matrix-saving alternative: transfer of a fixed 2D consensus target ordering.** Use `AdherentMean` as the frozen source ranking and evaluate its ordering errors across genes within Sanger organoids. This avoids fitting conventional-model predictors. It is a different question: consensus target prioritization, with no claim about loss of genotype/expression relationships or improvement beyond S3’s molecular baseline.
3. **Processing fallback: independent public measurements or pre-joint-correction processed outputs.** Retain the first route’s estimand but replace evidence whose processing crosses the development/evaluation boundary. This remains conditional on locating suitable public observations; “reprocess independently” is not a concrete solution when required inputs are unavailable.

A correlation between minipool effects and the downloaded Broad group-comparison table is useful development evidence. It cannot clear the independent-transfer gate.

**1. One primary estimand for the preferred route**

Choose **format**, based on its six model supports. The intervention bundle is **plastic culture versus Matrigel-dome culture, holding the recorded medium fixed**. It does not isolate geometry from matrix exposure.

For gene \(g\), define measured format lability:

\[
s_g=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{m=1}^{6}
       \frac{1}{|K_m|}\sum_{k\in K_m}
       \left|Y_{mgk,\mathrm{Dome}}-Y_{mgk,\mathrm{Plastic}}\right|.
\]

Here \(K_m\) contains the observed matched media. ACH-003040’s two medium-specific contrasts receive half its model weight each; every other model contributes one contrast. Each model therefore receives weight \(1/6\).

The target family is the **224 test genes outside the exact 200-gene selection tail**, subsequently restricted only by frozen identifier, assay-coverage and source-estimability rules. This is one selected family, with equal target weights.

For transfer:

- Train a molecular dependency predictor \(f_g\) using conventional models only.
- Reserve conventional reference donors \(R\) disjoint from training donors \(T\).
- Apply the **same fitted predictor** to \(R\) and donor-disjoint Sanger organoids \(C\).
- Evaluate within colorectal, oesophageal, gastric, ovarian and pancreatic groups, with equal prespecified group weights. Required source coverage must be demonstrated before locking these groups.
- Retain one sample/library per donor using an outcome-independent selection hierarchy.

For domain \(D\in\{R,C\}\), define target-specific donor-ordering accuracy:

\[
C_g^D=\frac15\sum_{\ell=1}^{5}
 P\!\left[
 (f_g(X_i)-f_g(X_j))(Y_{ig}-Y_{jg})>0
 \mid i,j\text{ distinct donors in group }\ell
 \right],
\]

with ties receiving half credit. Then define transfer loss:

\[
d_g=C_g^R-C_g^C.
\]

Positive values mean worse ordering in organoids. This compares ordering accuracy without subtracting Chronos from Sanger LFC.

The **single primary parameter** is the finite-panel linear-projection coefficient

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\beta=
\frac{a^\top M_Xd}{a^\top M_Xa},
\qquad a_g=s_g/\operatorname{IQR}(s).
}
\]

\(M_X\) removes the fixed baseline covariates: source dependency mean and SD, source ordering accuracy, signed and absolute Broad selection-table `MeanDifference`, and the library’s functional-class indicators. Use their fixed column space; overlapping classes do not justify adaptive variable selection.

**Interpretation:** additional loss of correct donor ordering per one-IQR increase in measured format lability, conditional on those baselines, this target family and these environmental supports.

The predictor comparison must include lineage-only, genotype-only, S3-style expression Elastic Net, and genotype-plus-expression models, using the same permitted observations. Select the predictor family and tune it entirely within \(T\), then freeze it before evaluating \(R\) and \(C\). Environmental scores enter the explanatory association, not external predictor selection.

This route still needs the individual-level source matrix. Published group means cannot supply \(C_g^R\).

**2. Selection circularity: exact exclusion plus conditional external evaluation**

The downloaded trace supports this reproducible rule:

1. In `organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tests_full.csv`, retain `DropEssential=False`.
2. Sort by signed `MeanDifference`.
3. Take the lowest 100 and highest 100 genes. **Do not substitute an FDR cutoff.**
4. Match the table’s `SYMBOL (EntrezID)` identifiers to library genes.
5. Exclude their intersection with `All test genes=True`.

That removes **26 of 250 test genes**, leaving **224** before other eligibility exclusions. The tail boundaries have no ties.

However, **224 does not mean selection-independent genes**. Whole functional classes were chosen using the same comparison. The [library documentation](/Users/bmarti44/github/bufferright/research/cancer-dependency-rsi/data/raw/broad_figshare/README.txt:1) and enrichment trace make that pathway-level selection explicit.

The remaining protection is therefore:

- Condition the claim on the entire historical panel-selection process and fixed family.
- Use the Broad comparison table only as development information and frozen baseline covariates.
- Obtain the evaluation outcome from Sanger donors excluded from all overlapping Broad environmental, selection, training and reference cohorts.
- Exclude uncertain donor matches from confirmatory eligibility.
- Establish that Sanger evaluation outcomes did not influence any source predictor, selection artifact or environmental-score processing artifact.

This can neutralize **reuse of the selection outcome as confirmation**. It cannot identify a genome-wide, selection-unconditional association. Adjusting for `MeanDifference` alone would not establish independence.

**3. Independent units and achievable precision**

Format supplies **seven contrasts across six models**, at most six independent environmental donors pending crosswalk completion. Medium supplies five contrasts across four models; restricting medium to dome gives four clean supports.

The 224 genes are correlated targets. They are not 224 environmental experiments.

There are two different inferential ambitions:

- **Conditional on the six measured environmental supports:** a panel-wide association is feasible in principle. External donors provide repeated evaluations of a fixed vector of measured lability scores. Cross-target dependence must be retained by resampling complete donor outcome vectors.
- **For latent biological sensitivity or new environmental models:** technical measurement error and environmental-model sampling matter. Neither is resolved by having many genes. With collapsed screen estimates and unaudited replicate uncertainty, the latent-sensitivity coefficient remains unidentified.

A rough precision check illustrates the limitation. If a model-cluster influence SD were \(s_u\), an approximate 95% half-width would be:

\[
t_{.975,5}s_u/\sqrt6\approx1.05s_u
\]

for format, versus \(1.59s_u\) for four-model medium. An influence SD of 0.10 already produces approximately ±0.105 for format, before other uncertainty. These are feasibility illustrations, not calibrated intervals for deliberately selected models.

For external ordering accuracy, under a simple independent-donor null, its SE is approximately \(1/(3\sqrt N)\): about 0.027 at 150 donors. A difference between two equally sized domains has SE around 0.038 per target under those assumptions. Donor pairs are dependent; their quadratic count does not provide quadratic precision.

A shared coefficient can be more precise than individual target losses, but that depends on the **actual joint covariance**, residual lability variation after conditioning, and environmental-score uncertainty.

**Verdict:** a conditional panel-wide parameter is plausible. “Only a bound” is not forced by \(n=6\), and a useful bound is not guaranteed. No actual precision claim is defensible before the eligible donor counts and joint uncertainty are established. A bound on *true biological sensitivity* additionally needs a defensible measurement-error model.
